News.title: Pub firm Greene King's record demand from wannabe landlords despite industry crisis
News.content:
Pub firm Greene King's record demand from wannabe landlords despite industry crisis

Pub firm Greene King says it has seen an average 26 applicants for every pub for let in the first six months of this year, which is said to be boosted by England’s thrilling run in the World Cup

View 4 Images Many people still dream of running a pub - despite all the challenges (Image: GETTY )

Pub giant Greene King has seen a record number of people wanting to become landlords - despite the crisis gripping the industry and large scale closures.

‌



During the first six months of 2026, it received 1,449 applications – a 26% increase compared with the same period in 2025.

‌



And each pub available to let in the first six months of the year generated 26 applications on average.

‌



The rush of wannabe-landlords and landladies comes in the face of a well publicised battle face by many ealier running pubs, wth 2,000 closures since 2020.

The summer heatwaves, combined with the England’s thrilling run in the World Cup, has delivered a much needed boost to the nation’s watering holes.

View 4 Images Greene King says it has seen record demand from prospective publicans (Image: jewhyte via Getty Images)

‌



Andy Burnham mulls Railcard changes in plan to cut high train ticket prices READ MORE :

However, industry chiefs say it does not make up for a host of other challenges, from soaring wage and energy costs to changing customer habits, and cheap supermarket competition.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has sought to help by promising to reduce business rates for pubs by 20% in a first step to further support the sector.

The Mirror has long championed the industry's cause with its Your Pub Needs You campaign. Greene King, which has around 2,500 pubs, restaurants and hotels, says nearly half of prospective publicans had not run a pub before.

‌



The majority of Greene King pubs available to let during the first half of the year were in Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Oxfordshire. However, data shows demand has been widespread across the country, with almost a quarter of applicants looking for opportunities to run pubs in London and the South East and a further 22% seeking pubs in the North West and Yorkshire. More than 10% expressed interested in Wales and the South West.

One in five said they wanted to run pubs exclusively in towns and city centres, while 14% were only interested in rural or coastal locations.

Charlie Brodie, 29, took over running the Royal George pub in Shildon, County Durnham, after three years delivering cars nationwide, and also previously worked as a teaching assistant for a short spell. However, he also has experience of working in pubs in the past.

‌



“I have been here for six months,” says Charlie, who completed a 12 week training programme with owner Proper Pubs. “It’s good to get to know all the customers when they come in.”

Dan Robinson, managing director of Greene King Pub Partners, said: “It’s incredibly encouraging to see record numbers of people wanting to run their own pubs in partnership with Greene King - demonstrating continued appeal and trust in this model. Running a pub is an incredibly rewarding opportunity, especially for those looking to build their own business.

View 4 Images Charlie Brodie has gone from delivering cars to running a pub

‌



“We’re fully committed to giving our partners the support, investment and expertise they need to succeed, so they can thrive in their local communities. Alongside additional support from the new Government, there is no better time to run a pub with Greene King.”

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, said: “It’s no surprise people want to run a pub, because who wouldn’t want to be at the heart of the community, pulling a delicious pint, and being part of a unique and brilliant British tradition.

“What’s important is that people can make a success of their pubs which is why we want the Prime Minister to build on his brilliant support for pubs by delivering permanently lower business rates bills, cutting beer duty and VAT, and reducing the regulatory burden our locals face.”

‌



View 4 Images Priyesh Bathia, a recent finalist from The Apprentice, says he always wanted to work in hospitality - and now runs a pub (Image: CREDIT LINE:BBC/Naked (A Freemantle Label)/Ray Burminston)

Priyesh Bathia, a finalist on the most recent series of TV hit shiow The Apprentice, has swapped Lord Sugar’s boardroom for the bar after opening a pub in south London in June.

Bathia, who worked in sales and marketing at accountancy giant PwC before entering the show, and two business partners have taken over running The Elephant & Barrel in Stockwell.

‌



“I went university, did a degree in maths and economics, and then the real thing of getting a corporate job, and that was it,” he says. “But I always had a passion to be in the hospitality industry.”

One reason for going on The Apprentice was to develop his business plan to transform a small mobile cocktail bar business he was running at the same time as being at PwC into a bigger business.

“Going on The Apprentice made me realise I didn’t want to go back into my corporate life.”

Article continues below

Bathia says the pub, which features a lifesize robotic elephant that squirts water, has been very busy since opening. Given his business idea, it also serves a range of cocktails.

“The hardest part is all the different moving parts that you need to manage, whether it be the kitchen to the beer, to the front of house,” he adds.

News.title: Train derailments show rail network 'unprepared for climate crisis'
News.content:
Train derailments show rail network 'unprepared for climate crisis'

EXCLUSIVE: Maryam Eslamdoust, General Secretary Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association, warned reducing investment would not help meet the issues caused by the 'climate crisis'

View 2 Images This week saw two derailments (Image: Jonathan Brady/PA Wire)

A transport union has called for urgent talks with Andy Burnham amid fears over rail safety and after two derailments in the heatwave.

‌



Maryam Eslamdoust, General Secretary Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association (TSSA), demanded more funding for staff, and warned reducing investment would not help meet the issues caused by the “climate crisis”.

‌



A Greater Anglia train derailed on Friday south of Wickford railway station in Essex, while an incident at Lewes on Thursday seriously injured two passengers.

‌



Investigations into the derailments are looking at all possible causes, but officials have said that hot weather presented the railway with a series of challenges.

View 2 Images Investigations into the derailments are looking at all possible causes for the derailments (Image: Lucy North/PA Wire)

In a letter to Mr Burnham seen by this newspaper, Ms Eslamdoust warned the 2025 Spending Review was a real terms cut in investment for Network Rail, who required more investment to handle the crisis.

‌



She said: “This summer has seen exceptionally high temperatures, placing additional stresses on railway infrastructure.

“Maintaining and adapting the network so that it can withstand increasingly frequent extreme weather will require sustained investment in infrastructure, maintenance and workforce skills, not less.

“The events at Lewes demonstrate once again that when something goes seriously wrong on our railway, passengers depend not only on the infrastructure and emergency services, but also on the railway workers who are there with them. Those workers must have the training, resources and support necessary to respond safely and effectively.”

‌



Concerns over the impact of the weather were also raised on Saturday by Martin Frobisher, group safety and engineering director at Network Rail, who there was “lots that we can do” to make the railway more resilient to climate change.

Mr Frobisher told BBC Radio 4’s Today: “We’re in the process now of putting together our case for our next five-year funding cycle and we’ll be making a very strong case for climate resilience.

“There’s more that we need to do in the future. We’re modelling that in a very technical way, so as to make the best possible case for funding in the future.”

Article continues below

It came as London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan warned the PM not to “slow down on net zero”. He said national governments around the world ”must choose action over apathy and commit to delivering Net Zero, reducing our reliance on oil and gas, and investing in the large-scale green projects we urgently need to cut emissions, adapt to extreme heat, and protect communities from flooding and wildfires”.

Downing Street has been approached for comment.

News.title: Granada earthquake - live: Tourists flee and homes wrecked as tremor hits Spain
News.content:
Residents fled their homes and tourists ran from hotels in panic in the city of Granada, Spain, after the powerful 5-magnitude earthquake struck

A powerful 5-magnitude earthquake has hit part of Spain popular with tourists, leaving a trail of destruction with panicking tourists running from their hotels.

The southern city of Granada, known for its stunning Alhambra Palace, was rocked by the tremor at around 1am local time. Homes and cars have been heavily damaged.

Antonio Sanz Cabello, vice-president of the Andalusian government, said in a post on X that authorities had declared an emergency.

"If you're in Granada, you've felt the earthquake, you're okay, and your home shows no damage, stay calm and avoid entering and exiting buildings unnecessarily," he said. "On the street, stay away from facades, cornices, balconies, walls, and other elements that could fall."

Today's earthquake follows another tremor in Granada in July which measured 3.7 on the Richter scale.

News.title: Michigan mass shooting leaves five dead as police issue 'avoid area' warning
News.content:
Michigan mass shooting leaves five dead as police issue 'avoid area' warning

Five people and a suspected gunman - named by police as 39-year-old Chad Hickman - have died after a series of shootings in the US state of Michigan today

View 2 Images Six people in total have been found dead in Michigan (Image: WPBN)

Five people and a suspected gunman have been killed after a series of shootings in Michigan.

‌



Police found three people dead at a home in Missaukee County, US, before officers then launched a manhunt for suspect Chad Hickman. They then found a fourth body at another address - before finding the gunman dead in a wooded area, along with another victim.

‌



Police spokesperson Lt Ashley Miller said: "This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved.

‌



"We are going to conduct a thorough investigation. And we want to make sure to keep our community members up to date on our current situation and what we're discovering throughout this process."

View 2 Images Shooting suspect Chad Hickman was found dead by police (Image: The Michigan State Police, Seventh District)

Earlier, Michigan State Police shared on social media that officers were investigating a shooting in the area that was reported just before noon local time. Authorities were hunting Hickman, 39, who they said should be considered "armed and dangerous."

‌



Officers later found the mna's vehicle near Whitlock Lake, where officers located his body along with a fifth deceased victim.

The force initially responded to a shooting at an address, where they discovered three people dead and one person wounded. The injuried person remains in hospital.

Investigators tracked the suspect's car, where but he and another victim were dead when they arrived. It is unclear what circumstances led up to the shooting.

‌



Court records indicate Hickman was in the process of a divorce.

He also had been previously sentenced to more than a year in prison after being charged with contributing to the delinquency of a child and child abuse in the fourth degree back in 2010.

State Representative Ken Borton offered his condolences to the victims.

Article continues below

He told the Detroit News: "Please join me in praying for our Northern Michigan community tonight after the unspeakable acts of violence we saw unfold today, especially send prayers for the six families who lost a loved one today and pray that an additional person, currently fighting for their life, will pull through and make a full recovery."

The names and ages of the people killed are not being released until their family have been notified, according to police.

News.title: Donald Trump dismisses fears for crew of US aircraft carrier with supplies and mental health issues
News.content:
Donald Trump dismisses fears for crew of US aircraft carrier with supplies and mental health issues

Thousands of US military members who have lived aboard USS Abraham Lincoln for more than 250 days are reportedly contending with major issues as leading lawmakers demand answers

View 3 Images USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea for 250 days (Image: Navy Office of Information/AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has downplayed fears over conditions on US aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln amid claims sailors tried to jump overboard during their extended deployment.

‌



His comments come after two American military news outlets reported suicide attempts and a shortages of basic supplies, safety concerns and mental health issues on the vessel. The warship has been at sea since November 2025 and has spent a record 250 days consecutively without making land.

‌



Worried families have registered their concerns about loved ones onboard with one of the outlets claiming the wife of one of the crew saying she received a message from her husband saying he "hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”.

‌



View 3 Images US President Donald Trump has responded to the claims (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump orders changes to aircraft carriers to use steam catapults to launch jets READ MORE :

USS Abraham Lincoln has been in the Middle East since January, supporting the war in Iran. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, reported the declining morale and thwarted attempts to jump overboard are just some of the issues as Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the aircraft carrier "will return home soon" in a social media post.

But as 5,000 sailors and marines endure a record-breaking time at sea, the US President played down reports of an intensifying crisis onboard.

‌



Mr Trump said the deployment is "not nearly long enough" when asked by reporters if it was excessive. He added: "That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it's being replaced with another very similar ship."

View 3 Images The warship's thousands of sailors have reportedly faced food shortages and difficult conditions (Image: Navy Office of Information/AFP via Getty Images)

When he was asked whether family members were worried about the situation on board, the president simply responded: “No, they’re not.”

‌



Mike Levin, a Democratic member of Congress from California, sounded the alarm over issues on X, describing the conditons as “moldy showers, broken toilets, laundry down for weeks, long stretches with no hot water, a meal that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas. No soap, deodorant, or toothpaste.”

America's defense secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed the suggestions as “more fake news”.

Mr Levin hit back at the response, writing: “These men and women signed up to serve their country. The least their country owes them is hot water, a working toilet and a real meal. Hegseth cannot even manage that, and he has the nerve to look their families in the eye and call them liars.”

‌



Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal also listed the reported hardships in a letter to Mr Hegseth.

"Shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months," the Democrat wrote.

The US Navy says it has "not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship", following the reports that sailors on the carrier are struggling with mental health.

Article continues below

Jason Crow, a Democratic Congress member who served in Afghanistan and Iraq, warned that the strain on service members and their families on the ship is “building week by week”.

Yesterday, Mr Trump has announced plans to declare the Strait of Hormuz a "territory of the United States."

Speaking at a rally in New York on Friday, Trump said: "After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”

News.title: 'Doting dad' died after 'exiting' from back of moving van during row with partner
News.content:
'Doting dad' died after 'exiting' from back of moving van during row with partner

David Rhodes fell from the back of the Peugeot Bipper van as it was heading along a road in Kirkham, Lancashire - now a coroner has returned a conclusion of misadventure

View Image David Rhodes died after falling from the back of a van (Image: Family photo)

A "doting" dad has tragically died after "exiting the rear doors" of a van during a row with his partner.

‌



David Rhodes, from Todmorden, fell from the back of the Peugeot Bipper van as it was travelling along Carr Lane in Kirkham, Lancashire, close to the junction with Dowbridge, at around 11pm on October 11 last year.

‌



The 40-year-old was taken to the Royal Preston Hospital where he died the following day and the cause of his death was recorded as a blunt force head injury, an inquest heard.

‌



After David's death his family paid tribute to the builder who had a "heart of pure gold" and they said that their lives "will be a much quieter and duller place without him".

Met Office issues grim drought warning as rain forecast to break heatwave grip on UK READ MORE :

Two found dead in plane crash after aircraft vanished on way to North Wales READ MORE :

The tribute read: “David was a doting dad to his beautiful seven-year-old-year old girl, a protective big brother and a much-loved son.

‌



“He was Todmorden’s best builder as he would always say! People who knew David would agree he was a ball of energy, a cheeky character with an infectious smile, and a heart of pure gold.

“All our lives will be a much quieter and duller place without him. We love you, forever and always. David tragically and suddenly lost his life on the 12th of October, in a road traffic accident in Carr Lane, Kirkham.

“Our hearts are breaking, we don't understand how this has happened, if anyone has any information or saw anything, no matter how insignificant it may seem, please contact the police.”

Article continues below

An inquest into David's death was held at Blackpool Town Hall on August 10 where Assistant Coroner Patrick Cassidy returned a conclusion of misadventure, reported LancashireLive. Misadventure is when a death occurs as an unintended consequence of an intended act.

The coroner concluded said: "On the 11th October 2025 on Carr Lane, Lancashire, Mr David Rhodes sustained a fatal head injury when he exited the the rear doors of a moving Peugeot Bipper Van whilst under the influence of significant alcohol and following a prolonged domestic argument with his partner who was the driver of the vehicle at the time of his exit.

"He was subsequently taken to the Royal Preston Hospital where he was pronounced deceased on the 12/10/25."

News.title: Fresh UK heat health alerts in place for 61 hours amid 'rise in deaths' warning
News.content:
Fresh UK heat health alerts in place for 61 hours amid 'rise in deaths' warning

A yellow heat health alert has been issued for the UK by the government and will now run until Tuesday for parts of the country as extreme temperatures continue

View Image Fresh yellow heat health alerts have been issued for parts of the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Fresh yellow heat health alerts have been issued for parts of the country as scorching temperatures continue.

‌



The UK has been sweltering under its fifth heatwave of the year with the country seeing its hottest day of the year of 38.1C at Kew Gardens in London on Thursday, while tinder dry vegetation has led to major wildfires.

‌



Now the government has issued a fresh yellow heat alert which running until 9am on Tuesday for the south east and south west of England and London.

‌



Met Office issues grim drought warning as rain forecast to break heatwave grip on UK READ MORE :

Two found dead in plane crash after aircraft vanished on way to North Wales READ MORE :

Temperatures are becoming more bearable this weekend and it has led to the end of the UKHSA's amber alerts for healthcare workers today which covered London, South East, South West, East Midlands, West Midlands and East of England.

The amber alerts meant that significant impacts were likely across health and social care services due to high temperatures. But new yellow alerts mean impacts are still likely across health and social care services, states the UKHSA.

These include increased use of healthcare services by vulnerable people, greater risk to life of vulnerable people, increased potential for indoor environments to become very warm and water-related incidents may increase, including risks from cold-water shock and drowning.

‌



With record dry conditions in July and a dry start to August, nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment.

Millions of people have been warned not to light anything that could spark a wildfire, including barbecues and garden incinerators, in “the most extensive use” of the UK’s mobile phone alert system.

The Government sent the emergency alert on Friday evening, which began appearing on mobile devices from 7pm.

‌



Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told members of the public to take the warning “seriously”, and said it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

Mr Burnham had earlier visited Stourbridge in the West Midlands, where a wildfire destroyed 19 homes on Thursday, the hottest day of the year so far.

The Stourbridge blaze spread across more than 500 acres, with the West Midlands Fire Service summoned to “hundreds and hundreds of incidents” throughout its patch, according to the area’s chief fire officer Simon Tuhill.

Article continues below

Friday is provisionally a record-breaking 10th day in 2026 where temperatures have exceeded 35C or more, according to the Met Office.

Frittenden, near Ashford in Kent, was among the hottest places, where temperatures reached 35.3C. In the West Midlands, Mr Burnham described Britain as “a tinderbox right now” with “37 fires smouldering around the country”.

News.title: Moment family run for their lives as doorcam captures home engulfed by wildfire
News.content:
Moment family run for their lives as doorcam captures home engulfed by wildfire

Footage shows the heartbreaking moment a young family’s home was destroyed by flames in Stourbridge as a quick-acting mum saved her children from the devastating fire

CCTV shows shocking moment wildfire destroys property

This is the heart-stopping moment a family were forced to run for their lives as their home was ripped apart by wildfire.

‌



Doorcam footage captures terrified Rose-Anne Vinten sprinting through the garden before just seconds later it catches on fire. She was in the living room and had her windows shut when nine-year-old daughter suddenly saw smoke.

‌



With dad Richard at work, they were forced to flee and the family, which included two young children Roman, 11, and Robyn, 9, have "lost everything" from their property in Stourbridge. They only moved into their new home five months ago.

‌



View 4 Images A young family's home is engulfed by an inferno (Image: ITV)

Met Office issues grim drought warning as rain forecast to break heatwave grip on UK READ MORE :

Around 30 homes were destoryed and dozens more damaged with scenes described as being like a war movie. A video shows terrified Mrs Vinten running from the flames as smoke fills the garden.

A friend helped the family find a hotel where they stayed whilst waiting to hear back from their insurance. The mum told ITV: "It was really scary. I knew at the same time I needed to be brave for my kids, because my daughter was really worried.

‌



View 4 Images Rose-Anne Vinten and husband Richard say they've lost everything (Image: ITV)

"When I went over to next door and saw them just standing there at the window, looking and they could see that their house was on fire, so I had to just hold it all in. I couldn't cry or anything."

Richard, who was out at the time, saw images of houses nearby on social media didn't know the extent of the damage until her returned.

‌



"It's heartbreaking, we'd only been there for five months. It's our forever home and it's gone," he said.

View 4 Images Smoke fills the garden of the property in Stourbridge (Image: ITV)

The dad told the Worcester News: "We knew the damage would be bad, but it was so surreal yesterday that the reality didn't really hit us. I was doomscrolling all night and when we saw a photo of our house, it was just devastating. It's been completely gutted. We've lost everything.

‌



"We only moved into the property five months ago and it was our forever home. There are sentimental things that we've lost, which is really sad, but we keep thinking it's only bricks and mortar. The important thing is that we are all safe. I'm so grateful to my wife for saving our children."

View 4 Images Dozens of homes have been destroyed in the town (Image: Getty Images)

The fire began in a popular children's park nearby before the flames quickly spread across grassland and tore through neighbouring homes. Six properties were devastated and around 50 residents had to be evacuated during the terrifying blaze.

Article continues below

Paramedics treated 54 patients, including 19 who were taken to hospital, as a result of wildfires across the West Midlands, the region's ambulance service said.

The prime minister, on a visit to Stourbridge, described the country as a “tinderbox right now”, adding that this weekend could be a really difficult one. A temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues has now been issued by the government.

News.title: Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
News.content:
Arday, 41, resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

A friend told the BBC Arday had described feeling "destroyed" and had told him his authorisation to travel to the US had been revoked.

Eamonn McCrystal, who became his friend at St Mary's University, Twickenham, tried to reassure him what he was going through would pass, but Arday replied "it does not feel like it will."

McCrystal told the BBC "He was the nicest person. So kind and such a gentle soul.

"We shared an office at university, when I set up the student radio station, and he used to speak on the station a lot"

"I'm in shock, I can't believe it."

The University of Cambridge vice-chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice led the tributes, saying the faculty was "desperately saddened" to learn of his death.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she added.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" and urged people to "remember there are real people with loved ones involved".

Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said Arday was subjected to unrelenting media scrutiny.

He said he had faced "an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse" and was the victim of "a pernicious public shaming".

"His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us," he posted on X.

Jo Grady, general secretary of the University and College Union said the "level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to has been sickening" and "must be investigated".

Lord Paul Boateng, who became the UK's first black cabinet minister in 2002, told BBC Newsnight he was "horrified, shocked and deeply saddened".

"Racism in academia is a fact of life and needs to be addressed," he added in a written statement.

In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to "a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism".

"The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target," he said.

Director of the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge, Prof Simon Baron-Cohen told the Today programme Arday had been "bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud".

"He was an incredibly, kind and gentle and caring man," he said.

He spoke to Arday the morning of his death, and said the academic had felt unable to leave the house.

"He has experienced what he described as a campaign against him, for the last three years," he previously told BBC News.

"What he was saying to me was 'they've destroyed my life' - it's not clear who they were but I think he was referring to the media.

"The personal attacks on him have been so immense."

News.title: Analysis: Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
News.content:
There was another reason this row had such a high profile. Jason Arday was a celebrity academic known as much for the remarkable life story he told, of an autistic child who didn't speak until 11, or learn to read and write until 18.

Other aspects of his personal narrative came under scrutiny, and he had to clarify that Â£5m raised for charity had been as part of a group effort, and that a 600 mile running challenge had taken twice as long as originally claimed.

Some who had signed a public letter of support quietly removed their names.

By the time he resigned his Cambridge position last week Jason Arday said the "relentless accusations" had taken a "profound toll" on him and his family. He suggested they had been racially motivated.

There are many unanswered questions which a coroner will no doubt be expected to consider about his circumstances and state of mind in the days before his death.

In the immediate aftermath of his death, his family said Jason Arday had been subjected to a "campaign of misinformation" that was too much for this "gentle man".

Others think that he attracted so much scrutiny because he was a black man in a prominent position.

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said Jason Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake up call for all of us."

There has been deep unease among some academics of colour who feel the ferocity of the debate was due to Jason Arday being a young black academic.

Professor of Black Studies Kehinde Andrews, a friend of Arday, told Newsnight in the wake of his death: "This is not just something that has happened in the past two weeks, we've seen the stories, this goes back three and a half years.

"The very day he got the position at Cambridge he had a Freedom of Information request asking about his credentials. He had all the right-wing people in America and the UK writing in to see if he was credible.

"Some people didn't believe a black man should be in that position at Cambridge.

"It's been a three-and-a-half-year toll which has come its head now."

What is certain is that Jason Arday had sought to defend his reputation, using a high-profile firm of lawyers to send letter to a journalist from Times Higher Education who first questioned his work.

The University of Cambridge initially robustly defended Jason Arday then announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure amid growing disquiet.

In 2023, as an elite university which had been criticised for a lack of diversity, Cambridge had been keen to make some high-profile non-white appointments. It had already made a huge effort to ensure admission of students was more diverse.

Whoever was appointed into such a high profile post would have faced scrutiny and Jason Arday had a slighter research track record than some others in the field.

Dr Jo Grady, General Secretary of the University and College Union, described Jason Arday's death as "devastating".

"There are so many questions that need to be answered. The level of harassment he suffered and the racism he was subjected to, has been sickening. It must be investigated."

For the University of Cambridge now there will be the difficult task of holding together an academic community divided and shocked by the controversy and now the death of Jason Arday.

It had announced an investigation into his appointment and tenure at the university and a review of how senior staff are chosen.

Now all of that has been overtaken by his sudden and shocking death.

News.title: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 women who say they were sexually abused by the late Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Scotland Yard confirmed to the BBC it copied in all those who had signed up to receive a monthly email update for victims instead of blind copying them.

The update revealed a further three suspects in their 70s and 80s had been interviewed under caution, bringing the total number interviewed to seven.

The force said it had referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). It is considering providing further support to the victims along with additional safeguards.

A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC a monthly update sent to victims on 11 August regarding Operation Cornpoppy had contained details of progress in the investigation.

Operation Cornpoppy is the Metropolitan Police investigation into people who may have facilitated or enabled sexual offending by Al Fayed.

The spokesperson said: "Due to human error, recipients' email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken.

"We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident.

"The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."

The force said the breach affected victims who had opted in to receive updates from the investigation team, but recipients had been split into smaller groups, meaning email addresses were only visible within those groups rather than across the entire cohort.

The BBC understands around 140 women have signed up to the updates.

The force has previously said 154 victims have reported allegations connected to Al Fayed and that supporting survivors remains at the heart of the investigation.

It said the incident had been formally recorded within the investigation records and they would continue to monitor the circumstances and impact of the breach, including reviewing alternative methods of updating victims that would reduce the risk of human error.

The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.

News.title: Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?
News.content:
But now, even this is being squeezed too. Recent rules say women have to ask men to take their products to market, and only men can sit at their stalls to show their wares at trade fairs. The Taliban gives various reasons for this, including claiming that women aren't wearing proper hijab or head covering.

"The world has to talk to the Taliban in a different way because it's just not working," says Najia. "The lives of Afghan women have to change because we're losing hope."

Five years after this ultra-conservative Islamist movement took charge, women are banned from much of the public sphere and girls are prohibited from going to school over the age of 12. Many inside and outside Afghanistan are asking the same pressing question: what's the best way to engage the Taliban to try to achieve meaningful change?

The issue is deeply divisive. There are fissures between many groups, with a huge array of conflicting issues at stake. These include women's rights, unpredictable Taliban edicts, international sanctions and aid cuts during a spiralling humanitarian crisis. The international response is split between Western countries often focused on human rights and others more interested in investment opportunities. And the West itself is divided on the best response.

Many now accept that whatever they're doing, it's not working.

News.title: Europe's scorched landscapes seen from space after summer heatwaves
News.content:
The impact of this summer's extreme temperatures on western Europe can now be seen from space after successive heatwaves since May.

Satellite images examined by BBC Verify show shrunken glaciers, scorched areas left by wildfires, green fields turned arid and lower river levels.

And some landmarks have been affected, too. The Palace of Versailles, south of the French capital Paris, appears as an island of trees surrounded by brown fields in these images.

News.title: When my dog died, my grief was overwhelming and complicated
News.content:
Gemma Champ, a writer from north London, rescued her cat Frankie as a kitten 17 years ago, when she lived in Abu Dhabi. Frankie died at home in January, and at first she felt "ridiculous for making such a fuss".

"I sent out a WhatsApp to all who'd known and loved him - and it turned out everyone had amazing memories of him. He wasn't just a cat. One friend said it was like 'a legendary beast from the great plains has left us.'

"We can see from social media that there's a whole community of people out there who have gone through the same experience and the same pain, so you don't feel like you're just being a drama queen - I think that's definitely how it would have been seen years ago."

After Greg James' dog died, the presenter said he wouldn't be on his show the next day. But getting employers to agree to this isn't always easy.

In 2019, Emma McNulty's 14-year-old terrier Millie died suddenly. Feeling sick with grief, McNulty, from Glasgow, said she was too upset to go into work. Unable to find someone to cover her shift, she said her part-time job in a sandwich shop was terminated. She then launched an online petition asking for employers to recognise pet bereavement.

No country mandates that employers offer paid time off after the death of a pet. Kara Stott, head of in-house legal and general counsel at law firm Peninsula, said more UK employers were starting to show flexibility with workers whose pets had died, even if a change to the law does not appear imminent.

But introducing formal pet bereavement policies has its challenges, Stott tells the BBC.

"Points to consider include how do you define a pet - does the policy just cover cats and dogs or would hamsters, rabbits, goldfish, horses, snakes, or other animals be included?"

Gemma, who is freelance, took a few days off work after Frankie's death, with the support of her "incredibly kind" client. "I doubt I could have done that if I'd been employed," she says, "and I think I'd have been weeping in the toilets at the office."

The reaction from friends and family to Frankie's passing confirmed that her sense of grief was real, she says, and she appreciated that people took it seriously.

"I do think, or hope, that people are learning not to dismiss this very profound and long-lasting relationship so easily."

News.title: Many Canadians are boycotting the US - here's where they're travelling instead
News.content:
Prior to US President Donald Trump's re-election, Kent Truscott and his family, from London, Ontario, had taken multiple trips south of the border, including to California and most recently New York in 2023.

But since late 2024, "my family and I have completely decided to boycott the United States", he told BBC.

That meant cancelling a trip last spring to Texas to watch the SpaceX Starship launch with his brother. The two had planned to fly down from Toronto, rent a car and stay a week to watch the launch, likely spending "thousands of dollars".

Truscott and his wife decided to spend that money in Canada instead â the Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, to be exact.

Their decision is a response to US tariffs and the president's comments about annexing their country. More than a year after Trump's return to the White House, many Canadians like Truscott are still holding firm on their boycott on travel to the US.

News.title: I wish I had been a more rebellious teenager, says Bella Ramsey
News.content:
Bella Ramsey spent many teenage years working with adults so never really went through the moody, rebellious phase often associated with being a teenager.

The British actor, who debuted in Game of Thrones aged 11 and uses they/them pronouns, says they had consciously decided not to behave like a stereotypical teenager after hearing criticisms from adults.

"I was like, I'm not going to be that."

So when Sunny Dancer, a film about a summer camp for young people affected by cancer, gave Ramsey seven weeks to experience teenage freedom, it was an opportunity to dive straight in.

"I got to be a teenager aged 21, which was brilliant," Ramsey tells BBC News. "It was really nice - and liberating."

Looking back, Ramsey says the experience made them wonder whether they had missed out by being quite so sensible the first time around.

"I kind of wish that I had made the most of being a teenager and getting away with things and being a bit rebellious."

In Sunny Dancer, Ramsey plays Ivy, a young female cancer survivor in remission who reluctantly heads to a "chemo camp" where she finds an unexpected group of friends and has a summer that changes her.

News.title: Fires prompt national alert as 19 homes destroyed
News.content:
Fires across England and Wales have prompted a national government alert warning people not to light anything that could spark a wildfire.

The warning on Friday evening came as it was revealed 19 homes were destroyed and a further 18 damaged in a huge fire in Stourbridge, West Midlands, that spread rapidly through grass and woodland on Thursday before damaging homes.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told members of the public to take the warning "seriously", adding it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

West Midlands Fire Service chief fire officer Simon Tuhill said the Stourbridge blaze was one of the most significant incidents the service had ever dealt with.

It was one of several fires being dealt with across England and Wales on Friday.

In Wales, a major incident was declared near Llandovery, Carmarthenshire, after dozens of homes were evacuated and roads closed

Overnight in to Saturday, four 14-year-olds from Porth, South Wales, have all been arrested on suspicion of arson and have since been bailed under investigation

In Hampshire, firefighters spent a sixth day tackling a wildfire in the New Forest, Hampshire, which broke out on Sunday.

Sixteen emergencies were tackled by Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service on Thursday afternoon, including a fire at Mousehold Heath, off Gurney Road in the city.

Elsewhere in the West Midlands fires caused extensive damage in Warstock and Kings Norton, Birmingham on Thursday. A 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of arson with intent to endanger life .

In Stoke-on-Trent on Thursday four homes in Sandyford were destroyed, with other properties damaged. Two people were arrested on suspicion of arson. Six firefighters were taken to hospital due to smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion.

In Willenhall, West Midlands, at least three homes and several gardens were destroyed in fires on Stonehouse Avenue and Harry Perks Street.

Investigators said they were working with other emergency services to establish how the Stourbridge fire started, with police saying they were keeping an open mind.

Some of the worst-affected areas have been cordoned off and many residents who were evacuated, including the Bishop of Dudley, the Right Reverend Martin Gorick, have not been able to return home.

News.title: Heathrow Airport roads reopen after mains burst
News.content:
All roads to Heathrow Airport have reopened after earlier disruption caused by flooding from a burst water main on a ring road.

The flooding along Inner Ring Road West prevented access by road to the central terminal area (CTA), which includes Terminals 2 and 3, a number of other buildings and the road network.

Heathrow Airport has confirmed the airport is now operating as normal and has apologised for the inconvenience after the road closures were made just before 06:00 BST.

Passengers are still being advised to use public transport where possible due to heavy congestion on the roads.

It is understood that there was no flooding within either terminal, and flights have not been disrupted.

The affected pipes are owned by Heathrow Airport which has been in charge of the repairs.

The disruption hit passengers amid the school summer holidays.

Heathrow said 19 July was its busiest day of the year so far as many schools broke up for summer, with 267,000 passengers passing through.

An airport spokesperson said: "Following earlier road flooding impacting access to Terminals 2 and 3, all roads have now reopened and the airport continues to operate as normal.

"We apologise for any inconvenience caused and we thank passengers for following the advisories we had put in place while our teams worked to resolve the situation as quickly as possible."

The airport was recently affected by disruption to railway services, after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel.

Additional reporting by PA Media.

News.title: Weekend to bring significant drop in temperatures as heatwave ends
News.content:
Temperatures are set to tumble this weekend as the fifth heatwave to scorch the UK this year comes to an end.

After Thursday marked the hottest day of 2026 so far, conditions will be noticeably cooler on Saturday and Sunday.

Temperatures will fall by 10-15 degrees Celsius by the end of the weekend, bringing them much closer to the seasonal average.

The change in weather pattern that is bringing this cooler air will also result in an increased chance of rain, including in areas currently in drought.

News.title: New Forest fire fully contained, fire service says
News.content:
A wildfire that broke out in the New Forest on Sunday is now "fully surrounded", says the fire service.

The blaze began when a van caught fire on the A31 last Sunday, with 23 drivers having to abandon their vehicles as the fire took hold.

The A31 will remain closed until at least Thursday 20 August, says National Highways.

In an update on Saturday, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said: "Overnight, firefighters continued working incredibly hard at the scene, and the fire is now fully surrounded. We will still be on scene for a number of days as we damp down and extinguish hotspots."

The fire service revealed on Friday evening that the blaze has affected an area of approximately 1.6 sq km (0.6 sq miles) and 169 fire appliances have attended from 93 fire stations.

In the update on Friday, assistant chief fire officer for HIWFRS Rob Cole said: "I'm pleased to say we are getting on top of this. However there are many days of work ahead of us to ensure that this fire doesn't spread when the wind blows or when other hotspots start to occur."

On Friday evening the UK's mobile phone alert system was used to warn people not to light anything which could spark a wildfire, including barbecues and garden incinerators.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told members of the public to take the warning "seriously" and said it was triggered at the request of firefighters.

News.title: Six people arrested after man abducted in Edinburgh
News.content:
Six people have been arrested in East Lothian after a man was abducted in Edinburgh.

Police Scotland said it received a report that a man had been abducted in the Canonmills area of the capital at about 22:30 on Thursday.

A 22-year-old man was later traced in Longniddry on Friday and taken to hospital as a precaution.

Five men - aged 21, 21, 22, 23 and 45 - and a 40-year-old woman have been arrested and police say inquiries are ongoing.

A section of the A198, which runs through the village of Longniddry, has been shut by police and a diversion is in place.

Officers believe this was a targeted incident and there is no risk to the wider public.

Det Insp Robbie Wallace said: "We understand an incident of this nature will be concerning but please be assured our inquiries are ongoing.

"Police will remain in the Longniddry area while this investigation continues and anyone with any concerns, or information, can approach these officers."

One report on social media said armed officers had been seen removing someone from a car.

Lothian Buses posted that some services were unable to serve the village and its routes had been diverted due to the road closure.

Longniddry is a coastal village about 15 miles (24km) from Canonmills.

News.title: Derailed Essex train leads to travel chaos
News.content:
Martin Frobisher, of Network Rail, said the summer's hot weather had "presented exceptional challenges to the railway".

In an interview with the BBC Transport Correspondent Katy Austin, Frobisher also confirmed speed restrictions were not in place in either Wickford or Lewes.

On the possible impact of the hot weather, he said "yes, that's one of the things that we're looking at.

"We've got our investigations underway. We've got technical engineers on site, our best experts who are on site with the Rail Accident Investigation Branch.

"They're looking very thoroughly at what's happened. And based on that, we will act on what we learn."

However, he added it was "too early to speculate on the full findings".

The investigation would specifically assess "whether or not this was weather-related", said Mark Francois, the Conservative MP for Rayleigh and Wickford.

The Department for Transport stressed Britain's railways were "among the safest in the world" as it reacted to the incident.

It said derailments were "incredibly rare" events.

An East of England Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "Our crews assessed 62 patients who were on board the train.

"Following assessment, all patients were discharged at the scene.

"We also assisted with the evacuation of a second train that was unable to continue its journey due to the derailment.

"There were no casualties among those on board."

A spokesperson for BTP also confirmed there were no reported injuries.

News.title: Bride dazzles in thrifty wedding with £2 charity shop dress
News.content:
A couple tied the knot in a thrifty-themed wedding with the bride dazzling in a Â£2 charity shop wedding dress.

Gina and Jacob Dodds, from Hoole in Chester, said "I do" in a ceremony held at the city's Storyhouse arts and cultural centre on Wednesday.

Both Gina's dress and engagement ring were bought from the Hope House Children's Hospice outlet while guests were also invited to wear outfits sourced from charity shops - raising money for a range of good causes.

"If we were going to have a wedding then we wanted it to be about more than just us - we wanted it to be about helping other people," she said.

News.title: Baby puffins make uninhabited island their new home
News.content:
Footage of a puffling - a baby puffin - bred on the Copeland Islands off the County Down coast has been captured for the first time.

The seabirds, synonymous with Rathlin Island off County Antrim, are not indigenous to the uninhabited Lighthouse Island, so no population existed there until an introduction scheme was launched around 2013.

There are now around 30 breeding pairs of puffins, which is being seen as a real success story.

They arrive to the island each April, and this year - in fact, just last month - trail cameras near their burrows in the ground filmed a young puffling out of its burrow, and an adult puffin bringing fish back to feed its young.

Attempts to attract puffins to Lighthouse Island included setting up fake "decoy" puffins, and a solar powered speaker system broadcasting its call.

News.title: Burnham says death of ex-Cambridge professor Jason Arday is a ‘tragedy’
News.content:
Former University of Cambridge professor Jason Arday has died after being found unresponsive at an address in Battersea.

The Metropolitan Police are treating his death as unexpected, though it is not believed to be suspicious.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the death as a “tragedy” and called for a moment of reflection on the circumstances leading up to it, adding: “A really sad, sad and sorry state of affairs and I think we all today think of Jason, his contribution, and his family and friends.”

Prof Arday recently resigned from his post following intense media scrutiny over plagiarism allegations.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI), email jo@samaritans.org , or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branchIf you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

The military-backed government in Myanmar announced on Saturday that it was willing to accept the return of around 300,000 Rohingya refugees currently housed in Bangladeshi camps, confirming they were former residents of western Rakhine state, once security conditions improved.

The statement from the foreign ministry comes as the Rohingya refugee crisis marks its ninth year.

A brutal military crackdown in 2017 forced nearly 700,000 Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, where they joined hundreds of thousands of fellow community members who had lived there for decades following earlier waves of violence carried out by Myanmar’s military and ethnic militias against the Muslim minority.

The overall scale, organisation and ferocity of the military campaign prompted the international community, including the UN, to issue widespread accusations of genocide and ethnic cleansing.

Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, doesn’t recognise the Rohingya as one of the country’s 135 official ethnic minorities. Instead, it labels them as Bengalis to imply that they are illegal migrants originating from Bangladesh.

Officials stated that Myanmar had processed a list of 828,824 refugees provided by Bangladesh as of the end of July. Of the 426,545 individuals verified, authorities established that 308,797 were former residents of Rakhine.

The foreign ministry noted that 113,507 individuals could not be successfully verified, while 4,241 had taken part in what it described as terrorist activities.

Rohingya refugees wait outside a distribution centre after collecting relief materials at the Kutupalong camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, on 20 December 2025 ( AFP/Getty )

According to the statement, Myanmar will keep working alongside Bangladesh to receive verified former residents as soon as the security situation in Rakhine stabilises.

The ministry further rejected claims that more than a million people had been displaced from Rakhine, arguing that over 540,000 people crossed into Bangladesh after the 2017 outbreak of violence, while more than 200,000 remained in northern Rakhine.

Myanmar and Bangladesh agreed a two-year repatriation framework in 2018. However, implementation collapsed following the 2021 military takeover that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, sparking widespread armed resistance against junta rule. Repatriation efforts have consistently failed to materialise.

Renewed conflict between the military and the Rakhine-based armed group Arakan Army over control of the region in 2023 caused further displacement, pushing more refugees towards Bangladesh and other countries in a desperate bid for survival. The Arakan Army now holds much of Rakhine after seizing swathes of territory.

In recent years, worsening camp conditions, sharp cuts to international humanitarian aid, and a lack of safe prospects for returning to Myanmar have forced large numbers of Rohingya to risk dangerous sea journeys to Malaysia and Indonesia on unseaworthy boats.

In July, Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar had agreed to accept 5,000 Rohingya refugees currently living in his country as part of a return initiative.

However, Han Win Aung, an official from Myanmar’s foreign ministry, told the Associated Press at the time that the programme was restricted to verified Myanmarese nationals held in detention centres in Malaysia, dismissing reports that the administration would take back any Rohingya.

AP

The cast of the new X-Men movie has officially been announced, putting to bed months of rumour about who will be joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most important new franchise.

The annual D23 fan convention is taking place over the weekend, with Disney announcing a slew of new projects and teasing films and TV shows due for imminent release, but all eyes were on the new X-Men cast on Friday night (14 August).

Adam Driver, who had been sought by a number of Marvel projects over the years, was confirmed to be playing villain Mr Sinister, while his former Girls co-star Christopher Abbott is officially signed on as Professor X.

Inde Navarrette, who has experienced skyrocketing fame this summer as the star of the surprise smash Obsession, will play Rogue in the new film, while Broadway actor Maya Boyd will make her feature film debut as Storm.

They join the previously announced Heartbreaker star Kit Connor and Ready or Not’s Samara Weaving as Cyclops and Emma Frost, respectively. Sadie Sink will also reprise her role as Jean Grey after debuting the character in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

open image in gallery Director Jake Schreier alongside Maya Boyd (Storm), Sadie Sink (Jean Grey), Christopher Abbott (Professor X), Samara Weaving (Emma Frost), Kit Connor (Cyclops) and Inde Navarrette (Rogue) ( Getty Images )

But the casting has also thrown for a loop many observers, who had been convinced in recent weeks that certain actors were all but signed onto the new movie.

Cailee Spaeny, the star of Priscilla, Civil War and the recent second season of Beef, was widely tipped to play Rogue in the new movie – with one report suggesting she had it in the bag after trouncing Marty Supreme actor Odessa A’zion in auditions.

One Spaeny fan account went so far as to tweet their excitement over the impending X-Men presentation at D23, only to post a follow-up tweet within minutes of the Navarrette announcement simply saying “LMFAOOOOOOOOO”.

“The amount of fake narratives and rumours the casting of X-MEN caused,” tweeted one person.

“I’m so glad I wasn’t keeping up with all the X-Men casting rumours and getting invested in them,” tweeted another person. “I’m seeing people crashing out over certain people and don’t even know over who.”

May December star Charles Melton had been linked with the role of Beast, but reports this week suggested he had dropped out of contention. The Long Walk’s Cooper Hoffman and Queer’s Drew Starkey had also been linked to Cyclops prior to Connor’s casting.

For weeks it had also been speculated that Storm would be played by actor Jayme Lawson, who appeared as the mayoral candidate in The Batman and the seductive vampire singer Pearline in the Oscar-winning Sinners – a further rumour suggesting that Sinners director Ryan Coogler was personally involved in the Storm casting, because he intends to introduce the character in his forthcoming Black Panther sequel, only strengthened the idea.

open image in gallery The new X-Men are announced at D23 ( Getty Images for Disney )

Of course, many of these names could still materialise somewhere in the new X-Men, as MCU chief Kevin Feige promised that the stars announced at D23 were not the entirety of the cast.

The new X-Men film, which will be directed by Thunderbolts’s Jake Schreier, is a significant next step for the slightly beleaguered MCU, which has struggled to replicate its early success in recent years with launches of superhero teams including the Thunderbolts, the Fantastic Four and the Eternals.

X-Men remains a much-loved property, with several cast members from the original films – among them Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, Alan Cumming and Rebecca Romijn – all due to reprise their roles in December’s Avengers: Doomsday. Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine has also been drafted into reprise his role in a number of additional movies over the years, including 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine, which grossed more than $1 billion at the box office.

Bryan Singer directed the original X-Men in 2000, which was credited with salvaging the superhero genre as a whole following the campy, critically reviled and commercially disappointing 1997 film Batman & Robin.

The movie revolved around a team of mutant superheroes led by the likes of Halle Berry’s Storm and Famke Janssen’s Jean Grey. A prequel series was launched in 2011 with X-Men: First Class, which cast James McAvoy as Professor X, Michael Fassbender as Magneto, Jennifer Lawrence as Mystique and Nicholas Hoult as Beast.

The new, currently untitled X-Men film will be released on 5 May, 2028.

South Korean leader Lee Jae Myung called for talks with rival North Korea to “pursue peaceful coexistence”, urging the need to replace the Korean peninsula's armistice with a "peace regime".

The Korean War of 1950-53 was stopped ​by a ceasefire and not a peace treaty.

In a speech marking the 81st ​anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese colonial rule at the end of World War II, the president called for dialogue to end the war once and for all.

Mr Lee said Seoul and Pyongyang must “sit down together to pursue peaceful coexistence and shared growth”.

“Rather than a concession,” the president said, “this would mark the start of coexistence.”

“We’ll embark on a journey to end war and transform the Korean Peninsula’s unstable armistice into a peace regime. Let’s drop all intentions of threatening one another and initiate dialogue among directly concerned parties in order to conclude this long war,” Mr Lee said, adding that talks could also explore ways to curb Pyongyang's nuclear capabilities.

open image in gallery South Korean president Lee Jae Myung speaks during a ceremony to celebrate the 81st anniversary of the Korean Liberation Day in Seoul ( AFP/Getty )

The president assured that Seoul would ​take the steps needed to ease tensions on the peninsula and ​build safeguards to contain escalation.

“Peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula is a duty, not a choice,” he said.

Pyongyang’s relations with Seoul remain broken, with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un labelling the rival nation ⁠as the most hostile state and ordering stronger frontline defences.

Pyongyang has criticised Seoul’s ⁠joint military drills with the US and its plan to build nuclear-powered submarines as grave provocations.

open image in gallery Lee Jae Myung and his wife Kim Hea Kyung wave the national flag ( AFP/Getty )

Speaking about his country’s ties with Japan, Mr Lee said cooperation between the two countries was “more important than ever”.

He said that Seoul and Tokyo had broadened cooperation in recent years in supply chains, energy and advanced industries.

“Guided by pragmatic diplomacy centred on national interests,” he said, “my administration will continue to broaden the horizons of cooperation in pursuit of our shared interests and pool our collective wisdom to resolve common challenges.”

The leader called for confronting the past while leaving open the ⁠future when it came to dealing with the memory of Japanese colonial rule and hoped to launch 60 years of peace and prosperity with the "close neighbour".

“Trust is formed through mutual empathy and a sincere recognition of one another’s pain,” he said. “To this day, victims and bereaved families are still living with the wounds and pain of the past.”

Spanish officials have launched a formal investigation after the matriarch of a famed Iberian orca pod was spotted with injuries consistent with shotgun or pellet gun fire.

The animal, named Toñi, is the oldest living matriarch of a critically endangered population known for jostling and ramming boats off the coast of Spain and Portugal.

Spain’s Ministry for Ecological Transition have since confirmed that Toñi was seen with multiple impact wounds along her dorsal fin in the Strait of Gibraltar.

Ministry sources have indicated that several projectiles remain lodged in the whale’s fin, creating a severe risk for infection.

open image in gallery Potential bullet wounds have been spotted on the dorsal fin of the orca ( Reuters )

Conservation group Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) tracked Toñi shortly after the injuries were spotted, describing the sight of "la abuela" (which translates to “the grandmother”) as devastating.

"If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.

"We were with her just a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there," said IOG co-founder Janek Andre.

Spanish authorities are now coordinating with Portuguese officials, as the injuries were first detected after the pod traveled from waters near Faro.

The Iberian orcas made international headlines in 2020 after sailors reported interactions where animals bumped rudders, spun vessels, and caused structural damage.

open image in gallery The pod have previously jostled vessels travelling across the strait ( Rafael Fernandez Caballero/Ocean Photographer of the Yea )

While the pod has been linked to damage on dozens of vessels and the sinking of at least four boats, scientists have repeatedly rejected claims that the behaviour constitutes an attack, suggesting instead that it represents social play or hunting practice.

However, tension between sailors and the pod has escalated significantly in recent years. Sailors have shared controversial methods to deter pods from approaching ships.

In 2023, video footage surfaced showing individuals throwing firecrackers into the water as orcas approached a boat's rudder.

Scientists warn that the tiny population, which is now estimated at just 30 to 40 whales — is already struggling for survival in one of the world's busiest maritime corridors.

Severe environmental stressors, including severe food scarcity, pollution, and dense commercial shipping traffic through the strait mean that human retaliation threatens to push the vulnerable pod closer toward regional extinction.

"Whatever someone's opinion about vessel interactions may be, shooting at these animals can never be acceptable," Andre added.

"These orcas need protection, not retaliation."

Spanish marine protection agencies have appealed for information from local sailors and boat operators as the investigation continues.

News.title: How to recycle old phones and electronics – and why doing so is good for your wallet
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Many consumers have drawers or closets full of old laptops, cellphones, fitness trackers and other electronic devices they no longer need.

But it's hard to know where to recycle these items, or it seems costly and inconvenient.

The world generates millions of tons of electronic waste, also called e-waste, each year. People worldwide produced 137 billion pounds (62 million metric tons) of e-waste in 2022, and only about 22 percent of it was properly recycled, according to the United Nations' most recent estimate.

The Environmental Protection Agency estimates that less than a quarter of e-waste is recycled in the U.S. each year.

Keeping e-waste out of landfills is important because the devices contain materials that can harm the environment. Electronics can also contain precious metals and rare earths that are hard to source, making recycling valuable to businesses.

If an item is newer and still in working condition, manufacturers may refurbish and resell it ( Getty )

“The way that we’re creating and using and disposing of these devices has generated this completely unsustainable waste stream,” said Rick Neitzel, an environmental health sciences professor at the University of Michigan.

“And there are no signs of that abating at all. In fact, the trend continues to accelerate.”

Experts say that if more consumers recycle their e-waste, it could even drive down the cost of some electronics. Here are some tips.

Why recycling e-waste is challenging — but important

While all recycling comes with challenges, it is often more confusing to recycle e-waste than a plastic bottle or cardboard box. Common containers can be recycled curbside or in public bins, but it often takes some research to figure out where to take an electronic device.

“Cardboard comes in many shapes and sizes, but at the end of the day, it’s still cardboard,” Neitzel said.

Electronics, on the other hand, can range from a small earbud to a large refrigerator, each with different materials inside, he said. Recyclers need to be able to extract each component and material efficiently. That is a complex, energy-intensive and expensive process.

But the efforts are worth it. Components such as steel, aluminum, copper, gold, silver, plastics and even glass can be recovered and reused, said John Shegerian, founder of Electronic Recyclers International. Keeping harmful materials out of landfills is another incentive.

“These electronics — which could and have historically ended up in our landfills or in other inappropriate places — can leak all the stuff that’s contained there within: Mercury, lead, cadmium, beryllium, arsenic. All these things are horrible if they get into our environmental ecosystem,” Shegerian said.

Experts say recovering precious metals from devices also helps the environment by lowering the need to mine more of those resources.

Preparing your device for recycling

Some consumers may be hesitant to recycle devices because of the personal data stored on them. Experts say that in order to protect your data, start with a factory reset — not just deleting files.

Resets restore the device to its original settings and thoroughly remove data. It’s important to follow the manufacturer’s guidance, as each device has different steps. Wiping an Android phone, for example, requires different steps than wiping an iPhone. The Cyber Security and Infrastructure Agency provides guidance on data protection, including where to look for manufacturer instructions.

Even factory resets may leave traces of data, so some recyclers will go as far as shredding a device's hard drive — and verify it's been destroyed. What's left goes through the recycling process.

Some devices can be refurbished and reused

If an item is newer and still in working condition, manufacturers may refurbish and resell it. Some charities and recyclers can also refresh devices so they can be given to those in need.

Look for major electronics and computer manufacturers that allow for their old equipment to be shipped back as part of buy-back offerings, or dropped off at a partnering site. Apple, for example, offers a credit toward a future purchase if your trade-in is current enough. Otherwise, they provide free recycling for older models.

Salvation Army and Goodwill Industries have donation programs that accept some used electronics, but it is important to check with your store to find out exactly what they need. Consumers should avoid inundating places with items that can’t be sold or disposed of properly.

For devices at the end of their life

Even if a device can't be refurbished, manufacturers are still a good first place to check, experts say.

“The manufacturers are where we want this stuff to end up because they know their products, they know best and most efficiently how to recycle them,” Neitzel said.

Retailers such as Best Buy and Staples accept devices big and small for recycling. Best Buy will also haul away televisions and larger appliances for a fee when new models are purchased, then work with electronics recyclers.

While local governments typically don't accept electronics in curbside recycling, many have drop-off locations that can be researched on their websites.

“Typically, if you’re dropping them off at a government-run electronic waste collection station, you can be confident in that," Neitzel said.

Recycle Nation allows consumers to look up specific items and find locations in their zip code that will take those items.

Other mail-in options include Amazon and Waste Management. Consumers can order boxes to their home, fill them up with their items, and ship it back.

Some programs charge small fees. Some return sites, for example, charge a few-dollar processing fee — such as $5 per monitor, or a set cost per the weight of returns or by the car-load if you drop off in person.

And even when a device can't be refurbished, recycling is important for the domestic supply chain of minerals and rare earths, said Terence Musho, an associate professor of engineering at West Virginia University.

He said improving the mineral recovery process and boosting recycling rates can also help consumers in another way: “It can also potentially bring down the price of your future electronics.”

News.title: Scientists mimicking the Big Bang accidentally turn lead into gold
News.content:
