Medieval alchemists dreamed of transmuting lead into gold.

Today, we know that lead and gold are different elements, and no amount of chemistry can turn one into the other.

But our modern knowledge tells us the basic difference between an atom of lead and an atom of gold: the lead atom contains exactly three more protons. So, can we create a gold atom by simply pulling three protons out of a lead atom?

As it turns out, we can. But it’s not easy.

open image in gallery Lead and gold are different elements, with three protons’ difference between them ( University of Seville )

While smashing lead atoms into each other at extremely high speeds in an effort to mimic the state of the universe just after the Big Bang, physicists working on the ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider in Switzerland incidentally produced small amounts of gold.

Extremely small amounts, in fact: a total of some 29 trillionths of a gram.

How to steal a proton

Protons are found in the nucleus of an atom. How can they be pulled out?

Well, protons have an electric charge, which means an electric field can pull or push them around. Placing an atomic nucleus in an electric field could do it.

However, nuclei are held together by a very strong force with a very short range, imaginatively known as the strong nuclear force. This means an extremely powerful electric field is required to pull out protons – about a million times stronger than the electric fields that create lightning bolts in the atmosphere.

The way the scientists created this field was to fire beams of lead nuclei at each other at incredibly high speeds – almost the speed of light.

The magic of a near-miss

When the lead nuclei have a head-on collision, the strong nuclear force comes into play, and they end up getting completely destroyed. But more commonly, the nuclei have a near miss and only affect each other via the electromagnetic force.

The strength of an electric field drops off very quickly as you move away from an object with an electric charge (such as a proton). But at very short distances, even a tiny charge can create a very strong field.

So when one lead nucleus just grazes past another, the electric field between them is huge. The rapidly changing field between the nuclei makes them vibrate and occasionally spit out some protons. If one of them spits out exactly three protons, the lead nucleus has turned into gold.

open image in gallery A man rides his bicycle along the underground Large Hadron Collider during its hiatus in 2020 ( AFP via Getty )

Counting protons

So if you have turned a lead atom into gold, how do you know? In the ALICE experiment, they use special detectors called zero-degree calorimeters to count the protons stripped out of the lead nuclei.

They can’t observe the gold nuclei themselves, so they only know about them indirectly.

About the author Ulrik Egede is a Professor of Physics at Monash University. This article was originally published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

The ALICE scientists calculate that, while they are colliding beams of lead nuclei, they produce about 89,000 gold nuclei per second. They also observed the production of other elements: thallium, which is what you get when you take one proton from lead, as well as mercury (two protons).

An alchemical nuisance

Once a lead nucleus has transformed by losing protons, it is no longer on the perfect orbit that keeps it circulating inside the vacuum beam pipe of the Large Hadron Collider. In a matter of microseconds, it will collide with the walls.

This effect makes the beam less intense over time. So for scientists, the production of gold at the collider is in fact more of a nuisance than a blessing.

However, understanding this accidental alchemy is essential for making sense of experiments – and for designing the even bigger experiments of the future.

News.title: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn
News.content:
Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Mowbray: It feels like a defeat

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Asian shares were mostly higher, powered by gains for AI-related stocks including computer chips as regional markets tracked a rally on Wall Street.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 advanced 1.6pc to 68,601.21. In South Korea, the Kospi jumped 4pc, climbing to 6,844.65, as shares in Samsung Electronics surged 5.4pcc. Computer chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 7.1pc.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

Sports.title: ‘We should have handled this better’ – Premier League club release statement after backlash over ‘disgusting’ email
Sports.content:
BOURNEMOUTH have released a statement following backlash from fans after firing a long-term employee.

The Premier League outfit emailed at least one employee confirming that they would not be renewing their contract for the 2026-27 season.

The employee – in his 70s – had been working at the club for nearly 60 years in multiple different matchday roles.



News of the sacking was shared on social media and the impersonal email sent to the long serving staff member received a huge backlash from fans.



A relative called the decision “disgusting” as they sent a message to Bournemouth ceo Jim Frevola.

The message on X read: “A relative of ours has been working on match days for @afcbournemouth for nearly 60 years.

“Programme selling, car park duty and various other roles. 2 weeks before the season starts he received this from the club.

“A disgusting approach @jimfrevola club should be ashamed.”

Frevola replied to the message on social media and insisted the matter would be looked into.

The club have now released a statement confirming it would be reaching out to the staff member and others who have had similar experiences.

Sports.title: Man Utd Treble winner reveals how Sir Alex Ferguson would have dealt with Amazon documentary series after filming begins
Sports.content:
EX–MANCHESTER UNITED star Wes Brown has given his verdict on whether Sir Alex Ferguson would have allowed Amazon cameras into the dressing room when he was in charge.

In June, the club announced Amazon cameras would be allowed into the dressing room for the critically acclaimed All or Nothing series, giving unprecedented access to Michael Carrick’s staff and squad.



SunSport reported how filming for the series had started as it charts their 2026/27 season, with the likes of Red Devils fan Gary Oldman in line to potentially narrate the fly-on-the-wall show.

The series has had critical acclaim with Premier League rivals Manchester City, Arsenal and Tottenham, while there have been similar success stories with Sunderland and Wrexham for shows on streaming rivals Netflix and Disney+.



Such a thing might have been unthinkable in the days of 13-time Premier League winner Ferguson, who ruled the club with an iron fist and was notoriously protective against media intrusion.

However, according to two-time Champions League and five-time Premier League winner Brown, Ferguson had changed towards the end of his legendary tenure at Old Trafford and would have been open to the idea.



Speaking ahead of the BOYLE Sports Cup at Croke Park, where Man Utd beat Leeds on penalties in front of a sold out crowd, Brown said: “He did change a little bit near the end.

“The gaffer always changed with the times and, yes, he is old school, but at the same time he understands when things change.

“So, I’m guessing if he was still managing now, he’d be okay with it. But it’s a different challenge again.”

Carrick is a media dream for the club, with his calm demeanour giving precious little away in press conferences – unlike his predecessor Ruben Amorim, who will be in the opposite dugout as United take on AC Milan, whom the Portuguese is now the manager of.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Carrick himself said the documentary, which had already began filming, had been “new and unique”, but insisted the squad had already grown “half-used to it”.

But Brown believes his former team-mate will remain the same, even if – given the tumultuous nature of the club in the past 13 years, it is a bit of a gamble.

The 46-year-old continued: “I think it’s brilliant for the fans because they see the inside of the club.

“They see meetings that they don’t normally see, so it’s brilliant. That’s the way it’s gone. I’ve watched many American football ones.

“It’ll be a little bit different. Will it change things? I think Michael will be the same sort of person he is. He understands the game, he understands Manchester United. But it’s a big difference.



“Is it a bit of a gamble, maybe? But at the same time, this is what the people want to see now.”

Sports.title: European golden boot winner who ended Messi run and went viral at Euro 2020 for embarrassing moment announces retirement
Sports.content:
ITALY icon Ciro Immobile has brought the curtain down on his stunning career after announcing his shock retirement.

The striker, 36, only joined Paris FC on a free transfer from Bologna in the final hours of the winter transfer window earlier this year.



But Immobile has decided to hang up his boots instead of gearing himself up for another season in the French capital.

The lethal finisher fought back tears as he told his team-mates he would not be extending his deal at the Stade Jean-Bouin.



Immobile said: “I know this is a difficult moment for me because I am ending a big part of my life.

“I love this job with all my heart, but I have to be honest with myself and say what the situation is now.

“For me, now is the time to be more with my family. They have been with me everywhere. I needed them for 17 years, and now they need me.”

Immobile got his hands on the European Golden Boot after notching a whopping 36 goals for Lazio in the 2019/20 season.

It ended Lionel Messi’s stunning three-year run of bagging the coveted award.

And Immobile, who found the net a sensational 201 times in Serie A, also played a key role in Italy breaking England hearts by winning Euro 2020.

Vuskovic made a £50m switch to Brighton despite never playing for Spurs while Lankshear will hope to become a star at Middlesbrough in the Championship.

Solomon crossed over to East London as he joined West Ham on a three-year deal.

The Israeli will be aiming to help the club fire themselves back into the Premier League at the first time of asking.

Djed Spence, whom Romero faced in the World Cup semi-final when Argentina beat England, is also leaving to join Inter Milan.

Sports.title: EFL club looking to replicate Man Utd’s academy revolution with former Sir Alex Ferguson coach overhauling youth setup
Sports.content:
RENE MEULENSTEEN upgraded Manchester United’s youth system while working under Sir Alex Ferguson – and now he has similar plans at Stockport.

The Dutchman, 62, has bagged a new role as the League One side’s director of football methodology.



And Meulensteen, who jetted out to the World Cup as Iraq’s assistant boss, is making a stunning bid to unearth hidden gems at Stockport.

He worked as United’s technical skills development coach before becoming Ferguson’s right-hand man.



Meulensteen now wants to mimic the academy revolution he oversaw at Old Trafford.

The former Fulham chief said: “I will try to help the academy as much as I can.



“We’re going to implement the skill development programme in the same way I did at United.

“That will be brought in at the foundation phase at grassroots level so all those coaches will get educated.

“We want to make sure Stockport has a skill development element that runs through all the age groups all the way up to the Under-18s, so that becomes an integral part of our performances on the pitch.

“You will then see our players have a good defensive structure and they are comfortable on the ball.

“We also want them to be able to change the angle when under pressure and to dominate in one-on-one situations.

“We want to align all of those things a little bit more in the longer term because that is what you should do with academies.”

Meulensteen’s arrival at Edgeley Park came a matter of weeks after his son, Joppe, joined Stockport boss Jimmy McNulty’s backroom staff.

And the Hatters will be looking to get their League One campaign off to a winning start when they head to Plymouth today.



Stockport narrowly missed out on promotion to the Championship after losing to Bolton Wanderers in the play-off final last season.

Sports.content:
Romero goodbye message

Cristian Romero has released an emotional goodbye message to Tottenham on his Instagram account.

He said: "Today, I say goodbye to a place that, for five seasons, was much more than a club. It was my home, my challenge and the place where my family and I built such an important part of our lives. I leave with a heart full of memories and enormous pride for everything we lived and achieved together.

"When I arrived, I had a clear dream: to leave my name in this club’s history. I knew the only way was through hard work, sacrifice and achieving something that had seemed so difficult for so long: lifting a trophy again. And we did it.

"The journey wasn’t perfect, but I don’t want that to define my goodbye. I choose to remember the happy moments, the lessons, the people who stood by me and, above all, the love I received during these five years. Thank you to everyone at the club who shared this journey with me. Coaches, teammates, staff and every person working behind the scenes you are all part of my story and have a place in my heart.

"And to the fans: Thank you for loving me, respecting me and making me feel like one of you from day one. Thank you for every hug, every song, every flag, every applause and for always being there. I know I wasn’t perfect, but one thing gives me peace: I always gave everything. I defended this shirt with pride and with all my heart.

"THANK YOU FOR EVERYTHING. I’m leaving the club, but a part of my heart will always remain here. Once I was one of you. Today, I leave as one of you forever. With all my love and respect. Thank you for everything. And goodbye @spursofficial."

Sports.title: Liverpool finally change transfer stance after breakthrough in negotiations
Sports.content:
Liverpool finally change transfer stance after breakthrough in negotiations

Liverpool are under pressure to complete sales with just 17 days left in the summer transfer window and have reportedly reached a compromise over the deal for Curtis Jones

View 2 Images Andoni Iraola needs player sales to fund transfers (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

Liverpool have subtly lowered their asking price for midfielder Curtis Jones following prolonged negotiations with Inter Milan. Jones' proposed move to Italy has been in the offing for months - and it appears a breakthrough has now been made.

‌



It was way back in June when Liverpool rejected a second bid from Inter worth £21.7million. The Reds had grown frustrated with their approach for the midfielder, who they have valued at £35m, despite being in the final 12 months of his contract.

‌



However, the growing pressure to offload players in the final stages of the transfer window is beginning to tell at Anfield. Jones is one of several players who are in the final year of their contract at Liverpool, who have so far failed to sell this summer.

‌



Ibrahima Konate, Andy Robertson and Mohamed Salah all left for nothing, while remarkably, Luca Stephenson, a 22-year-old midfielder, is the only player to pull in a transfer fee, having moved to Bolton for £700,000.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

There are just 17 days left in the transfer window, and eight days until the season starts for Andoni Iraola's side, they've been forced to seek a compromise. Corriere dello Sport say that Liverpool's €40m (£34m) valuation has softened for Jones, who has already agreed personal terms and will become Inter's third English signing this summer, following John Stones and Djed Spence.

‌



He will move for closer to €35m (£30m), bringing in valuable funds for the club. Stejan Bajcetic and Calvin Ramsay are also in the final year of their contracts at Liverpool and could also be moved on in the coming weeks.

Joe Gomez, Wataru Endo, Kostas Tsimikas, Virgil van Dijk and Alisson Becker are in the same boat, although Iraola wants to keep them, posing the possibility of losing them for nothing next summer. It's an obvious issue for the club to deal with, as they also try to add quality before the deadline.

View 2 Images Curtis Jones is poised to leave Liverpool this summer (Image: Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images)

‌



Ronald Araujo has joined Victor Munoz in joining the Reds this summer, but the signing of a world-class forward remains outstanding amid stalled negotiations with Paris Saint-Germain for Bradley Barcola.

"There are obvious situations that we know where we need to sign players," Iraola said last month. "A winger, for example – we definitely need to sign a winger.

"But there are other situations that we will have to analyse what the market gives you, what’s the cost, how we also see the players we have. We have some tricky positions where we have injured players that we trust but is still not the ideal situation. So, it will depend on a lot of things."

Sports.title: Victor Osimhen breaks silence on Arsenal transfer rumours after £58m talks
Sports.content:
Victor Osimhen breaks silence on Arsenal transfer rumours after £58m talks

Victor Osimhen is dominating transfer headlines yet again, with Arsenal being identified as a possible destination for the Galatasaray forward

View 3 Images Victor Osimhen could be set for a move to the Premier League with Arsenal interested in the striker (Image: Ahmad Mora/Getty Images)

Arsenal transfer target Victor Osimhen offered a 'wait and see' style response to speculation linking him to the Emirates Stadium. As is the case during nearly every transfer window, the Nigerian is being linked to the Premier League again.

‌



Having regularly been mentioned in the same breath as Chelsea, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur are now the two clubs believed to be interested. His name was brought up when the Gunners were in transfer talks with Galatasaray, who were looking to secure a move for Ethan Nwaneri and Gabriel Martinelli.

‌



While Martinelli rejected a move to Istanbul, Osimhen appeared to keep his options open when the rumours linking him to Arsenal were put to him. While stopping short of ruling out a departure from Galatasaray, he was equally keen to stress his mind is firmly fixed on pre-season preparations, with Arsenal said to be considering a move for the £58m-rated forward.

‌



FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

He said: "There are always rumours in transfer seasons. I will take care of my business. I am focused on my job, then we will see and think further."

Back in 2023, Osimhen made no secret of his ambition to one day play in the Premier League, at a time when he was in stunning form for Napoli as they stormed to the Serie A title.

‌



"I think playing in one of the top five leagues in the world is an amazing feeling for me," he said after being named 'Best Foreign Athlete of the Year' by the Italian Foreign Press Association in 2023.

View 3 Images Osimhen's future is uncertain (Image: Ferda Demir, Getty Images)

"A lot of people worldwide consider the Premier League as the best and the strongest league but now I'm in one of the best leagues in the world which is the Italian Serie A.

‌



"I'm working so hard to make sure that I achieve my dream of playing in the Premier League some day but like I said, it's a process and I just want to keep on this momentum and continue to do well."

Currently, Arsenal have Viktor Gyokeres spearheading the attack, with Kai Havertz and Gabriel Jesus also on hand as centre-forward alternatives. Defensive midfielder Mikel Merino has also demonstrated a talent for finding the net when utilised as a striker by Arteta previously.

View 3 Images Arteta and Arsenal are chasing back-to-back titles (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Arsenal have also been connected with a potential swoop for Atletico Madrid forward Julian Alvarez, though the Spanish giants are said to be holding out for upwards of £100m for the Argentinian. The Gunners have encountered considerable disappointment regarding their striking targets this summer.

They have already seen attempts to secure Morgan Rogers and Vinicius Junior fall through this summer, with them choosing to sign for Chelsea and stay at Real Madrid respectively.

Sports.title: 'I was the next Lionel Messi – now I'm making music after tough times on the pitch'
Sports.content:
'I was the next Lionel Messi – now I'm making music after tough times on the pitch'

The former Barcelona star turned to making music as a way of dealing with a hard period in his life

View 3 Images Ansu Fati was pnce viewed as Lionel Messi's successor (Image: Alex Caparros, Getty Images)

Being dubbed the next Lionel Messi is quite the burden. And for Ansu Fati, the former Barcelona prodigy now playing for Monaco, it hasn't worked out as hoped.

‌



The 23-year-old is looking to reignite his career in Ligue 1 after signing for the French side this summer following a successful loan period there last term. Fati has also turned to music as a form of therapy to help him navigate rocky periods and the expectation that came with his bursting onto the scene in 2019.

‌



At just 16 years and 318 days old, he became the youngest player this century to score and assist in the same La Liga fixture. Such was he a beacon of Barcelona's future, he was even given the No. 10 jersey after Messi's departure in 2021.

‌



Fati's promising career was blighted with injuries, however, including a meniscus tear in 2020 that kept him out for nine months. Consistent muscle problems followed. To jolt his career back to life he even joined Brighton on loan, getting a brief taste of the Premier League in the 2023/2024 campaign, where he managed four goals in 27 games.

And so music it is, as he attempts to anchor himself back to happiness. The attacking star has released a track titled Sea Como Sea" The song’s name means 'Whatever It Takes' and it has racked up a staggering 1.1million views on YouTube.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌

Fati said: “Singing is a hobby. I’ve always loved music, and people who know me know it’s something I’ve had since I was a child. But football is my passion, and I can’t compare it to anything, I have several songs I’m working on, and the idea is to release them soon.

“Sometimes when you’re alone, you just start writing and they just came out. I had some tough periods where it helped me get out of that rut.”

View 3 Images Ansu Fati was given the No.10 shirt once Lionel Messi departed Barcelona (Image: © 2020 Andrea Staccioli)

On the meaning of the song, he said: “A lot of people ask me if this song Sea Como Sea is about a girl or what. I’m not going to say. It’s a concept – everyone can interpret it as they feel it, as they feel at that moment. But basically it’s that with hard work and dedication you can achieve whatever you want, no matter what.”

He has fans in high places, too. Another Barcelona heir to Messi's throne, World Cup winner Lamine Yamal, is one. Fati added: “They weren’t surprised because I’ve always been one of those who plays music in the locker room or is always singing and dancing.

‌



"I shared them with several people, like Gavi, Lamine, [Alejandro] Balde, [Ronald] Araujo. They also gave me a big push, telling me to release it because people would like it. It would be a dream to one day be able to sing in front of so many people and show them my songs.”

Fati won two La Liga titles, two Copa del Rey titles and one Spanish Super Cup with the Catalan giants. Monaco forked out £9.3m for the player who scored 29 goals for Barcelona and once had a €1billion release clause.

In an interview with AS, he said: "The truth is that when I signed with Monaco, I felt both sadness and joy. I spent many years at Barça and left behind friends and people from La Masia (Barcelona's training facility). The first few days were sad, but that's life. You have to accept what comes and keep looking forward."

As of yet, Fati has not played a single minute of Monaco's pre-season, as his new permanent side looks to get him in shape ahead of their opening Ligue 1 clash with La Havre on Sunday, August 23. But after scoring 12 times for the French side last season, he looks to be on the right path.

Sports.title: 11 transfers that managers didn't want – but the club signed them anyway
Sports.content:
11 transfers that managers didn't want – but the club signed them anyway

Sometimes a manager is against a signing but the club still goes ahead and completes the deal - and it happens more often than one might think

View 11 Images Paul Pogba's blockbuster Manchester United move is one example where the manager was left irked (Image: Getty)

Transfers aren't always as straightforward as most of this summer window's moves have been. With less than a week left until the start of the new Premier League season, we've seen records broken and allegiances shifting left, right and centre.

‌



Morgan Rogers became the most expensive British player in history when he completed his £117million switch to Chelsea last month, following in international team-mate Elliot Anderson's footsteps after he swapped Nottingham Forest for Manchester City in a deal worth £116m.

‌



The window has been a relatively dramatic one with other stars like former Newcastle United trio Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon all changing hands for sizable fees, and more moves are on the cards too as clubs reinforce ahead of the new campaign and the September 1 deadline day.

‌



But with all those transfers, it's highly likely the club's managers either sanctioned the purchases or will at least be overjoyed to welcome new faces to their squads. This isn't always the case. Mirror Football takes a look back at instances where a transfer wasn't the manager's decision, but the club still went ahead with the deal.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Xabi Alonso steps in as new Chelsea set-piece coach in heated clash with rival READ MORE :

Man Utd in driving seat to beat Arsenal and Aston Villa to wonderkid transfer READ MORE :

Joshua Zirkzee

When Manchester United purchased Joshua Zirkzee from Italian side Bologna in 2024 for £36.5million, he became the first signing of the INEOS era at Old Trafford. Then-manager Erik ten Hag was given a new promising striker to work with. But the only issue? He'd requested a different type of forward.

‌



View 11 Images Zirkzee has flopped at United (Image: Getty)

Not long after Zirkzee's arrival, the under-pressure Ten Hag was relieved of his duties after a dismal start to the season and was replaced by Ruben Amorim. After his dismissal, reports broke suggesting that the Dutch boss was frustrated at the Zirkzee signing, as it was driven by INEOS, to whom he had requested a proven Premier League striker.

Zirkzee could do nothing to save Ten Hag's job and even under Amorim, he barely showed glimpses of the talent that shone in Italy. He could leave the club this summer, with Amorim supplanted by Michael Carrick. Zirkzee started just five games last term.

‌



Djed Spence

Tottenham defender Djed Spence was one of World Cup 2026's brightest lights and he made his mark in an England side that fell at the semi-final stage. But his path to becoming a Three Lions hero was not a straightforward one.

In 2022, Spence was snapped up by Spurs for £20m from Middlesbrough, having impressed the season prior on loan at Nottingham Forest. Antonio Conte was the manager at the time and he sensationally admitted that the full-back wasn't his signing, it was the club's.

View 11 Images Spence was not wanted by Conte (Image: Getty)

‌



"Spence is an investment of the club," said Conte. "The club wanted to do it. I said OK, this player is young but he showed he can become a good, important player for us. The club decided to buy him."

Under Conte, Spence played sparingly and in January 2023 he was sent out on loan to Rennes. In the summer, he joined Leeds United, but this loan was cut short. Genoa took him on for the second half of the 2023/24 campaign. These moves somehow paid off as the 2024/25 campaign was a breakout one and he played admirably last season before earning a World Cup call-up.

Paul Pogba

There was barely a United supporter alive who wasn't thrilled at the prospect of bringing Paul Pogba back from Juventus in 2016 — yet Jose Mourinho wasn't quite so enthused.

‌



View 11 Images Pogba was an expensive buy (Image: Getty)

At least, that's according to Mourinho's close friend and former adviser Eladio Parames, who lifted the lid in 2018 on what went on behind the scenes as 'The Special One' looked to stamp his authority.

"Sometimes there are reasons beyond sports that lead the clubs, and not always the coaches, to gamble on hiring players," he told Record at the time. "Pogba, for example, is worth a lot in the advertising market, so much so that in just six months Manchester United had already recovered what they had invested in him [£89million].

‌



"However, without terriers like Blaise Matuidi and N'Golo Kante at his side, he is worth ­virtually nothing on the field. United did not give Mourinho terriers despite advice given to Ed Woodward last summer."

Olivier Ntcham

Marseille's decision to bring in Celtic playmaker Olivier Ntcham proved such a bitter pill to swallow for Andre Villas-Boas that it ultimately cost him his job.

View 11 Images Ntcham is a former Celtic star (Image: Getty)

‌



The former Chelsea and Tottenham manager not only walked away from his role at the Velodrome following Ntcham's loan arrival in February 2021, but sensationally quit management for good.

"I have resigned because I don't agree with the sporting policy of the club," Villas-Boas told reporters in 2021. "I said no to the signing of Olivier Ntcham. He wasn't on our list. I had nothing to do with this decision. Ntcham is a player I said no to. I was not aware [he had signed], I learned it in the press this morning when I woke up."

Joelinton

Newcastle fans would have been forgiven for considering Joelinton a waste of money following his £40m switch from Hoffenheim in 2019. Former Magpies owner Mike Ashley once disclosed that Rafa Benitez was among those unconvinced about sanctioning the transfer in the first place.

‌



View 11 Images Joelinton went on to become a Magpies fan favourite (Image: Getty)

"He thought the £40m for Joelinton wasn't worth it. It's too much and the club shouldn't spend it," Ashley told the Daily Mail in 2019. "Very occasionally, I get to be me in this world. So here's the deal. I'll pay £20m of it personally. Nothing to do with the club. Above and beyond the budget.

"Rafa valued him at £20m. So that's what would come out of the club budget. The rest, £23m – I'll pay. And he still didn't sign it off. Looking back, I think he knew for a long time he was going to China because it was like we couldn't do anything. Joelinton was the test."

‌

Winston Bogarde

Chelsea's haphazard approach to recruitment is still a topic of discussion. Yet, any contemporary chaos would struggle to rival the shambolic scenes witnessed at the turn of the millennium when an ageing Winston Bogarde rocked up from Barcelona.

Reports at the time suggested that then-manager Gianluca Vialli had been kept in the dark over the transfer, with director Colin Hutchinson having actually overseen the deal.

‌



View 11 Images Bogarde's transfer was kept a secret from the manager (Image: Getty)

The late Vialli was dismissed by Chelsea shortly after Bogarde's arrival and he rounded off his four-year stint at Stamford Bridge as a notorious flop after Claudio Ranieri showed no interest whatsoever in the defender.

"You may have seen reports in the press that Vialli never wanted to sign me in the first place and it was my arrival that quickened his departure," said Bogarde following Vialli's exit. "As far as I am concerned, I was not aware of any of this."

‌



Andriy Shevchenko

A 29-year-old Andriy Shevchenko ought to have been music to the ears of virtually any manager, but then Mourinho was never your typical boss.

Having netted 173 goals in 296 appearances for AC Milan, Ukrainian legend Shevchenko was brought to west London by Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich, yet managed just 23 goals during a dismal two-season stint at Chelsea.

View 11 Images Shevchenko is a Ballon d'Or winner (Image: Getty)

‌



"He was like a prince in Milan and at Chelsea our philosophy was different, we had no princes," said Mourinho upon leaving the club in 2007. "Everybody needs to work like everybody else and everybody needs to prove he deserves to play. I think maybe he lost some self-confidence. Step by step a player goes in the wrong direction. He was not my first option."

Mario Balotelli

For all the indications that Brendan Rodgers enjoyed ultimate authority over Liverpool's transfer activity during his Anfield tenure, Mario Balotelli is one acquisition he's sought to distance himself from.

Stepping into Luis Suarez's shoes in 2014 proved a daunting challenge, but the Reds eventually settled on former Man City striker Balotelli as their solution - though Rodgers hardly wanted his arrival.

‌



View 11 Images Balotelli's Liverpool stint was short-lived (Image: Getty)

"What we wanted and what we needed was a player who could really press at the top end of the field. It wasn't just a goalscorer we were after," the Northern Irishman subsequently admitted in 2016. "I felt Mario was someone who wouldn't work for us. But come the end of the summer, we were struggling to get someone who could do the role we wanted."

Xisco and Ignacio Gonzalez

The late Kevin Keegan's second stint as Newcastle boss was not one to remember. Matters reached a breaking point following the 2008 summer transfer window, when the manager learnt that the Spaniard Xisco and the Uruguayan Ignacio Gonzalez were being imposed upon him.

‌



View 11 Images Xisco's arrival didn't please Keegan (Image: Getty)

Keegan wrote in his 2018 autobiography, My Life In Football: "It wasn't Mike's beer-guzzling that upset me that day. It was the fact that Tony Jimenez, the executive who had been put in charge of Newcastle's transfer business, had informed me we were spending £5.7m on a Spanish player called Xisco whom nobody from the club had ever seen play.

"On the same day the Xisco bombshell was dropped, I had also found out a Uruguayan by the name of Ignacio Gonzalez was joining us as a 'favour' for two South American agents.

‌



"When I rang Dennis [Wise] to explain it was out of the question, he seemed determined to change my mind. Gonzalez, he said, was a 'great player,' and our contacts in South America meant we had the chance to get him on a season-long loan. He was adamant we should give him a go and suggested that if I clicked on YouTube I might find some footage to change my opinion."

Timo Werner

Frank Lampard faced no shortage of obstacles during his first spell as Chelsea boss, not least the fact that he had little say over incoming transfers.

That power rested primarily with former director Marina Granovskaia and The Athletic reported that the fractured relationship between the pair played a significant role in Lampard's eventual departure from the club.

Article continues below

View 11 Images Lampard didn't request Werner's transfer (Image: Getty)

One such signing Lampard reportedly never requested - or at least not at that particular time - was RB Leipzig striker Timo Werner. Arriving in the summer of 2020, Lampard had previously lobbied for the Blues to bring in Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang that January, but was instead left with an alternative who failed to live up to expectations in west London.

"The two German players [Kai Havertz and Werner] have been massive disappointments, massive," said Harry Redknapp of his nephew's signings that summer. "I'm not even sure Timo Werner is cut out for Premier League football, the physical side is too much for him. I doubt very much whether Frank had a big say over in who came in."

Sports.title: Bangladesh edge closer to historic Test win in Australia
Sports.content:
Bangladesh moved to within sight of one of the biggest wins in their Test history after Australia stumbled to 161-4 at stumps on day three of the first Test in Darwin, still 67 runs behind.

Cameron Green (43 not out) and Alex Carey (19 not out) dug in to keep Australia afloat, but the hosts face a huge task to first erase the deficit and then build a competitive total to defend.

Bangladesh could even secure an innings victory if they take six more Australia wickets quickly, which would secure their first Test victory on Australian soil and arguably their biggest win in Test cricket.

Resuming at 351-6, Mehidy Hasan Miraz calmly shepherded Bangladesh's tail to another 75 runs, taking the visitors to 426 all out and extending their first-innings lead beyond 200, before returning to make the crucial breakthrough with the ball by removing Steve Smith late in the day.

Mehidy shared partnerships of 46 with Hasan Mahmud, 18 with Taijul Islam and a useful 46 with Taskin Ahmed before eventually falling for 65 from 154 balls.

Australia were their own worst enemy at times with three dropped catches, including an inexplicable miss by Smith in the deep, taking their tally for the match to five.

Josh Hazlewood claimed all four wickets to fall on Saturday and finished with 6-89 from 28 overs.

His dismissal of Mehidy was also his 300th Test wicket, making him the fourth member of Australia's famed "Big Four" bowling attack to reach the milestone and the ninth Australian overall.

Image: Travis Head walks from the field after he was dismissed

Australia lost both openers cheaply as Bangladesh tightened their grip on the match at Marrara Stadium before tea.

Jake Weatherald (0) and Travis Head (17) both chopped on attempting to cut paceman Hasan Mahmud as Australia slumped to 37-2.

It took Mahmud's match tally to eight wickets after his first-innings return of 6-55 helped dismiss Australia for 198 and set the tone for the tourists' dominance over the following two days.

Image: Hasan Mahmud celebrates taking Australia opener Travis Head's wicket

Marnus Labuschagne, also searching for runs after a lean spell, looked busy at the crease until he missed a straight ball from spinner Taijul Islam (1-28) and was bowled for 31 from 59 deliveries.

Australia's hopes of salvaging the match rested on Smith's shoulders and the veteran looked composed as he characteristically accumulated his runs with minimal risk.

The match swung firmly in Bangladesh's favour, though, when Mehidy (1-20) snaffled a sharp caught-and-bowled chance to dismiss Smith for 44, leaving Australia 122-4 and still 106 runs in arrears.

Image: Bangladesh's Mehidy Hasan Miraz, centre, is congratulated by team-mates after his caught and bowled dismissed Steve Smith

The largest first-innings deficit Australia have overcome to win a home Test is 206 runs, achieved against Pakistan at the Sydney Cricket Ground in 2010.

Sports.title: Never So Brave headlines Hungerford Stakes
Sports.content:
We have a busy day’s racing on Saturday with flat action from Deauville, Doncaster, Lingfield, Newbury and Ripon, live on Sky Sports Racing...

3.10 Newbury - Group Two Hungerford Stakes - Never So Brave and Coppull head competitive feature

Never So Brave and Coppull head a very competitive feature Visit Malta Hungerford Stakes at Newbury this afternoon.

Never So Brave holds the strongest form, having enjoyed a fruitful campaign last year, with wins in the Buckingham Palace Stakes at Royal Ascot, the Summer Mile and then topped off his season with success in the City Of York. Andrew Balding's gelding is nought from four this year but has been keeping good company and far from disgraced himself in the Sussex Stakes last time out. Bold bid expected.

Coppull is still lightly raced and produced a career best last time out in the July Cup where he came home strongly to finish a narrowly beaten fourth of 11. He steps up to seven-furlongs for the first time today and there could yet be more to come.

Like Coppull, Symbol Of Honour is stepping up in trip and hasn't been seen over this trip since his first start as a three-year-old. He has a fine record at Newbury, winning here on both starts and most notably last time out in the Group Three Hackwood Stakes.

William Haggas sends Extremely Zain went into the International Handicap at Ascot unbeaten and was a short-priced favourite to continue his winning sequence, however he could only manage fourth. He remains very unexposed and could take another step forward here.

1.25 Newbury- Group Three Geoffrey Freer Stakes - Dubai Honour returns to take on five rivals

Dubai Honour takes on five rivals as he returns in our opening race at Newbury today, the Highclere Thoroughbred Racing Geoffrey Freer Stakes.

This gelding is a credit to William Haggas and connections having won 12 races from 37 starts, winning four Group Ones and accruing over £5 million in earnings. We last saw him back in April when he finished a credible fourth in the Group One Queen Elizabeth Stakes at Randwick.

Mount Atlas and Tabletalk represent worthy adversaries and are set to clash for a fourth time. Mount Atlas, has got the better of his old foe on two of the three occasions that they've bumped heads but is three pounds worse off at the weights here having outbattled Tabletalk in a gripping finish to the John Smith's Silver Cup.

Gamrai remains unexposed after being pipped to the Copper Horse Stakes at Royal Ascot. He has since been bought by Victorious Forever, duly switching yards to George Scott from John and Thady Gosden and there could be plenty of improvement left in the tank.

Rebel Rocket is the only three-year-old in the field and takes the step up in trip on his fourth start after last being seen finishing sixth in the Derby. He is of interest.

3.25 Ripon - Great St Wilfrid - Fast Track Harry, Lord Roxby and Dark Cloud Rising clash

Fast Track Harry, Lord Roxby and Dark Cloud Rising all clash in what looks to be a typically open renewal of the William Hill/MND Association Great St Wilfrid Handicap.

Clive Cox sends just his second runner in the last five years to the 'Garden Racecourse' this afternoon and could have a winning chance with Fast Track Harry who arrives here after a fine run behind Amazing Journey, who went on to win the International Handicap on King George Day. Having already won off of this mark of 95, he rates a danger to all.

Lord Roxby arrives here off the back of a course and distance success where he saw off the reopposing Dark Cloud Rising in convincing fashion. Both hold good claims here with the David O'Meara runner four-pounds better off at the weights, with a win over the track and trip of his own, and bids for a fourth win in the coveted contest for his handler.

Best of the rest

12.45 Deauville - Group Two Prix Alec Head - Rabbit's Foot returns having not been seen since June where she beat recent Group One scorer Tiffany.

1.33 Deauville - Group Two Prix Guillaume d'Ornano - Daryzan and Montreal lock horns in a fascinating affair.

2.55 Ripon - Go Vince Go and Educating Rita clash in the Silver Cup.
