Sports.title: How insiders feel about the Ruben Amorim-Marcus Rashford Manchester United rift as the two prepare to meet again this weekend, writes NATHAN SALT
Sports.content:
It was inside the tight-knit press room at Craven Cottage following a 1-0 win over Fulham where Ruben Amorim completely took Marcus Rashford apart.

This was late January 2025 and by this point Rashford had not been in a Premier League matchday squad for approaching two months since being dropped by Amorim ahead of the Manchester derby.

Privately the tensions at management level had been brewing over the Rashford issue for some time. There are those who, still, point fingers at others for being the driving force behind forcing him out. Others still pin a lot of the blame on Amorim’s man-management skills.

But that night in south west London, Amorim went nuclear on Manchester United’s greatest academy player since Sir Alex Ferguson departed. In that moment, it totally changed the path for the two of them.

'It's always the same reason: the training, the way I see a footballer should do in life,’ Amorim said that night.

‘It's every day, every detail. If things don't change, I will not change.

Marcus Rashford is set to come up against Ruben Amorim this weekend as Man United take on AC Milan in a pre-season friendly

During his time at Old Trafford, Amorim froze out Rashford and put him in the 'bomb squad'

‘You can see on the bench we miss a bit of pace on the bench. But I would put [Man United goalkeeper coach Jorge] Vital before a player who doesn't give the maximum every day.’

It was the last line that was the kicker.

Amorim was sat in front of many microphones and television cameras claiming he would rather play a 63-year-old, who suffers from a noticeable limp, over a £325,000-a-week international calibre footballer. It looked categorically then like Rashford’s Manchester United story was done for good.

Sources speaking to Daily Mail Sport later questioned whether his handling of the situation called into question his ability to manage elite players.

Fast forward to December 2025 and following a 1-1 draw at home against West Ham, this time it was Kobbie Mainoo, yet to start a Premier League match at that point last season, who was to be hung out to dry by the Portuguese. Rashford was on loan at Barcelona by this point. No doubt he could empathise better than most as to how it felt.

‘I understand what you are saying,’ Amorim said in a really spiky press conference centred around his lack of trust in Mainoo, another shining light that emerged from the academy years prior.

‘You love Kobbie, he starts for England. But that doesn't mean that I need to put Kobbie [in] when I feel that I shouldn't put Kobbie [in], so it's my decision.’

And now, remarkably, we are here, heading to Poland for Manchester United’s final pre-season friendly before the start of the 2026-27 season in which Amorim is managing the opposition, AC Milan, and both Rashford and Mainoo are primed to line up against the very man who kicked them to the curb.

There are sources close to both players who are eager to draw a line under the uncomfortable episode and that is understandable. Amorim is gone. They have not. In theory, they won.

But there are staff members at United working in backroom roles that spoke freely in Dublin after the penalty shootout win over Leeds United about just how much determination is inside the group to get one over Amorim, more so than Milan. That, too, is understandable.

Particularly on Rashford, there has been a real push at United not to make this weekend a sideshow. Amorim put Rashford into a ‘bomb squad’ last summer and news that seven AC Milan players have been told they are surplus to requirements won’t come as any surprise inside a highly-motivated United dressing room.

Fellow United academy graduate Kobbie Mainoo also barely featured under Amorim

The pair are now back with United, adding extra spice to this weekend's friendly in Poland

Rashford doesn’t want a sideshow, though, neither does his current boss Michael Carrick, and after a pre-season in which he hasn’t won a single game - including a damning 3-0 loss to Chelsea which Italian newspaper Corriere dello Sport claimed ‘sounded the alarm’ - it’s unlikely to be top of Amorim’s wish list either.

It is, however, inescapable at just how much has changed since that staggering undressing of Rashford at Fulham last year.

Days later Rashford was at Aston Villa on loan, and a secondary loan to Barcelona followed following his ‘bomb squad’ treatment, where he went on to win LaLiga and the Spanish Super Cup, all while Amorim unravelled at Old Trafford and was kicked out at the start of the year following an explosive press conference at Leeds.

Now, having edged out Leeds in Dublin, there is an irony that Amorim and United meet again with two players he cast aside set for central roles at United and he’s in the role of the opponent. It’s funny how football works like that.

Rashford’s return to the group - which didn’t always seem likely, not least when his No 10 shirt was given away to Matheus Cunha - in Ireland over the past week has been extremely well received by players. To many, he is far removed from the arrogant and lazy figure he was painted out to be.

‘He was great,’ new signing Youri Tielemans, who worked with Rashford while he was on loan at Aston Villa, said.

‘There had been so much talk about him and bringing pressure and the media around him, but I thought he was just so good, you know. He was very humble, he was just hard working, and from the first training you could tell his touch, his acceleration was just amazing.’

‘In some ways, it feels a fresh start, you know, with new players coming into the building, new challenges, new things to try and win, it's quite exciting,’ Carrick said this week when asked about Rashford’s mindset.

What happens between now and the end of the window with Rashford remains up in the air. Carrick was noncommittal when asked categorically if the 28-year-old would be here following the transfer deadline, while figures upstairs, eager to trim the wage bill, have long been open to a move with a handful of Premier League rivals watching from afar with interest.

But nobody expected us to be here, with Amorim in the opposing dugout and Rashford, along with Mainoo, ready to be front and centre once more.

With an arm around the shoulder from Carrick, both players are ready to go and there’s no better storyline that going up against the very man who wrote you off as not good enough to play for your boyhood team.

Yes, both players are keen to draw a line under the whole thing, but revenge is sweet. No wonder some staff members at United are so desperate to win on Saturday.

Sports.title: WEST HAM FAN VIEW: The Championship could be a perfect reset button, but with a lack of new blood and nagging ownership doubts we know how quickly things can go wrong...
Sports.content:
WEST HAM FAN VIEW: The Championship could be a perfect reset button, but with a lack of new blood and nagging ownership doubts we know how quickly things can go wrong...

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

West Ham fans braced themselves for the worst following relegation from the Premier League in May.

Justified pessimism, you would think, after a season in which they won ten games, drew nine and lost 19.

The star players will soon be gone and so perhaps the financial burden and emotional turmoil of being a West Ham season ticket holder would be hard to justify.

And yet, instead of desperation and despair, there has been an unprecedented sense of unity with fans, players, owners all rallying around the club.

There is even a feeling that a season in the Championship could be the reset the club needs and could act as a catalyst for long-term change.

However, West Ham fans like myself know full well that things can soon take a turn for the worse…

Nuno Espirito Santo is pictured on the day West Ham were relegated - he remains in charge

Ownership, or one-upmanship?

The most significant change has been at the top with Karren Brady and latterly David Sullivan stepping down.

The Czech billionaire and Royal Mail owner, Daniel Kretinsky, is both director and major shareholder of the club. Kretinsky helped generate hope and optimism as he took steps to retain two of West Ham’s key components ‑ their talisman and their manager.

Skipper Jarrod Bowen said of his decisive meeting with Kretinsky: ‘I flew out to Prague in the Czech Republic to meet Daniel and Jiri (Svarc, his right hand man) and the ambition that I got from them, certainly in terms of the direction the club wants to move in, it interests me a lot.’ He stayed.

Similarly, while many West Ham fans thought Nuno’s departure was a foregone conclusion and something that Sullivan had pushed for, Kretinsky placed significant emphasis on persuading him to stay.

Nuno remaining is vital for West Ham. Having a Premier League-calibre manager, who helped to get Wolves promoted with 99 points in 2018, provides much needed stability at the London Stadium.

West Ham United owner Daniel Kretinsky (centre) helped to generate some optimism

Everything seemed to be looking stable and there was a clear connection between the board and the club. However, West Ham would not be West Ham if there wasn’t some turmoil at the top.

On August 1, Vanessa Gold, daughter of the late West Ham co-owner, David Gold, announced that she planned to sell the family shares to a consortium led by ex-Newcastle co-owner Amanda Staveley.

What followed was a frenzy of back-and-forth, with loaded statements by Kretinsky, saying: ‘The agreement with the Gold family provided stability at crucial time. This does the opposite.’

Whether this Succession-style conflict will spell trouble for the Hammers is unclear, but the reshuffling behind the club is coming at the wrong time, as West Ham begin their Championship season at Burnley on Sunday.

Fan power

It is thought that the departures of Sullivan and Brady, combined with Kretinsky’s promising start, played a huge role in the rush to buy season tickets. West Ham announced that over 50,000 season tickets had been sold, a figure that dwarfs previous Championship attendance records and shows a set of resilient fans backing their team.

There were glimpses of this connection last season, especially when West Ham won three consecutive home Premier League games, a feat they had not achieved since March 2019.

Fans are treating this season as a restart and a new era away from the clutches of Brady and Sullivan, no VAR, two fixtures against Millwall and an opportunity to win plenty of games.

There was also a growing expectation that in the Championship the club would draw on the fabled Academy that has produced down the years stars like Bobby Moore, Rio Ferdinand, Frank Lampard and Joe Cole.

Freddie Potts is one of a number of young players at the club to have moved on

Surely players like George Earthy, Callum Marshall and Freddie Potts could use their experience in the EFL to provide cost-effective options in West Ham’s promotion push.

However, Marshall has joined League One Luton Town and Potts left for Club Brugge for £10million. Potts' departure stings the most as fans believed his experience on loan in the Championship at Wycombe and Portsmouth would have been invaluable.

Former great Kevin Nolan, who scored 31 goals in 157 appearances for the Irons, expressed his concern.

‘I think this probably could turn out to be a bit of a mistake, but it's good money for Freddie,’ Nolan said. ‘I thought that he could be one of the players who could stand up this year for West Ham.’

This sentiment is echoed by former Hammers striker Tony Cottee, who says: ‘I don't get it…I played with his dad (Steve), and I want to see the Academy players.’

The loss of academy players could yet see the good faith that Kretinsky built up to begin to ebb away.

Ins and outs

This faith was never at a higher level than on July 17 when Bowen announced he was committing to another season. ‘We're going to need a real tight knit, a real togetherness, a real understanding of what we want from each other,’ the forward said.

This sense of togetherness and commitment seems to be echoing around the locker room where the Hammers have been able to keep their core group intact ‑ with only two big-name departures confirmed.

Midfielder Mateus Fernandes joined London rivals Tottenham for an eye-watering £85m, almost £50m more than West Ham paid Southampton for him a year earlier.

Winger Crysencio Summerville joined Al Hilal for £60m, a good mark-up again after arriving from Leeds for £25m only two seasons ago and scoring just six goals in 50 appearances for West Ham.

Both departures were seen as inevitable but gaining close to £150m for the duo was seen as a shrewd bit of business.

Jarrod Bowen chose to stay with the Hammers in a huge boost to promotion chances

There were fears that Dinos Mavropanos, a man reborn last season, and newcomer Taty Castellanos would follow the pair out the door. However, both seem committed to the club and prepared to fight for promotion next season, another reason for optimism.

On the down side, the club have been quiet in the transfer market except for signings of Keiber Lamadrid and Joel Veltman.

In midfield, we have an ageing James Ward-Prowse, an injured Tomas Soucek, the inconsistent Soungoutou Magassa and an unproven Mohamadou Kanté.

West Ham’s relegation to the Championship led to restructuring at each level of the club, a renewed connection between the club and its fans and stability in all the right places.

However, recent developments around ownership and a backtrack on youth policy seem to have set them back. The jury is out.

Sports.title: The season hasn't even started but Arsenal already look way ahead of the chasing pack. Their rivals, shrouded in uncertainty, have stood still this summer, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
The curtain will rise at the Principality Stadium on Sunday afternoon and the champions will walk out on to the stage ahead of the Community Shield. Arsenal’s cast will not look radically different. There will be a few extras and one or two new stars but nothing dramatic. There has been no need for drama. Just steady growth.

Arsenal did not need to have a spectacular summer in the transfer market. It was important that they strengthened from a position of strength and they have started that process calmly by recruiting Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle. With two weeks of the window remaining, there is an argument that it is the best signing of the close season so far.

Other arrivals are being discussed. The champions need reinforcements in defence where long-term injuries to William Saliba and Jurrien Timber are a concern and have led to an as-yet fruitless pursuit of Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa.

Arsenal are said to be interested in Jarell Quansah, at Bayer Leverkusen. They have spoken about prolific striker Victor Osimhen from Galatasaray and hope they can lure Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid.

If they add more quality in the next fortnight to supplement the signings of Guimaraes and Greece forward Christos Tzolis, then it will probably be enough to put them out of reach of the rest for another year.

They are already strong favourites with the bookmakers to retain the title they won by seven points from Manchester City last season. They have a solid look, just as they did last season, when solidity got them over the line.

Arsenal and Man City go head-to-head once more in the Community Shield on Sunday

The Gunners have strengthened from a position of strength and new signing Bruno Guimaraes will likely be involved

They are the favourites because of their own virtues, because of the depth and the quality of their squad and because, now they have ended a title drought that lasted for more than 20 years, much of the pressure that impeded them in the second half of last season will have fallen from their shoulders.

But they are also favourites because uncertainty shrouds their rivals. They are favourites because City have lost manager Pep Guardiola and the rest have not done enough to close the gap.

Manchester United looked like the coming club at the end of last season but an underwhelming summer in the transfer market so far has led many to question whether they can take the great leap forward they would need to unseat the champions. It feels as if their momentum has stalled.

City, Arsenal’s opponents in Cardiff, pushed Arteta’s side close last season but since then, they have lost Guardiola, one of the greatest managers English football has ever seen, and they are struggling to keep hold of the man many still see as their best player, Rodri.

It remains to be seen whether Guardiola’s replacement, Enzo Maresca, can handle the pressure of following Guardiola and the increased demands he will face at a club like City that is used to winning.

Maresca considered it such a great achievement finishing fourth with Chelsea in 2024-25 that he was emboldened enough to tell the club’s critics to ‘F Off’. Finish fourth with City and he may find himself booted out on to the east Manchester pavement.

Andoni Iraola is widely seen as a progressive managerial appointment for Liverpool but their defence of their title under Arne Slot last season was so disappointing that it may be too much to expect them to bridge the gap to Arsenal.

They have been linked consistently with Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola but even if they sign him, is that an improvement on Mohamed Salah? Much will depend on whether we see the real Florian Wirtz during this campaign.

Arsenal are favourites to win another Premier League title because of their quality and depth

It is yet to be seen whether Man City boss Enzo Maresca can handle the pressure of following Pep Guardiola

Amid that blaze of uncertainty, Arsenal are operating with the closest thing to certainty in the league. Everything about them says they are trading up. Leandro Trossard was an important player for them last season and Gabriel Martinelli scored goals, too, but Trossard has gone and Martinelli’s future is uncertain.

As Arsenal try to reach higher, they are identifying areas where they can improve and acting with requisite ruthlessness. Tzolis is seen as an upgrade on Trossard and Martinelli, if Osimhen arrives, he will be seen as an upgrade on Viktor Gyokeres. Guimaraes, wherever he fits into midfield, is proven quality.

And then there is Max Dowman. Until now, Dowman has been seen as a wonderkid, a startlingly brilliant and precocious teenager, a tantalising curiosity rather than a title game-changer. Dowman is still only 16 but he is so good and so exciting that his progress signifies another reason why Arsenal should be stronger this season than they were last year.

Many believe he has the kind of talent that justifies him being mentioned in the same bracket as Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal. His development means Arsenal will get the equivalent of a new superstar signing every season for the next couple of years.

There is still time for others to make inroads into the advantages Arsenal hold over them but there has been a studied maturity about the champions’ summer that carries a sense of foreboding for the rest. When the curtain rises in Cardiff, their lead over the rest will not have diminished since the end of last season. It will have grown.

Sports.title: Horrifying pictures emerge in aftermath of Finlay Tarling's fatal crash as report suggests car was travelling on the correct side of the road despite previous claims
Sports.content:
Fresh questions have emerged over the death of British cyclist Finlay Tarling after a Portuguese journalist disputed initial reports that the car involved in the fatal collision was travelling on the wrong side of the road.

The 19-year-old Welsh rider, who had raced for Great Britain on the road and track, died during the Volta a Portugal on Friday.

Posting on social media, Portuguese cycling commentator Paulo Martins shared pictures of the damaged white van which appeared to show the collision with the windscreen, and Tarling's shattered bike.

In the caption he wrote: 'Initial reports indicated the vehicle was driving on the wrong side of the road, but images seen on various TV channels show that the car was going in the right direction.

'For this reason, I feel obligated to clarify what I had written incorrectly, as these were news reports that had been given by various TV channels in Portugal.

'Now it's a matter of understanding how that vehicle ended up in that location.

'Was it authorized to continue its journey by the police? Did it break through the security cordon?

'Nothing will bring this boy back to the world of the living, and may everyone in the future respect human life, because there is a brother, a son, a father, friends, girlfriend or wife who will suffer immensely, and I have no doubt that the driver himself, even if he may not be at fault, will also be scarred for the rest of his life.'

The 19-year-old Welsh rider (second from left), who had raced for Great Britain on the road and track, died during the Volta a Portugal on Friday

Terribili le immagini della scena dell'incidente e della bici accartocciata del povero Tarling, via @RTPNoticias #ciclismo pic.twitter.com/rLkcDkmV3U — Stefano Rizzato (@stefanorizzato) August 14, 2026

Tarling was on the eighth stage of the race when the incident occurred on a 166.8km route to Fafe, in the north of the country.

In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been 'a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle' and that an investigation was under way.

According to Portuguese media Tarling was given immediate medical attention but died shortly after the crash. The race was neutralised about 20km from the finish line.

Tarling's team NSN said in a statement: 'We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

'Fin was a much-loved member of our team but, most importantly, he was a son, a brother and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

'Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents, Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend.'

Tarling's older brother Josh is a world champion cyclist on the track and a stage winner at last year's Giro d'Italia. Josh made his Olympic debut at Paris 2024, where he came fourth in the men's time trial.

Portugal's President, Antonio Jose Seguro, said Tarling's death 'saddens the peloton, the race, and the country that welcomed him'.

He offered his 'deepest condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates at NSN Development Team, and to the entire cycling community, joining in their grief with deep emotion'.

A statement from world governing body the UCI read: 'The UCI is deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today's eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

'The UCI extends its deepest condolences to Finlay's family, friends and team-mates.'

Tarling looked to be following in the footsteps of his older brother Josh - who made his Olympic debut at Paris 2024 - as a time trial specialist

Meanwhile, the sport's governing body in Wales added: 'We at Beicio Cymru (Welsh Cycling) are absolutely devastated to hear the news of Fin Tarling's passing today while competing at the Volta in Portugal.

'Fin was an incredible athlete, role model, friend, brother and son. We send our love and deepest condolences to Mike, Dawn and Josh at this incredibly difficult time.

'Rest in peace, Fin. You were incredible, and we will always remember you.'

The Volta a Portugal got under way in Lisbon on 5 August and is raced over 10 stages, concluding in Porto on 16 August.

Tarling looked to be following in the footsteps of his older brother Josh as a time trial specialist.

He finished in third in the under-23 men's individual time trial at the British Championships in June and competed in the Tour of Britain just under 12 months ago.

Sports.title: Golden girl Keely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as British star loses her 800m European Championship crown with second-place finish - with Olympic champion jokingly removing her medal in disappointed post-race interview
Sports.content:
Audrey Werro is fast becoming an unsolvable riddle for the leading lady of British sport. For the second time in 10 weeks, this Swiss phenomenon left Keely Hodgkinson staring at her heels in a race that lived up to its billing as the best of the European Championships.

To the most talented Audrey since Hepburn went the 800m gold medal. To Hodgkinson, there was presumably no silver lining to be found in finishing a close second on home soil.

If there is to be any consolation, it is that Werro, aged 22, clocked a championship record of 1:54.81 on a chilly, breezy evening in Birmingham to beat her. But warmer thoughts will be harder to find for Hodgkinson.

Instead, the Olympic champion must process the dawning of a serious rivalry and one that is not currently swinging in her favour. This one was settled by the margin of 0.2sec.

In the long run, Hodgkinson might view such moments as the competitive nectar needed for the breaching of new frontiers, of course, but the sting in the present will be real. Not many athletes have the finishing speed to match Hodgkinson, but in their past two races Werro has kicked away from her with the force of a donkey.

The decisive move here came after 500 metres, when Werro put the hammer down.

Hodgkinson, who had been near enough level at the bell after a 56sec opening lap, went with her, and they both separated from Femke Broeders-Bol in third, but the Brit had no answer. She never got her nose in front, and those moments of futility can leave lasting doubts in an athlete.

The 24-year-old, who was chasing a third straight European title, was evidently in little mood to indulge the celebrations of on-track interviewer Iwan Thomas. He assumed she would be thrilled with silver, but Hodgkinson responded: ‘I think I would be happier with a gold.’

Kely Hodgkinson was forced to settle for second in the women's 800m final on Friday

Hodgkinson jokingly took off her silver medal at the European Championships in Birmingham

She later added: ‘I think with that level of competition, any medal is a really good achievement and another one to add to my collection so I can never be disappointed with that. But I'm defending champion so I wanted to do that.

‘I knew it was going to come down to the wire but I really thought I was going to win today. But it wasn't meant to be. I didn't do anything wrong, it was just one of those things.

‘Congrats to Audrey. I am sure we will have more battles.’

That much seems certain. And for two women striving to break the oldest world record in track athletics, that will be a good thing.

But Werro has the edge. Having been beaten twice by Hodgkinson during the indoor portion of the season, she gained spectacular revenge in Stockholm in June when the Brit set a personal best of 1:54.33. Not only was that a win against a full-form Hodgkinson, Werro’s time of 1:53.98 was the third quickest in history. A month later, Werro ran quicker again with a 1:53.80 – if anyone is to better the dubious mark of 1:53.28 set by the Czech Jarmila Kratochvilova in the Eighties, Werro might have the edge.

To think, Werro was only cleared to race in this final on appeal after being tripped in her semi-final. It was a marginal call but also the correct one, so there should be no controversy around what it led to.

For Hodgkinson, the bigger picture will make for strange viewing. After the injury troubles of 2025, her times in 2026 have moved sharply on an upward trajectory, including the indoor world record in February, so she rightly resents any suggestion of ‘failure’ at losing a race or two. She was borderline tetchy in using that label prior to these Championships.

But in athletics, the clock is a secondary adversary to the field and Werro’s emergence is a huge fly in the ointment. For the rest of us watching, we can presumably take great pleasure in where it leads, because athletics needs rivalries. In these two gifted runners, it has one that has the potential to go on for years.

Sports.title: MMA star Ian Machado Garry eyes more than an upset at UFC 330 amid promoter Eddie Hearn's bitter rivalry with Dana White
Sports.content:
MMA star Ian Machado Garry eyes more than an upset at UFC 330 amid promoter Eddie Hearn's bitter rivalry with Dana White

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Top UFC welterweight Ian Machado Garry could be fighting for more than a triumph in the octagon on Saturday night.

After signing with Matchroom Chairman Eddie Hearn - the bitter rival to UFC and ZUFFA Boxing frontman Dana White - Garry, 28, is set to face off against two-division UFC champion Islam Makhachev this weekend.

And, should Garry pull off the major upset in UFC 330’s main event, it could mark more than achievement for the fighter alone.

A potential victory will see English promoter Hearn have two UFC champions in his stable of athletes - something that would certainly irk UFC brass.

Hearn previously signed UFC heavyweight champion, Tom Aspinall, 33, as a counter move to White stealing away longtime Matchroom athlete, Conor Benn, 29.

Benn got his feet wet by winning his first ZUFFA Boxing fight against Regis Prograis back in April and now has a massive fight lined up against polarizing boxing superstar, Ryan Garcia, 28, on September 12.

Top UFC welterweight Ian Machado Garry is set to enter the octagon on Saturday night

Garry is set to face off against two-division UFC champion Islam Makhachev at UFC 330

Now, it's Garry’s turn to bolster Hearn’s revenge. If Garry beats Makhachev tomorrow, it would soothe much of the pain the Matchroom chief felt when he lost Benn to White earlier this year.

It would also give Hearn some momentum towards finally booking a Ciryl Gane and Tom Aspinall rematch – a fight that could be set amongst the scenic views of the Eiffel Tower in Paris.

Garry understands on many levels what a win over the current world’s pound-for-pound number one fighter would do not only for his career, but also for the growth of his brand in the Europe market which is controlled and operated by Hearn and his sports agency team.

‘For me, it was an absolute no-brainer,’ the Irish fighter said of the partnership. ‘As someone who grew up in Ireland and is living in England right now, when you talk about the biggest sports promoter in our region, it is Eddie Hearn, it is Matchroom, and they've been successful at it for God knows how long at this point.’

When it comes to working with Hearn it’s more than just about money and opportunity for Garry, it’s about respecting the person you are conducting business with.

‘I love [the Hearn’s] family bond. I love Eddie's relationship with his dad. I love how they work. We've known their team for a while,’ he said.

Garry can’t deny Matchroom’s generational success, and the effect they’ve had on the European market.

‘[Signing with Matchroom] was the right decision at the right time to help grow my brand, grow my name and do it together so that we can bring more eyes to all of my fights,’ he added. ‘We can bring more attention to when I compete and that's my focus.’

The Irish fighter is signed with Matchroom Chairman Eddie Hearn's agency

UFC 330 will take place inside the Xinity Arena located in the heart of Rocky’s hometown - Philadelphia.

Garry is facing a swift and technical champion in Dagestan’s Makhachev - a longtime teammate of all-time great fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov.

For Makhachev, after moving up from the lightweight division, the New Jersey-living grappling phenom and all-time great is attempting to achieve UFC history by winning 17-straight fights inside of the octagon for his first title defense at 170-pounds.

Both men aim to outthink and outwill the other in what has the makings to be one of the most competitive fights of the year, even though Garry is a major underdog despite his incredible performances over the division's two bogeymen, Carlos Prates and Shavkat Rakhmonov.

Will Garry get the upset and become the newly crowned champ or will Makhachev have his way with the elusive striker and enforce his vice grip squeeze?

Hearn will likely be saying an extra prayer for his guy to shock the world and swipe out one of White’s bishops.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
