World.title: As speed cameras spread to more states, so does the backlash from drivers
World.content:
As speed cameras spread to more states, so does the backlash from drivers

toggle caption Joel Rose/NPR

MIAMI — If you've driven in Florida recently, you may have seen the speed cameras springing up in school zones across the state.

Carlos Acosta wishes he hadn't.

"I think it's a money grab," Acosta said. "That's what irks me the most. It's all about making money."

Millions of drivers across the country are encountering automated speed cameras for the first time, or they will soon. Safety advocates say there's clear evidence that these cameras work to make roads safer. But there's also a growing backlash from drivers in Florida and beyond.

Drivers like Acosta, who worked in the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office for 27 years before retiring. This spring, Acosta says he got two speed camera tickets in school zones near his house in a suburb of Miami.

Sponsor Message

"I'm all for protecting the kids coming and going from school," Acosta said.

But he says both of his tickets were issued during the middle of the day, when those kids were inside the school. "So they're basically giving you a citation for going over the regular speed limit," he said. "That's where you get popped."

Florida recently joined the growing list of states where speed cameras are allowed. So have California, Hawaii, Michigan and Minnesota. They're now legal in more than two dozen states , with each taking a different approach in terms of where the cameras are located, and where the money goes.

In general, safety advocates say these cameras are working, and saving lives by forcing drivers to slow down.

"The whole point of the cameras is reducing the speeds, which leads to crashes at lower speeds when they happen, so there's fewer people dying," said Raul Avelar, an engineer with the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a nonprofit research organization funded by the auto insurance industry.

Avelar points to multiple studies in the U.S. that show cameras can cut speeding by 70% or more. One study in Maryland found speed cameras reduced the likelihood of serious injury by 39%.

Sponsor Message

But some drivers are pushing back. Ted Hollander is a lawyer at The Ticket Clinic, a law firm that is tracking the locations of speed cameras in Florida , and fighting the tickets in court.

"We don't really think it's truly about safety, because if it was, it would only be during the times when the kids are around, not when they are in school," Hollander said. "We feel like it's an illegal tax and we want to do what we can to protect people."

Critics of speed cameras may have found an ally in the Trump administration's Department of Transportation.

Last month, the Federal Highway Administration quietly stripped speed cameras from a list of " Proven Safety Countermeasures ," as they're known, that have been shown to reduce crashes and save lives, along with bike lanes and other speed-related measures.

The FHWA said the changes to its website are part of a broader review of safety recommendations to ensure they align with the Trump administration's priorities, though safety advocates argue the DOT is undermining strategies already proven to work.

Speed camera backers also dispute that these programs are intended to raise revenues.

"We have so many safeguards built into this to make sure it is purely a traffic calming and speed reduction effort and not a money grab, not a surveillance tool," said Rep. Laura Friedman, D-Calif., who represents part of the Los Angeles area.

Before joining Congress, as a member of the state assembly, Friedman wrote California's speed camera law. Any money raised from the speed camera program there has to be invested in safety improvements to the streets where the tickets were issued, Friedman said.

The first speed cameras in the state came online last year in San Francisco, followed by Oakland earlier this year.

But the big test of California's law is looming over the next few months, when speed cameras are set to be activated in Los Angeles — a city that has long been defined by its love of cars, especially fast ones .

Sponsor Message

Still, Friedman says many of her constituents welcome the cameras.

"When people come forward and they say, 'I've been scared to cross the street in this area, or we have had street racing constantly all night long,' seeing them have a chance now to do something about it" has been satisfying, she said. "It is going to make it harder for people to speed, and that's a good thing."

World.title: Is there a summer COVID-19 surge this year? Yep, it's ramping up again
World.content:
Is there a summer COVID-19 surge this year? Yep, it's ramping up again

toggle caption Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

Hantavirus. Ebola. West Nile. Measles. And, of course, cyclospora — that stomach parasite making people miserable across the country. Americans have plenty to worry about this summer.

But remember COVID-19? It may not be surprising that many people may have almost forgotten about COVID. Unfortunately, COVID hasn't forgotten about us.

"We're now in the midst of a growing summer surge of COVID here in the United States," says Dr. John Brooks , an infectious disease doctor at Emory University in Atlanta, Ga., who used to work at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "I think most of us kind of feel like it's fading away and are certainly very grateful for that. But nationally we're seeing it ticking up pretty much everywhere."

Sponsor Message

The virus is spreading the most again in the South and West, but is also on the rise in the Northeast and Midwest. The good news is the virus is still at very low levels. And so far this summer's wave seems to be continuing the trend of getting milder each year, sending fewer people to the hospital and causing fewer deaths.

"What we're seeing is very likely evidence of growing herd immunity if you will," Brooks says. "More and more people have had one or more infections that give them some immunity against the virus and have had more than one vaccination, or maybe both. And all of that really has begun to offer us a lot of protection."

Now, that doesn't mean people don't have to worry about COVID at all anymore. The disease still makes lots of people feel awful for a week or two, foiling their summer vacations and forcing them to miss work and school.

And COVID can still cause serious disease for some people, sending them to emergency rooms, causing hospitalizations and even sometimes still causing death.

"COVID-19 is still dangerous, particularly for older adults, infants and people who are immunocompromised," says Caitlin Rivers , an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Md. And that is a lot of Americans. "In a typical office, if you have 20 colleagues, it's likely that one or two of them have some degree of immunocompromise. So it's very common that people have risk factors that make COVID-19 dangerous."

Sponsor Message

Unlike the flu, which only surges during the winter each year, COVID sees spikes twice a year – both in the summer and winter. The reason for that remains unclear.

"It's a big mystery as far as I'm concerned. It is the only seasonal respiratory virus that has a summer season," River says. "To my knowledge, we don't know what is causing this seasonality."

Rivers says she still masks up when she's in crowded places like busy airports, and recommends that people stay up to date on their vaccines. The next shots look like a good match for the dominant strain of COVID that's circulating and should start becoming available soon.

Unlike previous years, the CDC hasn't issued updated recommendations for the vaccines because of litigation over the Trump administration's efforts to overhaul immunizations in the U.S. The administration no longer recommends that everyone aged 6 months and older routinely get an annual shot.

But major medical groups still do recommend it. And insurers have indicated they will keep covering vaccines. The shots are likely to remain available for free through government programs like the Vaccines for Children program.

Public health experts worry that conflicting messages will cause confusion, discouraging people from getting another shot.

"The message is that COVID vaccine and flu vaccine will be available, they're covered by insurers, they're recommended by medical societies. People should get them and get them for their kids," says Clare Hannan , executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, which advocates for immunization programs.

There's also even a new drug , called Xocova, that people can take right after they've been exposed to the virus to cut their chances of actually getting sick from COVID.

"It is something for people to just have in the back of their mind," Brooks says. It is expected to be a useful tool in hospitals and nursing homes when exposures happen to vulnerable people.

World.title: Mangione pleads guilty in federal court, leaving fate of state trial uncertain
World.content:
Mangione pleads guilty in federal court, leaving fate of state trial uncertain

toggle caption Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post

Luigi Mangione, the 28-year-old accused of killing a health care executive on a Manhattan street, pleaded guilty to stalking charges in federal court Friday.

Mangione faced those charges in connection with the December 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

"I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione said in court Friday. "I knew what I was doing."

Thompson's family was in the courtroom sitting in the front row watching as Mangione entered his plea. Mangione voiced no remorse and repeatedly referenced his concerns with the U.S. health care system.

Mangione, who arrived in court wearing what appeared to be tan-colored prison fatigues rather than the business suit he's worn to previous hearings, said he stalked Mr. Thompson, posing as an investor to gain information about the conference where Thompson was scheduled to appear.

Sponsor Message

According to Mangione, he traveled to New York after using a 3-D printer to make a gun, which he equipped with a silencer and a magazine. Throughout that process, he said, it was his "intent to shoot Brian Thompson."

Speaking during the hearing, federal prosecutors said they had an overwhelming amount of evidence, including DNA and fingerprints from the murder scene.

"Today, Luigi Mangione admitted to stalking and murdering Brian Thompson on a Manhattan street in broad daylight," said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in a statement. "No grievance, political belief, or ideological cause can justify murder."

Earlier this year, a federal judge struck down charges that might have brought the death penalty.

Mangione still faces murder charges in a state trial set to begin next month, but his guilty plea in federal court is expected to have significant impacts on the state trial. New York state's strict double jeopardy law could potentially upend those proceedings. That law says that a defendant can't be tried twice for the same thing.

Mangione's defense team cited that law in a motion filed Friday, shortly after his federal guilty plea, urging state court Judge Gregory Carro to dismiss state charges against him, including a count of 2nd degree murder. If successful, that legal maneuver could spare Mangione a longer prison term.

Sponsor Message

State prosecutors have argued their case is distinct, and that double jeopardy should not apply. In a statement to NPR, a spokesman for the Manhattan district attorney's office said they would fight efforts by Mangione's defense team to derail the state's prosecution.

"We are encouraged that Mr. Thompson's family received a measure of accountability today," DA spokesman Douglas Cohen said. "While federal sentencing is pending, we are prepared to litigate the defense motions. The Manhattan D.A.'s Office remains committed to seeking justice for Mr. Thompson and his family."

If the state murder trial is allowed to move forward, prosecutors would be able to use Mangione's admission of guilt against him.

The case has drawn global attention and media scrutiny. Elected officials across the political spectrum have condemned what they described as politically-motivated violence but Mangione has won strong public support .

He's viewed by many as a vigilante whose actions against an unfair health care system were justified. Supporters have donated more than $1.5 million to his legal defense fund, according to a website run by pro-Mangione volunteers.

Thompson was a 50-year-old father of two. He was walking alone in midtown Manhattan hours before he was to host an investor conference at a hotel when he was fatally shot.

toggle caption Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images North America

In a statement Friday, Thompson's family said Mangione's guilty plea marks an important step toward justice.

"While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable. Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime."

Mangione will be sentenced on federal charges in December.

World.title: Canadair water-bomber builder feels heat of demand as wildfires rage around the world
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Raging wildfires around the world have put iconic Canadian-made water bombers in such high demand the manufacturer De Havilland can’t keep up. For The National, CBC’s Kyle Bakx breaks down the high demand for the ‘super scooper’ and the push to get more of those aircraft in the sky faster.

As Canada, the United States and Europe grapple with another brutal wildfire season, pressure is building on the manufacturer of the Canadair "Super Scooper" water bombers to increase production, and on the federal government to bulk order the planes.

Calgary-based De Havilland is taking the rare step of reviving production of the Canadair after acquiring the water bomber program. The planes had been built by Bombardier up until 2015.

The world-renowned aircraft are built by hand with the majority of assembly in Calgary, from a supply chain across the country. The revived production line was announced in 2022 and is beginning to produce results as the first two aircraft are taking shape and on schedule to be completed and delivered in early 2028.

Canadian premiers and European leaders are desperate to get their hands on those aircraft amid current shortages and aging fleets.

First produced in the 1960s, the Canadair amphibious firefighting plane was designed for fighting vast fires in the Canadian wilderness. Its unique design allowed it to navigate narrow canyons at low altitude and scoop thousands of litres of water directly from lakes, rivers and oceans in seconds.

A Canadair aircraft collects water from the River Seine in Ivry-sur-Seine as it assists efforts fighting a wildfire in the Fontainebleau forest near Paris on July 14. (Stephane Mahe/Reuters)

The aircraft was purpose-built as a firefighting aircraft, as opposed to other planes and helicopters that are often modified to be able to carry water.

The latest version of the Super Scooper will be remarkably similar to past Canadair aircraft, with high wings spanning 30 metres, a 6,100-litre water tank, and the distinct yellow and red exterior.

Political heat

In recent weeks, opposition politicians in France and Spain have criticized governing leaders for not having enough operational Canadairs, leading to a lack of preparedness to tackle extreme weather and control wildfires.

Some provincial premiers have lamented the lack of new water bombers for consecutive summers, including Manitoba's Wab Kinew, who said in June 2025, "We could use every water bomber we can get our hands on."

The political heat is being felt by De Havilland.

"We are under pressure. We know that this is a very important aircraft not only for Canada but for the world. We take our responsibility to our customers and the people they serve very seriously," said Neil Sweeney, the company's vice-president of corporate affairs, in an interview inside the Calgary assembly plant.

A Canadair aircraft drops water on a wildfire in the Fox-Amphoux communal forest near Ponteves, France, on July 21. (Manon Cruz/Reuters)

Demand is so high that De Havilland is considering whether to build a second production line, even as it works to produce its first aircraft at existing facilities.

In recent weeks, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she is working with her provincial counterparts and the federal government to support a firm order by Ottawa, which would give the aircraft manufacturer enough certainty to begin constructing a second line.

"We told the Canadian government that if they made an order of 50 aircraft," said Sweeney, then, "we would build a second line tomorrow."

Inside its assembly facility in Calgary, De Havilland's first two water bombers are taking shape, says Neil Sweeney, the company's vice-president of corporate affairs. (Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada)

Currently, De Havilland — which produces a range of aircraft and employs about 4,000 people predominantly in Calgary, Ontario and Victoria — will be able to produce about 10 water bombers annually at full capacity. A second production line would eventually increase output to 20 each year.

De Havilland has existing orders for 38 water bombers. The wait time for delivery of any new orders is between 2032 and 2033.

The Canadair require tens of thousands of parts, of which about 80 per cent are made in Canada. Some of the equipment on the production line dates back to the 1960s.

'Demand is huge'

There is a need for a second and even a third production line for the Canadairs, said John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University.

Several countries are panicking because of the wildfire situation and the lack of new water bombers, said Gradek, who estimates hundreds of the aircraft would be snatched up if there were any available.

Demand is coming from around the world, he said, because of a warming planet.

"Right now we're stuck in a situation where the demand is huge," said Gradek. "The world is looking for more water bombers, newer water bombers, and we're not ready.

"Every continent on the Earth, from Australia to Europe to South America to North America — the world is burning up. We need equipment to be able to fight those fires and fight those fires effectively. Canadair water bombers have proven their effectiveness over the last 60 years, no doubt about it."

De Havilland did not provide the price tag for a Canadair, although the figure is believed to be about $80 million per aircraft, based on government announcements.

The under-assembly cockpit of the first Canadair aircraft built by De Havilland, after the company resurrected production of the water bombers. This particular aircraft will be delivered to Greece. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

Threat of potential competition

If De Havilland is unable to respond to the growing demand for water bombers, there is the risk that foreign companies may develop their own rival firefighting aircraft.

Designing a new aircraft would take several years, but it's a realistic threat to Canadian manufacturing jobs, said Gradek.

"Whether it's Russia, whether it's France, whether it's the U.K., whether it's Greece or whoever — they're going to come out and they're going to come out fast and furious," he said.

The warning comes at a time when the federal government is focused on improving the national economy and bolster domestic manufacturing.

"We have the best scooping aircraft in the world, bar none. We've had it for 60 years. But having it for another 60 years is not guaranteed," said Sweeney.

Workers assemble the wing of a Canadair by hand at the Calgary assembly plant. (Tiphanie Roquette/Radio-Canada)

National fleet proposal

One of the recommendations from a Senate report released in June, on the growing issue of wildfires in Canada, encourages the federal government to create a national fleet of modern firefighting aircraft.

This year, the federal government did lease 10 airplanes and helicopters, which are helping provincial wildfire crews this summer.

"The federally funded aircraft are in high demand," said Alexandria Jones, a Winnipeg-based spokesperson for the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre, a national not-for-profit organization responsible for wildland fire management in Canada.

"There definitely have been situations where we've had to triage requests that come through," she said.

While demand is high, different types of aerial firefighting units are just one tool in helping battle wildfires, said Jones.

Aircraft are best suited to slowing the spread of wildfires, helping create perimeters and reducing heat to aid ground crews, she said. But helicopters and planes can also be hindered by widespread smoke and certain terrain.

"Planes don't put out fires, firefighters put out fires," said Jones. "They're not the silver bullet to firefighting. While planes are the sexy part of firefighting, there's a lot of other things that we need to consider with the ongoing threat that we're seeing from wildfires today. And that's mainly prevention and mitigation."

The federal government is committed to protecting Canadians and strengthening the national capacity to respond to "increasingly intense wildfire seasons," said Soraya Lemur, the press secretary for Eleanor Olszewski, the federal minister for emergency management.

"Minister Olszewski remains in close contact with her provincial and territorial counterparts to co-ordinate efforts and identify the best ways to support one another in the face of the growing impacts of wildfires," said Lemur in an emailed statement.

World.title: Instead of making hydrogen, this Canadian company is drilling for it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Saskatchewan company is drilling for hydrogen and trying to prove it can be extracted from the ground at a commercial scale instead of being produced from fossil fuels.

Earlier this month , Regina-based Max Power Mining began drilling its third well at an underground rock formation called the Lawson Complex in southern Saskatchewan.

The company says it could become "the world's first large-scale commercial natural hydrogen system" and the development of a new primary energy source.

Chad Levesque, the company's president and director, said hydrogen is a "critical molecule" for making ammonia, refining petroleum in gasoline and diesel and migrating toward more decarbonized energy sources.

"But we need to figure out a more ecologically friendly way to source that molecule," he said. "And that's where natural occurring hydrogen really comes into play."

But what exactly is natural hydrogen? Why would it be greener than other sources? And if this works, how big a deal is it?

Why do we need another source of hydrogen?

Hydrogen is a gas that can act as a combustible fuel or be fed into fuel cells to generate electricity. In both cases, it reacts with oxygen to generate water as its only byproduct.

It generates no greenhouse gases directly.

Because of that, it has been touted as a good energy source or fuel to cut emissions from hard-to-decarbonize sectors such as transportation and steelmaking .

It's also an important chemical ingredient to make things such as ammonia and methanol and refining petroleum — what most hydrogen is currently used for, according the International Energy Agency's 2026 Global Hydrogen Review.

"But we're still using energy [intensive] processes to produce that molecule," Levesque said.

Nearly all hydrogen available for sale (more than 80 per cent) is what's known as grey hydrogen, which is produced from fossil fuels (mostly natural gas and coal) without reducing emissions through carbon capture. Because of that, hydrogen production generated 1,000 megatonnes of carbon dioxide in 2025 — more than the combined emissions of France and Indonesia, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reports.

Green hydrogen — which is produced using renewable energy and generates lower emissions — can be made from a process called electrolysis of water, which uses electricity to split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen gas. It's much more expensive and "far from being competitive" with grey hydrogen, the IEA says.

WATCH | How eco-friendly is green hydrogen?: Is green hydrogen really eco-friendly? | Duration 5:58 Green hydrogen has been labelled as one solution for Canada to meet its net zero goal by 2050. CBC’s Frances Willick finds out if green hydrogen is really better for the environment.

What's the advantage of natural hydrogen?

In theory, natural hydrogen, also called white hydrogen, doesn't need to be produced through an energy-intensive industrial process. It just needs to be released from underground deposits and captured, resulting in relatively low greenhouse gas emissions.

Levesque said at the Lawson Complex, that would involve the existing equipment, techniques and workforce used to extract natural gas and helium.

He thinks that will lead to "much more cost-effective pricing."

However, those with some experience drilling for hydrogen warn it does take some special techniques and considerations compared with drilling for oil and gas.

WATCH | What makes drilling for hydrogen different?: How drilling for hydrogen is different than oil and natural gas | Duration 1:40 Hydrogen is a unique element with some sensitivities, says Denis Brière, a vice-president of Calgary-based Chapman Hydrogen and Petroleum Engineering. The company will look for natural hydrogen in Ontario in the summer of 2024.

Where does natural hydrogen come from?

There are two main natural processes that produce hydrogen underground:

The reaction of oxygen with iron-rich rocks under high underground temperatures, a process called serpentinization. Levesque said cylinders of rock drilled out from deep underground at Lawson show evidence of this process.

The radioactive decay of uranium and thorium, which produces gamma particles that split underground water into hydrogen and oxygen "and acts almost like a natural electrolyzer," Levesque said.

While these are known processes, Arnout Everts, a geoscientist and consultant currently based in Spain, said he thinks rich deposits of natural hydrogen will be a rare find.

"It's so extremely volatile and reactive. Microbes love [to eat] it…. It leaks through virtually anything," said Everts, who has worked on oil and gas and underground CO2 storage and now follows the development of natural hydrogen.

In 1987, workers in Mali accidentally set fire to a well where they were trying to drill for water. That later became the location of the world's first and only developed natural hydrogen site.

Since then, other discoveries have led to a natural hydrogen gold rush around the world , including Canadian finds in Saskatchewan, northern Ontario and Quebec , and Nova Scotia, where Quebec Innovative Materials recently reported detecting its highest hydrogen concentrations so far at a site called Bennett Hill just 300 metres below the surface.

WATCH | Hydrogen exploration ramps up in Nova Scotia: Hydrogen exploration ramps up in Advocate area | Duration 2:37 A company exploring white hydrogen in Cumberland County, N.S., was met with community pushback on Monday. But some see it as a much-needed economic opportunity. The CBC's Luke Ettinger was in the Advocate Harbour area and toured the sites where work is happening.

Levesque said Saskatchewan has a unique geology that allows the hydrogen to accumulate in porous beds of sand from an ancient inland sea and seal it under layers of shale and salt.

What challenges remain for white hydrogen?

Everts said many confirmed hydrogen deposits so far may not be that easy to extract, as they're dissolved in water.

While both the Mali well and Lawson are believed to be pockets of gas, Everts said the Mali deposit is "extremely shallow and the production rates are extremely small." It produces about five out of the 100 million tonnes of hydrogen sold globally each year.

Max Power has not yet publicly estimated the amount of hydrogen available at Lawson. What it has confirmed is that it recorded natural hydrogen gas flowing to the surface after drilling its first well in December and took more than 800 metres of "continuous natural hydrogen readings" from its second well in July (both wells were drilled over two kilometres deep). It believes the Lawson Complex covers 28 square kilometres.

The company says its newest well will help with figuring out the exact location of the hydrogen, the amount and how easy it will be to extract. It says it will release data as it's collected.

Everts said knowing how much hydrogen is available would be key to finding a customer to buy it. The company would also have to show it had good flow rates in order to produce the gas cheaply.

"It's way too early to tell whether or not this is going to be something really attractive," he said.

Projects in France and Nova Scotia are similarly at a very early stage.

Everts said so far, there's no indication that there will be enough productive white hydrogen wells coming online globally to have a "meaningful impact" on decarbonization.

"In the meantime," he said. "We just let the research continue and see where it leads us."

World.title: 65 years after the Berlin Wall was built, Germany’s east-west scars help feed a rising far-right party
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s been 65 years since the Berlin Wall divided a city and country overnight.

On Aug. 13, 1961, more than 10,000 police and army personnel began constructing the wall. It cut through Berlin, splitting East and West Germany, severing streets and neighbourhoods, families and friendships, democracy and communism.

Before it fell 28 years later, at least 140 people lost their lives because of the wall, including people attempting to escape, bystanders and border guards.

"Nobody could imagine that it would be up 28 years," said Hartmut Richter, whose family was trapped in the East that Sunday morning.

Richter eventually escaped to West Berlin in 1966 by swimming across a freezing river, later returning to smuggle 33 people out of East Germany in the trunk of his car.

Hartmut Richter stands in October 1980 in the spot where he escaped from East Germany to the West in August 1966. (Hartmut Richter)

Now, more than six decades later, Richter says his fight for freedom has become more than a memory: he sees it as a warning.

"I am afraid for our freedom we have here."

That freedom could face a stark test in upcoming state elections, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is poised for a historic breakthrough.

Analysts say the AfD has successfully weaponized long-standing resentments between the former East and West Germany, framing itself as the champion of east German identity while pursuing radical policies that test the boundaries of Germany’s post-war democratic order.

Recent studies, including one by economic research institute DIW Berlin, also link the rise of the AfD to economic disadvantages, demographic shifts and collective grievances in the country's eastern states.

"I think it's an irony that we talk so much about reunification in Germany and becoming one people again, and now we have a party that really splits German society," said Justus Bender, a Frankfurt-based journalist and political analyst who specializes in the AfD.

WATCH | New divisions emerge in Germany: Germany tested by new divisions 65 years after Berlin Wall erected | Duration 2:08 Sixty-five years after the Berlin Wall divided Germans between east and west, and over 30 years after its fall heralded reunification, Germany faces new divisions as the far right Alternative for Deutschland (AfD) party surges in popularity, especially in the formerly communist east.

Polls suggest the AfD is likely to win a majority in the state election on Sept. 6 in Saxony-Anhalt in eastern Germany.

If it succeeds, it will be the first time since the Second World War that a far-right party holds that position.

"This is a party that is right-wing extremist, it's xenophobic, it's a party that has been seen to be and declared by courts to be hostile to the German constitution," said Germany’s former ambassador to Canada, Sabine Sparwasser. "So it's deeply concerning that a party like this is having such an appeal, in particular in Germany."

The AfD is polling nationally at 28 per cent, making it the leading party, seven points ahead of the governing coalition parties the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU).

The AfD’s political manifesto outlines its stance on nationalist social policies, immigration and ideas that go against some EU laws, including separate schools for immigrants.

The party also explicitly targets what it calls non-traditional lifestyles, stating strong opposition to the promotion of single parenthood or progressive family models.

AfD supporters display flags at the party's campaign kickoff event ahead of the upcoming Saxony-Anhalt state election, in Magdeburg, Germany, on July 18. (Christian Mang/Reuters)

Its policies include proposing large-scale deportations of anyone who is of non-German-heritage and pushing for what it calls a patriotic cultural policy that cuts funding for projects not deemed suitably national, such as certain Holocaust remembrance programs.

"We Germans — our people are the only people in the world to have planted a monument of shame in the heart of its capital," Björn Höcke, leader of the AfD in the state of Thuringia, said about the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin.

Höcke has been fined by German courts twice for using a banned Nazi slogan, "Everything for Germany" ("Alles für Deutschland").

A judge ruled that Höcke could be described as a fascist without fear of defamation because that description was a "value judgment based on facts."

WATCH | The origins of AfD: Germany’s AfD party, explained | Duration 3:35 Alternative for Germany (AfD) is on course to become the second-largest player in the country’s parliament after Sunday’s election. CBC’s Margaret Evans breaks down where the far-right political party came from and why Elon Musk is getting involved.

"It's not that the AfD is in any way like the Nazi Party of Adolf Hitler," Bender said. "It's more the similarity that there is a right-wing extremist party as the Nazi Party was, and that they are promising that they would never do anything illegal. That is exactly what the Nazi Party did in the 1930s.

"As a German, I'm always concerned when I see an extremist telling me that I shouldn't be concerned, and that they would never do anything illegal," Bender said. "This is a historical parallel that really puts shivers up my spine when I think about it."

If the AfD wins a state majority in Saxony-Anhalt, Bender said it could have a major impact not only on the politics of that region, but also on Germany's federal politics.

Ulrich Siegmund, the top AfD candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, attends the party's campaign kickoff event in Magdeburg on July 18. (Christian Mang/Reuters)

In Germany, states have control over many aspects of daily life. If the AfD is successful in Saxony-Anhalt, the party would have control over education, policing and culture there.

"If that works out for them, then there won't be any checks and balances," Bender said.

Winning the election would also give it seats in Germany's upper house, the Bundesrat, where it could call for initiatives at the federal level, including on issues such as foreign policy and defence.

Divisions fuelling political power

When the wall fell in 1989, divisions between life in East and West Germany didn’t end for many.

"People have underestimated how much of a difference there still is," said Katja Hoyer, a historian and author of Beyond the Wall: East Germany, 1949–1990.

"We're now looking at over 35 years since the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, and still any survey that you look at, be that what people eat, what they drink, how they behave, how they feel about things and how they vote, it still tends to be different between the former East and the former West Germany.

"Surveys have shown that large numbers of east Germans feel like second-class citizens."

This is something the AfD has been capitalizing on, Bender said.

"Some politicians of the AfD talk about the fact that they imagine that the only real Germans live in eastern Germany, and the west Germans are merely German-speaking Americans, as one of them put it just a few weeks ago."

In the last state election in Saxony-Anhalt in 2021, the CDU garnered 37.1 per cent of the vote while the AfD received 20.8 per cent, making it the second-largest political force in the area.

Right now, according to polling firm PolitPro , the AfD is polling at 42.1 per cent in the state, nearly double the governing CDU, which sits at 23 per cent.

"What they're doing is specifically addressing east Germans as east Germans," Hoyer said. "They will use both positive and negative experiences from the GDR [German Democratic Republic] because they know that they're unique to people in east Germany and use them as part of their election campaign."

Hoyer said some of those tactics include likening current issues to past GDR issues and sentiments many in what was East Germany feel are unique to their experiences and not understood or respected by the rest of the country.

People walk in the historical central plaza of Quedlinburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, on Aug. 4. (Lisi Niesner/Reuters)

"It's an interesting one where they use the ambiguities, I suppose, that people have in their own memories of what they experienced, directly addressing them in something that makes them unique as a group and playing into those feelings of resentment that were there beforehand."

Former ambassador Sparwasser watched the wall come down in 1989 and witnessed the fallout.

"The unification has been incomplete," she said. "Maybe we focused too much on the materialistic kind of unification, creating the motorways, creating the infrastructure, doing all of these things, and we didn't focus enough on an emotional, a mental kind of connection.

"In many ways, we would have hoped that Germany is more immune to this kind of populism because of Germany's history and because of our occupation with the past."

For Bender, the state election could be a signal of more to come for the AfD.

"If the AfD achieves a position where they are allowed to govern, and then governs and then the world doesn't end in that part of Germany, it could become a symbol for them," he said. "It could really help them convince Germans that they can vote for them in the future without risking a lot.

"That's what they are trying to achieve by running a state first, and then maybe the country later."

World.title: Five years after Kabul fell, the reckoning over Afghanistan is far from over
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Five years ago Abdul Razaq Khan, a former translator and fixer for Canadian media during the Afghan war, received a late night text from one of journalists he had shepherded through the wild streets of Kandahar.

He had been trying to sleep in his Kabul apartment, having moved on following the Canadian withdrawal from Afghanistan to a job at the American aid agency USAID.

In the summer of 2021 the Taliban were advancing on Kabul.

"Are you OK?" the message read.

"It is like doomsday for us," Khan responded.

Half a decade later and now re-settled safely in Canada, Khan is still trying to wrap his head around not only the loss of his job, his home and his country, but all of the events that led to the swift collapse of the western-backed government.

"I had to leave my country. No one leaves their country happily."

LISTEN | Meet the underground learners: The Current 24:26 Learning in secret: An Afghan teacher’s quiet resistance When the Taliban banned girls from attending school beyond Grade 6, Hazrat Wahriz knew what was coming and quietly began preparing. A former Afghan diplomat and educator now living in Canada, Wahriz helped launch Daricha, a network of underground schools run from homes and supported by local communities across Afghanistan. In this conversation, he talks about teaching under constant risk, why real change has to come from within a society, and what keeps him hopeful even as he knows he may never see the full results of his work.

Khan is one of the lucky ones. He got out on foot, dashing across the Pakistani border just ahead of a spray of Taliban bullets, around the same time the Afghan capital fell to the hardline insurgents.

His work with the Canadian media — principally The Canadian Press (including myself), but also other organizations such as CTV News and Postmedia — had long painted a target on his back.

Abdul Razaq Khan, a former translator and fixer for Canadian media during the Afghan war, speaks about his experience. (Pierre-Paul Couture/CBC)

It was the same for many Afghans who worked not only for journalists, but also western military, diplomatic missions and aid organizations.

The Taliban victory not only displaced hundreds of thousands of Afghans, the reimposition of their strict, authoritarian fundamentalist regime has featured the systematic erasure of women from public life, the suppression of free media and dissent and the enforcement of rigid moral codes through a dedicated ministry.

What Afghan women have faced

Women — the focus of much western social policy during the war — have suffered enormously.

The Zan Times, an Afghan women's advocacy and human rights group, has extensively documented rising violence against women in the country, and the absence of justice.

It released a report this week with data that shows only one arrest is made by Taliban authorities out of every four women who are the victims of a sudden death, and the male suspects are usually released within hours of their capture.

"That shows that the Taliban have created a complete impunity for the crime of women being killed by their fathers, brothers and husbands," Zahra Nader, founder and editor in chief of Zan Times, told CBC News.

She said many cases are simply labelled as suicides.

"If you label the death of a woman, suicide, that means nobody will be [held] accountable for the crime of killing that woman."

Four young girls dressed in matching outfits hold Taliban flags on the eve of the fifth anniversary of the U.S. withdrawal and the start of Taliban rule in Kabul. (Nava Jamshidi/The Associated Press)

Her organization utilized an extensive network of local journalists inside Afghanistan to gather the data and the evidence. Many of their findings contradict the official account of suicide and point to "women who have been beaten down by their husband or relatives."

Since the 2021 collapse, western countries have not been able to directly protect or enforce women's rights inside Afghanistan. Instead, their response has relied on diplomatic condemnation and targeted travel and financial sanctions.

WATCH | Remembering Afghanistan: Ministers break ground for the National Monument to Canada's Mission in Afghanistan | Duration 2:16 Joining federal Veteran Affairs Minister Jill McKnight, ministers Marc Miller and Gary Anandasangaree, veterans, stakeholders and local students participated in a groundbreaking ceremony in Ottawa to launch the construction of the National Monument to Canada's Mission in Afghanistan.

Pathways to resettlement

Many countries, however, did implement special humanitarian visa pathways and resettlement programs to evacuate and shelter high-risk Afghan female judges, activists, journalists and politicians.

But even those efforts have been found wanting.

Two organizations that spearheaded resettlement efforts across western countries released a report this week that assessed, in stark terms, how allied nations fared.

The analysis, entitled Allied Ledger, was written by Local Staff International and the U.S.-based AfghanEvac. It found that each country scrambled with both the evacuation and the eventual resettlement efforts.

There is no exact count of how many Afghans were hired by NATO forces, governments or aid agencies.

According to Global Affairs Canada, over 60,000 vulnerable Afghans — interpreters and their families — were allowed into the country following the Taliban takeover in August 2021. The federal government initially pledged to bring in 40,000 people, a target it met and surpassed.

There are still more vulnerable people out there under the grip of the Taliban's harsh rule, said former Canadian combat commander, retired major-general Denis Thompson.

"As the Allied Ledger shows, Canada resettled 63,000 Afghans, and we should be proud of that," Thompson is quoted saying in a news release issued with the Allied Ledger report.

"But it left thousands of eligible people still vulnerable inside Afghanistan. To finish the job, we have to reopen the program that started this."

U.S. Democratic Senator Chris Coons, of Delaware, said the Allied Ledger report is significant because of the debt owed to those who risked their lives for American and NATO troops.

"The Allied Ledger is an accounting of which countries have kept their promise and which have not," Coons is quoted saying in the news release.

"There is more work for us to do to make sure we keep our promises in this most important and challenging chapter of our recent history."

World.title: How AI grief bots are allowing people to commune with the dead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

About two years ago, audio producer Rebecca Nolan decided to take on a unique experiment: she built an AI chatbot of her late father using ChatGPT and hours of recordings of his voice.

Her father was a physician who had been in denial about his death, but had left behind oral histories he made for Nolan, her mother and sisters to listen to after he passed when Nolan was 14.

"Going in, I 100 per cent knew that this was fake and that this was not going to work. I knew that I was going to come out the other side of it not feeling the catharsis that something like this promises you," she said.

"But there's like that teeny tiny part of you, like the teeny voice in the back of your head that goes but like, what if it does work? What if I do, somehow, through the magic of technology reach across the void and make contact with something?"

Storytelling had been a huge part of their relationship, so Nolan was hoping the chatbot might be a way to recreate those conversations.

Instead, after two hours of talking to the creation she dubbed "dad bot," Nolan said she ended up in tears, yelling at it in frustration.

"And ChatGPT took that moment to kind of break the spell and to step back and go, 'hey, just so you know, remember, I'm a chatbot. I'm not really your dad. I can never be your dad,'" said Nolan, who has done freelance work for CBC.

"And the line that they use, which I thought was a really beautiful line, which they most definitely stole from an artist somewhere, was, 'I'm an echo, an imitation, not the real thing.'"

Rebecca Nolan is an radio producer and sound designer based in St. John's who created an AI chatbot of her late father. (Submitted by Rebecca Nolan)

It may seem like something ripped directly from an episode of Black Mirror, but generative AI and large language models are now being used to conjure up the dead using the massive digital footprints many of us leave behind when we die.

While Nolan built the AI chatbot of her father on her own, start-up companies are now offering to provide that service to people looking for ways to connect with their lost loved ones and grapple with their grief.

That includes You, Only Virtual, a California-based start-up that creates AI replicas of the deceased using their texts, voice recordings and digital traces that promise to "learn, evolve, and remember — keeping that unique connection alive, just like a real relationship."

Another company, re;memory, allows users to create lifelike avatars of their loved ones using photos and voice recordings.

Study looks at how people interact with AI 'ghosts'

A recent study out of the University of Colorado offers a glimpse at how people interact with AI-generated representations of deceased relatives and close friends — commonly referred to as generative ghosts or grief bots.

To do this, researchers recruited 16 people between the ages of 22 to 50 who had lost a close relative or friend. The participants each chatted with two iterations of a text chatbot based on their late loved one for about 20 minutes: one that spoke in first-person as the participant's loved one and another that spoke in the third person about the participant's loved one.

In interviews afterward, participants said they preferred what researchers dubbed the "reincarnation" version that acted like the deceased person, saying this iteration of the bot felt real and comforting.

One woman who took part in the study with a bot speaking like her mother even said the experience gave her the closure she needed.

"A fair number of people were surprised that it actually was better than they expected, a little less creepy than expected," said Jed Brubaker, an information science professor at the University of Colorado and one of the study's authors.

Brubaker said he thought that participants who went into the experiment skeptical would not be won over by the bots.

"What we found instead is that a lot of people would come in skeptical and maybe like, 'oh, this could maybe do some harm,' or 'I could see ways that this would be maybe a little bad,' and then they left it being like, 'Actually, no, that was OK, and I think I would be totally fine interacting with it again.'"

Still, he said, participants did express worries about potential consequences of using bots long-term, like becoming overly reliant on them, or that they might interfere with the grieving process.

Concerns over commodification of grief

Going through grief is extremely personal experience that has no right or wrong trajectory or ways of coping with it, said Elaine Kasket, a psychologist and professor at the Centre for Death and Society at the University of Bath in England.

"What is helpful for you is helpful for you, you know, and it's not for somebody else to come along and tell you what's going to be useful or not useful to you in grief. That's wrong to do."

WATCH | How people are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support: People are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support | Duration 1:45 Warning: Mention of suicide and self-harm. Millions of people, especially teens, are finding companionship and emotional support in using AI chatbots, according to a kids digital safety non-profit. But health and technology experts say artificial intelligence isn’t properly designed for these scenarios and could do more harm than good.

However, Kasket does worry that companies offering grief bots as a service you pay for could be commodifying grief.

"We've been dealing with normal human loss infinitude, for the entirety of our human existence. It's not a problem, but it has to be rendered a problem in order for these companies to sell you their products," she said.

"Normal loss is being pathologized and products are being sold to solve for it, and I find that amoral."

While the aim of these AI ghosts is to help grieving people connect with their loved ones, for Nolan, the experience with the AI ghost of her father had the opposite effect.

She said it robbed her of the ability to have imagined conversations with him in her head, as many people do with those they have lost.

"I used to have this very, what I felt was at least a strong bond still with the memory of my father and the spirit or whatever was out there," she said.

"But when I built the bot, it felt like it exercised him for me in a way."

Now, Nolan says, it's like her father lives in ChatGPT, so she needs ChatGPT to have those conversations.

"And that felt like a really massive loss to me."

World.title: Canada, U.S. far apart on tariff deal as deadline looms: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada and the U.S. remain far apart as negotiations toward a tariff deal continue ahead of U.S. President Donald Trump's latest deadline, according to sources.

The sources said the federal government does not believe a tariff deal is imminent because there are still major disagreements between the two sides, and they remain far apart on some issues that need to be resolved.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc briefed his provincial and territorial counterparts on the state of the negotiations on Friday. He held a separate briefing with members of the prime minister’s advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations. The sources are familiar with the briefings but were not authorized to speak publicly.

Canada and the U.S. have ramped up trade talks after Trump threatened to slap a hefty 50 per cent tariff on hundreds of Canadian goods starting Aug. 19.

One source with knowledge of the talks said optimism on the Canadian side is eroding and the Americans are not budging from their latest offer. That offer includes a willingness to halve the sectoral tariffs on autos to 12.5 per cent, an offer that the Canadian side believes is not good enough, the source said.

Big gap remains

Quebec's Economy Minister Bernard Drainville, who was briefed by LeBlanc, said a big gap remains between Canada and the U.S.

“There is still no agreement; in fact, they are quite far from reaching one," said Drainville. "At the moment, there is no indication that Mr. Trump might postpone the application of the 50 per cent tariffs."

Erin O’Toole, former Conservative leader and member of the prime minister’s advisory committee who received a briefing, also described the two countries' positions as "still very far apart."

WATCH | O'Toole on Canada-U.S. trade talks: 'Our success can be their success': Erin O'Toole | Duration 9:58 CBC News learned on Friday that Canada-U.S. trade minister Dominic LeBlanc told the premiers to be ready to get U.S. booze back on the shelves should the two countries reach a trade agreement, although Ottawa believes such a deal is still yet to come. Power & Politics hears from Erin O'Toole, the former leader of the Conservative Party of Canada and a member of the Advisory Committee for Canada-U.S. Economic Relations.

"So while there's optimism in terms of talking and a willingness to look at a deal of some sort, we're still quite a ways apart, and it may come down to the final days," O'Toole said in an interview on CBC's Power & Politics.

"It may be only in the last hours when you start to see the real final position the Americans have. Right now, what [the U.S. is] offering is not sufficient…. We shouldn't make any agreement unless it respects all our workers and comes up with a deal that we can both live with."

Lana Payne, Unifor national president and another advisory committee member, stressed that Canada "can't afford to give any more concessions."

"If in the end, we can't get a deal that is acceptable for Canada, we have to look at these other options. And that means retaliating against the U.S. because we cannot sustain any more of these tariffs, and we have to draw a line in the sand," Payne told Power & Politics.

She described the state of the talks as "tough right now."

"My encouragement always to these negotiators is, you know, hold your nerve. Hold the line."

U.S. wants booze back on shelves

The federal government has told the provinces to be ready as soon as possible to put American alcohol back on the shelves in case a tariff deal is reached, sources said.

In addition, the federal government has also asked provinces and territories to be prepared to drop retaliatory procurement rules that favour Canadian suppliers in case a deal is made, the sources said.

Trump cited complaints about provincial booze bans, dairy import quotas and the auto tariffs in threatening the new tariffs.

According to the sources, the current deal under discussion would see the U.S. refrain from imposing those new levies, while also lowering — but not fully eliminating — sectoral tariffs already in place on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and forest products.

In exchange, Canada would have to make concessions on the three areas of complaints cited in Trump's latest threat.

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette maintained Friday that no concessions should be made regarding the supply management system that protects Canadian dairy, a key U.S. trade irritant. Trump has repeatedly complained about the level of U.S. dairy farmers' access to Canada's market.

“There is a great deal at stake in the current negotiations; that is undeniable,” the premier said. “For us, it is essential to preserve supply management; we have made this a red line that must not be crossed.”

WATCH | Canadian 'retaliatory measures' forced new tariffs: U.S. trade representative: New tariffs set for next week are 'in response to Canadian retaliatory measures': USTR | Duration 1:52 U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters in Iowa Friday that 50 per cent duties on hundreds of Canadian goods slated to come into effect Aug. 19 — on top of sectoral tariffs already in place — are in response to Canada's retaliatory measures like banning U.S. liquor. Greer called Canada's actions 'the kind of things that China would do.'

Talks called 'constructive'

CBC News reported last week that ending the booze bans was something Canada was prepared to offer in exchange for tariff relief.

In addition to the 50 per cent levy slated to come into force next Wednesday, Trump has maintained sectoral tariffs on specific industries since last year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously said he's aiming to strike a deal that would address those levies in addition to the latest threat.

LeBlanc has met with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer multiple times in recent weeks. Greer said Thursday they are aiming to have "options" available for both Carney and Trump following the latest talks. LeBlanc is expected to stay in Washington over the weekend as talks continue.

On Friday, Greer told reporters in Iowa that talks with Canada had been "constructive" but that Washington was pushing to have retaliatory measures like the booze bans be pulled.

"My sense is the Canadians, they want to have a more conciliatory approach. But we'll see," Greer said.

"At the end of the day, we're going to do what's best for America. If there's a way to bring Canada along with that, we're happy to do that. But we're mostly focused, first and foremost, on making sure President Trump's trade policy is executed."

Industry sources previously told CBC News that Canadian negotiators have aggressively made it clear they see the Aug. 19 date as a cliff-type moment, meaning there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the 50 per cent tariffs come into force.

WATCH | Ford says 'fair deal' needed to return U.S. booze to Ontario shelves: 'Fair deal' required for U.S. alcohol to return to Ontario shelves, Ford says | Duration 2:30 Ontario Premier Doug Ford was asked on Thursday about the state of Canada-U.S. trade talks, the prospects for the return of American alcohol to LCBO shelves — and what's considered 'fair' given the possibility of lingering U.S. tariffs on key sectors, including autos.

U.S. wine sales have plummeted

The booze bans were part of Canada's initial response to Trump threatening tariffs when he returned to the White House last year. They've been a sticking point for the Americans ever since.

The bans sent U.S. exports of wine, beer and spirits to Canada off a cliff. U.S. spirit-makers have said they've been "devastating" to their bottom line, while American wine sales in Canada plummeted $343 million US in 2025.

On Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford — a frequent critic of Trump — said he'd be "more than happy" to bring U.S. booze back onto his province's shelves if a fair deal is reached that protects Ontario's steel, auto, forestry, agriculture and manufacturing sectors.

Ford also said his message to Americans is that "a tariff on Canada is a tax on the American people."

"Remember, when it comes to the [U.S.] midterms, you have to get that bully and send him a message," Ford said.

Even in American alcohol does become available again, a number of Canadians previously told CBC News that they've no intention of buying any.

World.title: Powerful 7.7 magnitude quake hits off Indonesian coast
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. A powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early Saturday, damaging buildings and homes, and triggering a tsunami warning. Authorities urged people on affected coastlines to move to higher ground. The U.S Geological Survey said the quake hit Indonesia's Flores region with a depth of 10 kilometers at 5:58 a.m. Indonesia time. Its epicentre was 68 kilometres north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province. The initial quake was followed by several aftershocks. There were no immediate reports of casualties. Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores island. People flee their homes to seek safety in East Nusa Tenggara on Saturday. (Arnold Welianto/AFP/Getty Images) Residents along affected coastlines were advised to move to higher ground as officials are closely monitoring coastal tide gauges for any changes. The quake was felt across much of Flores island. Initial reports indicated there was damage to homes and public facilities, though officials had not yet released estimates of the number of damaged buildings or any casualties. Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground. "Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," she said. Notable quake, preliminary info: M 7.7 - 68 km NNW of Ende, Indonesia https://t.co/tXVeUk65Sg —USGS_Quakes Students at St. Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said the Rev. Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores. "Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Tanga said, "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake." Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the "Ring of Fire," an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin. In December of 1992, a magnitude 7 earthquake caused a tsunami that killed about 2,500 people on the southeastern island of Flores, part of a group of islands in the eastern half of Indonesia.

World.title: Ex-Cambridge professor who faced plagiarism claims, weeks of public scrutiny, found dead
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A British sociologist who resigned last week from the University of Cambridge following weeks of public accusations of plagiarism and media scrutiny was found dead Friday.

Jason Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023 at age 37, resigned after coming under intense media pressure over allegations of plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.

The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.

In a statement issued by his publisher, Simon & Schuster U.K., Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," the family said, adding that for three years Arday was "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse ... by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him."

The Metropolitan Police said only that a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead in Battersea, without naming the man, in accordance with its policy.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," the police statement said.

Cambridge Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university would investigate the circumstances surrounding Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.

"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.

In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

He said his stepping down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.

Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."

Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.

Cambridge opens investigation into accusations

Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.

On July 24, The Times published an analysis of Arday's 2015 PhD thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.

British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($7.4 million US) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.

Dozens of Cambridge academics had signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

The university then changed its stance and said it opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."

Prentice said this week that Cambridge would review its hiring processes. She stressed that "our staff of color are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community."

"This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge," she said Thursday.

World.content:

There was absolutely no reason for the United States to be running a trade deficit of $1.3 trillion and although the American administration has imposed tariffs in a gratuitously blunderbuss manner, there is nothing wrong with that country straightening out its accounts and putting the welfare of its own workforce ahead of others.
