World.title: Gibraltar orca Toñi found with 10 holes in fin: suspected shotgun blast
World.content:
Toñi is around 60 years old and is known among researchers as the "grandmother" of the orca population that moves between the Strait of Gibraltar and the Gulf of Cádiz. This week she has appeared with as many as a dozen marks on her dorsal fin and back which, according to the organisations that monitor her, were not there in the photographs taken a few weeks earlier.

 

It was the conservation group WeWhale that raised the alarm after comparing the animal’s current condition with its previous photographic record. Janek Andre, founder of WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians, said that the wounds now visible on the fin and back are, in his view, consistent with the impact of a shotgun blast.

The Atlantic Orca Working Group has gone further in its technical assessment. According to this collective, the injuries could correspond to lead pellets of around 9 millimetres, similar to those used in buckshot cartridges for wild boar, and it notes that this type of ammunition usually spreads nine projectiles in three rows of three, a pattern they consider to match the arrangement of the marks found on the animal.

Investigation under way

The Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge learned of the case on the afternoon of 11 August, through information submitted by WeWhale (source in Spanish), an organisation authorised to operate in the area. The following day, the Directorate-General for Biodiversity, Forests and Desertification opened preliminary proceedings to clarify the facts and, if appropriate, to launch a sanctions procedure against those responsible.

The vice-president and minister for the Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, confirmed via the social network Bluesky that the orca showed marks consistent with pellet shots and stressed that this is a vulnerable species, so any harm caused to it constitutes a serious offence.

La orca más longeva del Estrecho de Gibraltar ha aparecido esta semana con marcas compatibles con disparos de perdigones. Es una especie vulnerable y cualquier daño contra ella es un delito grave. 🔹 Desde el MITECO hemos abierto ya actuaciones de investigación para esclarecer lo ocurrido.



[image or embed] — Sara Aagesen (@saraaagesen.bsky.social) 14 de agosto de 2026 a las 8:04

CIRCE, the organisation that has been carrying out scientific monitoring of Iberian orcas since 1999 and holds a photographic archive of Toñi spanning more than two decades, has also joined this work.

The organisation has pointed out that, before determining the origin of the injuries, it is necessary to examine the available images in detail, compare them with the historical series and carry out fresh direct monitoring of the animal and its group.

For the time being, none of the authorities involved has officially confirmed that the wounds were caused by a shot, although this remains the main working hypothesis.

What the law says and how to act around an orca

The orca population of the Strait of Gibraltar and the Gulf of Cádiz is listed as vulnerable in the Spanish Catalogue of Endangered Species. Article 57 of Law 42/2007 on Natural Heritage and Biodiversity prohibits any action aimed at killing, capturing, pursuing or harassing the specimens included in that catalogue.

The specific rules on cetacean protection add further restrictions: no vessel may approach closer than 500 metres, make contact with the animals, swim with them, feed them, obstruct their path, split up groups or emit loud sounds to attract or scare them.

In the critical area of the Ensenada de Barbate, Conil and the Banco Majuán, orca watching is also banned between 1 March and 31 August. Anyone who breaches these measures faces fines of up to two million euros and criminal liability, according to MITECO itself.

Orca sighting areas in the Strait and Gulf of Cádiz MITECO

Since 2020 there has been an increase in interactions between these orcas and vessels sailing through the Strait and the Gulf of Cádiz. For this reason, the Ministry of Transport and MITECO recommend avoiding navigation in the area between April and August and, if there is an encounter with the animal, heading for the coast, avoiding any manoeuvre that could harm it, keeping people away from the gunwale and alerting the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.

The case of Toñi has once again turned the spotlight on this protected population. The organisations working in the area insist that these animals need protection, not reprisals.

World.title: Gut viruses are evolving new tricks to beat bacteria — and could help fight superbugs
World.content:
Viruses that selectively target and kill bacteria — also known as bacteriophages or simply phages — infect bacteria but leave human cells alone. Once they attach to a bacterial cell, they inject their genetic material, hijack the cell's machinery and force it to produce new phages until the bacterium bursts.

 

The problem is that bacteria can evolve defences against phages, just as they evolve resistance to antibiotics.

The new research suggests that phages have their own evolutionary countermeasure.

Some of the viruses living in the human gut can rapidly generate genetic variations among their offspring, increasing the chances that at least some will survive when bacteria fight back, according to the study, published Thursday in Nature Microbiology.

The finding could offer a new route in the search for alternatives to antibiotics, as drug-resistant infections become harder to treat.

Researchers at Michigan State University have identified previously underappreciated regions of bacteriophage genomes that act as genetic “hotspots”, allowing the viruses to repeatedly alter key genes as they replicate.

This suggests these regions help phages hedge their evolutionary bets against bacterial defences. Rather than producing a population of genetically identical viruses, they generate a diverse collection of offspring with different characteristics — increasing the odds that some can continue infecting and killing their bacterial hosts.

“This changes our understanding of how phages evolve,” said co-author Chris Waters, a faculty member in Michigan State University’s Ecology, Evolution, and Behavior program. “Instead of hijacking their hosts to mass produce exact copies of themselves, they are actually using these mutation hotspots to make a zoo,” he said, adding that phages are “essentially hedging their bets.”

Viruses that selectively target and kill bacteria — also known as bacteriophages or simply phages – infect bacteria but leave human cells alone. Canva

A genetic escape route

The researchers studied bacteriophage T2, which infects E. coli, after examining a bacterial defence system that can recognise and destroy invading phage DNA.

The team transferred the defence system into E. coli in the laboratory and exposed the bacteria to phages.

The protection did not last.

Within hours, the phages began overcoming the bacterial defences.

“Within a few hours, the phages always started to win,” Waters said. “We couldn’t understand why,” he added.

When researchers sequenced the resistant viruses, they found repeated mutations in a gene called agt, particularly in a stretch of repetitive DNA. “When I saw the data, I thought, oh my gosh,” Waters said.

That sequence turned out to be what scientists call a contingency locus — a highly mutable region where the DNA-copying machinery can slip when replicating repeated sequences.

The result is a reversible frameshift mutation that can change how the gene's instructions are read.

Some phages gain an extra repeat; others lose one. The result is a population containing different versions of the virus, potentially with different abilities to evade bacterial defences.

The researchers found that these repetitive regions accumulated mutations thousands of times faster than the rest of the phage genome.

And the mechanism is not confined to a single virus.

Using experimental evolution and genome sequencing, the researchers found similar contingency loci in E. coli phage T4. They also found that simple sequence repeats were widespread across diverse E. coli phages, although their abundance varied between genes with different functions.

Could it help treat superbugs?

The research comes as scientists and policymakers look for alternatives to antibiotics.

Phage therapy is not new. Phages were used therapeutically as early as the 1920s to treat bacterial infections, but interest in the approach declined after antibiotics such as penicillin became widely available.

Now the rise of antimicrobial resistance has revived interest.

The appeal is partly down to specificity. Whereas many antibiotics can kill beneficial bacteria alongside the pathogen they target, individual phages can be highly selective for particular bacterial species or strains.

But that specificity is also a weakness: bacteria can evolve resistance to a phage, potentially rendering a treatment ineffective.

The Michigan State findings raise the possibility that scientists could eventually exploit the viruses' own evolutionary strategies to make phage treatments more resilient.

“If we can harness these kinds of evolutionary tricks, we might be able to make more effective phage therapies in response to the antibiotic resistance crisis,” Waters said.

“We’re never going to be able to completely get rid of resistance,” he added. “But if we can better understand how bacteria protect themselves from phage infection and how phages fight back, we might be able to minimize it.”

World.title: From Gaza condoms to 'Your mom': Outgoing White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt's most divisive moments
World.content:
The Trump administration unexpectedly lost its megaphone this week, with the news of White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt resigning from her post to spend more time with her family.

 

Some have joked that her departure came days after Donald Trump left her and several members of his cabinet on a decoy plane that was supposedly targeted by a terrorist threat, while he was smuggled onto a secret flight out of Turkey.

The official line is that Leavitt will leave for personal reasons, saying on social media that since the birth of her second child, she’d realized she "cannot be the best mom" while devoting the “constant time, energy, and attention,” her job requires.

Regardless, what is certain is that she has outlasted many of her predecessors like Sean Spicer and Kayleigh McEnany. Throughout her 18-month tenure, the 28-year-old - and youngest person to ever hold the job - has proven to be a valuable asset for Donald Trump, who described her as "one of my most trusted aides".

She's also been incredibly divisive. For some, she's a staunch and unwavering Trump loyalist; others describe her as a dishonest and verbally abusive MAGA zealot.

The news of her quitting has been met with both disappointment from Trump's base, who know he will have a hard time replacing someone so fiercely dedicated to defending him throughout his many controversies, and cheers from those who routinely refer to her as "KKKaroline Leavitt".

Her time behind the White House podium has not been without controversy.

Whether it's attacking journalists and wishing to control press access to the White House, affirming proven falsehoods or hyperbolically praising Trump's achievements when opening her briefings, here is a lookback at five of Leavitt's most contentious moments.

Condoms in Gaza

Karoline Leavitt AP Photo

Even some of Karoline Leavitt's harshest critics have admitted that her vociferous defence of Trump has been impressive by the administration's standards. Some have also pointed out online that her deviations from facts and the truth have made then-Trump advisor Kellyanne Conway's "alternative facts" look innocent by comparison.

At her first-ever White House briefing, Leavitt announced that the Trump administration had foiled a plan to use taxpayer dollars to "fund condoms in Gaza.”

She stated that DOGE and the US Office of Management and Budget had “found that there was about to be 50 million taxpayer dollars that went out the door to fund condoms in Gaza.”

Trump repeated the claim, but added that the condoms were for Hamas.

Leavitt’s comments made headlines around the world - specifically because there was no evidence offered for this outlandish federal plan to spend millions on condoms in Gaza. Experts on US aid to Gaza and global health aid were baffled by the claim, with Steve Fake, a spokesperson for aid nonprofit Anera, telling CNN at the time that there was “definitely no purchase of condoms”.

“We have asked around, and no one is sure what this is referring to.”

The Associated Press beef

Karoline Leavitt AP Photo

In March 2025, AP reporter Josh Boak challenged Leavitt over Trump’s tariff policy, arguing that tariffs function as taxes on importers.

“He’s actually not implementing tax hikes,” said Leavitt. “Tariffs are a tax hike on foreign countries that, again, have been ripping us off. Tariffs are a tax cut for the American people, and the President is a staunch advocate of tax cuts.”

Boak pushed back by saying: “I’m sorry, have you ever paid a tariff? Because I have. They don’t get charged on foreign companies; they get charged on the importers.”

Leavitt replied by calling the question “insulting” and added: “I now regret giving a question to The Associated Press.”

For context, the exchange occurred during a broader dispute between the Trump administration and AP over the press agency's terminology.

Indeed, the Trump administration blocked them from accessing press events due to AP continuing to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by its actual title, as opposed to Trump's desire to rename it the "Gulf of America".

“It is a fact that the body of water off the coast of Louisiana is called the Gulf of America," said Leavitt, who defended AP's restrictions by saying she was holding news outlets accountable for reporting "lies".

The sanctions on AP were later lifted, but the incidents proved how keen Leavitt was on taking control over the press pool system, wishing to arbitrate who got access and who didn't. She later added MAGA personalities to the permanent press corps – podcasters and allies who didn't fall under her description of media outlets: "The press does only want to make the president look bad. That's it. That’s a fact."

Critics described these attempts as the "introduction of propagandists" and a way of undermining the core functions of the "Fourth Estate".

Leavitt defended herself and the administration by saying it was part of an effort to broaden access beyond traditional news organizations.

The viral "Your mom" jab

Karoline Leavitt AP Photo

Leavitt has constantly sparred with journalists she deemed to be "left-wing extremists" or "Trump haters", but one exchange went down like a lead balloon – leading many to label the president's inner circle as “moronic”, “childish” and “juvenile”.

Leavitt went viral last October when she shared an image of a text exchange with the HuffPost’s White House correspondent, S.V Dáte, on X.

At the time, Trump was planning to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Hungary.

"Is the president aware of the significance of Budapest?” asked Dáte in his message to Leavitt, adding: “In 1994, Russia promised, in Budapest, not to invade Ukraine if it gave up the nuclear weapons it inherited when the Soviet Union dissolved. Does he not see why Ukraine might object to that site?”

Dáte finished the message with the question “Who suggested Budapest?”, followed by a polite “Thanks.”

Leavitt replied: “Your mom did.”

She followed that up by labelling Dáte as a “far-left hack who nobody takes seriously" and added: “Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bulls*** questions."

In one trending reply, Leavitt showed to what extent she was keen to dismiss the press' function of holding presidents to account, and how little she cared about being measured in her responses to journalists she saw as being "anti-Trump".

The response also saw countless commentators online highlighting the hypocrisy of accusing a journalist of lacking seriousness and professionalism for a newsworthy question and answering with a reply more commonly found in playgrounds.

The Epstein files: A "hoax"

Karoline Leavitt AP Photo

Last November, Leavitt described the Epstein files as a “hoax that is being perpetuated by opportunistic Democrats”.

She went on to say that Trump knew Epstein because they both lived in Palm Beach and that Trump kicked him out of his Mar-a-Lago club because “Jeffrey Epstein was a paedophile and he was a creep.”

Earlier this year, in February, reporters pressed Leavitt about Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s relationship with Epstein, as Lutnick had acknowledged visiting Epstein’s private island in 2012 - despite previously saying he had ended the relationship years earlier.

Leavitt immediately responded by defending the Commerce Secretary as "a very important member of President Trump’s team" before criticising reporters for their questions.

“I will just point out that there are a lot of wins in the news this week that people in this room have not asked about because you continue to ask questions about the same subject so let me point them out for you,” Leavitt said.

She then began to recite recent stock market results and abruptly ended the press briefing with: “The President is very busy today and you will see him all tomorrow at the event in the East Room touting his Administration’s energy policy.”

She walked off stage to the bafflement of the press pool.

The ICE question by a "left-wing hack"

Karoline Leavitt AP Photo

In January 2026, The Hill columnist Niall Stanage questioned Leavitt about ICE, following the fatal shooting of Renee Nicole Good by an ICE agent.

Stanage listed statistics that 32 people died while in ICE custody in 2025 before referencing Good’s death.

Leavitt asked him: “Why was Renee Good unfortunately and tragically killed?”

Stanage replied: “Because an ICE agent acted recklessly and killed her unjustifiably.”

Leavitt's response was seen my many as deflection 101 and unacceptable.

“Okay, so you’re a biased reporter with a leftwing opinion,” she said. “Because you’re a leftwing hack. You’re not a reporter, you’re posing in this room as a journalist. And it’s so clear by the premise of your question. And you and the people of the media who have such biases but fake like you’re a journalist - you shouldn’t even be sitting in that seat.”

“You’re pretending like you’re a journalist, but you’re a leftwing activist,” she continued. “The question that you just raised and your answer proves you’re biased. You should be reporting on the facts.”

Leavitt will depart from the position as White House Press Secretary at the end of August. As of writing, there is no indication on who her replacement will be.

World.title: UK hits back after Netanyahu labels it 'the Islamic republic of Britain'
World.content:
The British government has reportedly hit back at comments by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu describing the UK "the Islamic republic of Britain."

 

A government spokesperson has labelled the remarks as "completely unacceptable" and said that the issue had been raised with the Israeli government.

Netanyahu made the comments during an army radio podcast interview, in which he also joked that the UK was the "first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons."

During the interview, the Israeli leader praised Randolph Churchill, the son of former British PM Winston Churchill, for positive coverage of Israel during the Six-Day War of 1967.

"Try and find that now, in what is called the Islamic republic of Britain," he said.

The host encouraged the point, saying: "Isn't all of Europe like that now?"

To which Netanyahu agreed, adding: "Yes, but someone said, 'the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons will be the Islamic republic of Great Britain.'"

"So, we'll make sure there isn't a second one here in Iran," he continued.

The Islamic Republic of Pakistan has been a nuclear power since 1998.

Netanyahu's comments echo similar claims made by politicians and activists on the British and international right, who claim that Britain is becoming increasingly influenced by Islam.

The UK and Israel's relationship has come under increasing strain in recent months, particularly since new British PM Andy Burnham's arrival in Downing Street.

A few weeks before taking over as prime minister, Burnham apologised for his Labour party's initial response to the war in Gaza and said that it needed to "do better."

While he condemned the Hamas militant group's "monstrous" October 7 attacks and "appalling" antisemitic incidents in the UK, he said it was vital to "be clear in our criticism of what has happened in Gaza."

"The unbearable suffering in Gaza is a scar on our collective conscience," Burnham said in early July.

"It's completely unacceptable that innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed," he continued, adding that Westminster must put more pressure on the Israeli government.

World.title: Crowds at Mont Blanc: will hiking soon require reservations?
World.content:
On particularly popular sections of Mont Blanc, hiking groups are now so close together that there is hardly any distance between them. At the same time, not all visitors show respect for nature. Local residents are complaining and consider the situation untenable.

 

Today we're moving along in single file. People can only see the backsides of those in front of them. Jean-Marc Peillex Mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains

"Today we're moving along in single file. People can only see the backsides of those in front of them. That's hardly ideal," said the mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, Jean-Marc Peillex, speaking to Swiss public broadcaster SRF. He is calling for access to the route to be restricted from next spring and for this to be enforced through checks and sanctions.

Saint-Gervais-les-Bains is on the French side of the Mont Blanc massif, in the Haute-Savoie department of the French Alps.

The town is an important starting point for tours in this area. The French access route to the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB) also runs through the region.

In future, anyone doing the Tour du Mont Blanc will have to reserve a place in a hut or an authorised bivouac zone. A bivouac zone is an officially designated area where hikers or mountaineers are allowed to spend the night outdoors on a temporary basis or pitch their tent.

Unlike in a hut, there is usually no infrastructure there, or only very basic facilities.

"If that is not possible, you postpone your plans to the following year," suggests Peillex.

Only a small part of the Tour du Mont Blanc runs through the municipality of Saint-Gervais. However, the other municipalities along the French section of the route are working together on the new rules and want to ensure that they come into force next spring.

Switzerland opts for coordination

Switzerland currently has no comparable plans to restrict access. Joachim Rausis, mayor of Orsières in the canton of Valais, also sees a need for action, but does not speak of pronounced overtourism. "There are warning signs, and we need to regulate things. But above all we need coordination between Switzerland, Italy and France," says Rausis.

Related Tourist guides raise the alarm as Europe braces for another heatwave

One thing is clear: the huge influx of visitors is also creating difficulties for mountain guides. "You have to reserve hotels and huts a year in advance. For someone self-employed, that is almost impossible," because as a self-employed mountain guide you rarely have clients who book a year ahead.

The debate highlights a fundamental problem of mountain tourism: how can the international popularity of the Alps be reconciled with the protection of nature and the interests of local people? A reservation requirement could slow the flow of visitors, but at the same time it would call into question the traditional idea that the mountains are freely accessible to everyone.

A mandatory reservation system would not be entirely new on Mont Blanc. On the French normal route to the summit, overnight stays in the Nid d’Aigle, Tête Rousse and Goûter huts already have to be booked via a special reservation system. The names of all participants must be provided, and the booking confirmation must be shown during checks.

The Goûter and Tête Rousse huts were open for the 2026 season until recently, but have been temporarily closed since 11 August 2026 because of the risk of rockfall.

World.title: In Turkey, one of the world's longest conflicts reaches a turning point
World.content:
Turkey stands on the threshold of closing a conflict spanning almost 50 years, after the Turkish parliament this week passed a law allowing exiled Kurdish militants to return home and rejoin society. The legislation aims to end the war with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has battled the Turkish state for independence since 1984.

Advertising

On Monday, legislators voted 468-88 in favour of a law detailing how the PKK will lay down arms, disband and guide most members back into civilian life.

Many see this legislation as a turning point after decades of bloodshed.

“This law in question is going to make a giant contribution,” predicts sociologist Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

“If the PKK militants are convinced that they can be safe in Turkey, it's estimated that some 15,000 people in Europe, in Syria, in Iraq and in the prisons in Turkey are going to be either released or are going to be able to come back home.”

The PKK leadership, based primarily in Iraq, is not covered by the legislation. Nor is the group's founder and leader Abdullah Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999 in a Turkish jail.

He initiated the peace process and last year called for the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK.

People hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Hope, caution

Istanbul, now the city's with the world’s largest Kurdish population, became a sanctuary in the 1990s as hundreds of thousands fled the violence raging in Turkey's southeast. At the conflict’s peak, the Turkish army destroyed villages in relentless scorched-earth campaigns.

In Istanbul's Bagcilar district, home to a vibrant Kurdish community, conversations reveal a fragile mix of hope and caution.

“This law seems good for the honour of the Kurds and to stop bloodshed,” said 31-year-old Ahmet, who only wanted to be identified by his first name. “Mothers should not shed tears anymore.”

But others were more wary. “The state has been delaying our rights for decades; I do not believe this process will be different,” said Kava, who also preferred not to give his full name. “I do not trust an arrangement in which Kurds do not have legal status.”

Kurds make up around a fifth of Turkey’s population, but are not legally recognised as a minority.

Emotions appear equally divided among Turks. “If they’re agreeing to live under the Turkish flag and love our country, that’s fine – let them,” said 51-year-old Mehmet Tas.

But 40-year-old Ertugral Zengin is unconvinced. “They committed a crime – and now they are to be pardoned? Do I want something like that? No, I won’t accept it.”

PKK ends 40-year fight but doubts remain about the next steps

Political momentum

The decades-long conflict has claimed 40,000 lives and forced more than 3 million people from their homes.

While major political parties support the peace process, hardline nationalist groups remain staunchly opposed, insisting it rewards a PKK they see as already defeated.

The process hinges on the laborious task of disarming the PKK and verifying its weapons are gone.

Maintaining the current political momentum is vital, warns Asli Aydintasbas, a Turkey expert at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC.

“If this drags on, political support for the legislation and for the return of former PKK members, seen by many Turks as terrorists, would become politically problematic for the government. Timing and moving fast is very important to achieve reconciliation,” she says.

The government is expected to face growing pressure to address Kurdish rights, including Kurdish-language education in schools and local autonomy, along with broader democratic reforms.

Social media buzzes with questions: how can PKK members walk free while critics of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan remain behind bars?

Kurdish demonstrators in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Peace or politics? Turkey’s fragile path to ending a decades-long conflict

Yegen warns that since the new legislation fails to address Kurdish rights and democratisation reforms, the government needs to move swiftly.

“The fact that these two issues are not touched upon by the law has created many doubts on both Kurdish and Turkish sides about whether disarmament will be the government's only agenda,” he says.

For Erdogan, steering the peace process to success could secure the vital Kurdish vote in the 2028 elections. Yet extending Kurdish cultural rights risks alienating Turkish nationalists, and relaxing pressure on the opposition brings its own perils as their electoral strength grows.

For now, the negotiations present a rare window for reconciliation and lasting peace.

World.title: Afghan allies still waiting for the safety Germany promised
World.content:
After the Taliban retook power on August 15, 2021, Berlin promised to bring Afghan staff to Germany. But people are still waiting to leave in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

It is hard to know which promise from German politicians the "local staff" — Afghans who assisted German efforts in the country — relied on most. Perhaps that from then-Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, who on August 26, 2021, 11 days after the Taliban took power, said: "Our work continues until all those for whom we carry responsibility in Afghanistan are safe."

By June 2026, more than 37,000 Afghan nationals had arrived in Germany since the Taliban retook power. These are people who worked alongside Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces or German aid programs, plus their relatives. It also includes people who are especially at risk, such as activists and journalists who advocated for human rights and against the Taliban.

For Ahmad Samid, who worked for the Bundeswehr as an audio engineer, Germany kept its promise. For Javad Niazi, who worked for the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), it did not. He remains stuck in the city of Peshawar in Pakistan. Both are using false names because they still fear the Taliban and possible repercussions for themselves and their families.

Hundreds of Afghans still waiting

Samid works as a receptionist at a hotel in a large German city and told DW in very good German: "I am very grateful to Germany. But if someone says, 'I will help you,' then it must remain that way. One must keep a promise."

In August 2026, 5 years after the Taliban quickly seized back power in Afghanistan, it seems that Germany no longer wants to know about the big promises it made.

In the case of Javad Niazi, Germany has, one must say, broken its promise. He is in the same position as 600 other Afghans who are desperately holding out in Peshawar and in Kabul, continuing to hope that they can leave for Germany. He and his family say they feel trapped in a small cage, he told DW. Their savings have been used up, he has no residence permit for Pakistan and he cannot leave his temporary accommodation for fear of Pakistani security forces, who arrest and deport Afghan nationals daily.

"My 14-year-old son goes shopping when it gets dark here. We cannot go to any bazaar, park, or hospital; my children cannot go to school. It is an enormous strain on us. We never would have thought that a country like Germany would take back its decision, it's unbelievable."

Afghan refugees at risk as deportations surge in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

New government does not want to take in any more local staff

Taking back its decision, as Javad Niazi put it, is what the new German government, comprising the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz did in May 2025 with its coalition agreement to scrap the resettlement programs.

Half a year later, those who had been left behind appealed to the chancellor directly for help in a two-page letter calling for help: "We wanted and needed to escape Taliban rule to survive. We cannot go back to Afghanistan. It would end brutally and violently for many of us," they wrote.

But the German government remains firm and, in the meantime, is cooperating with the Taliban "on a technical level" via the Afghan diplomatic mission in Germany to send Afghan nationals who have committed crimes in Germany back to Afghanistan — and recently also the first person from Afghanistan with no criminal record.

German Foreign Minister Alexander Dobrindt offered the waiting Afghans money in exchange for forgoing their departure to Germany. A one-time payment of up to €2,500 ($,2887) before departure, up to €10,000 for a return to Afghanistan or a third country, plus medical care, board and lodging for several months. So far, 300 people have accepted this offer and in doing so given up on a future in Germany.

Afghan migrants stuck in Pakistan reject German cash offer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fate of local staff also depends on German courts

Since then, the issue of the future of the 600 waiting Afghans has been primarily dealt with via the court system. In July 2026, Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled: The German government's blanket decision revoking the admission programme for at-risk Afghan citizens is in breach of the constitutional prohibition of arbitrariness. Each person's specific case and individual interests must be considered.

In response to questions from DW, the German Interior Ministry maintains it is in the right: "The Federal Constitutional Court largely aligns with the Federal Government's argument that declarations around admissions can be revoked if political interests change. However, the Federal Constitutional Court also instructs the Interior Ministry to consider affected people's individual circumstances when making such decisions."

According to the Interior Ministry, the Federal Constitutional Court allows broad leeway for political decision-making when deciding on the admission of foreign nationals.

German aid organization continues support

For Javad Niazi, the trepidation about his and his family's future continues. He would probably have given up long ago if not for the support of Kabul-Luftbrücke (Kabul Air Bridge). In response to the chaos at Kabul airport 5 years ago, the German non-governmental organization arranged a charter plane to fly 18 people out of Afghanistan. Since then, it has rescued 4,424 people from the Taliban, mostly overland to Pakistan.

Eva Beyer, who had worked as a filmmaker in Afghanistan, recalled the organization's 2021 beginning to DW: "We chartered this plane, flew to Kabul and could haul out a few people. And then we realized, actually the work is just beginning. From early 2022 — I was then in Pakistan — there I organized the land transport on the Pakistani side, took in the people at the border and looked after them in Islamabad. What was originally planned to be 4 weeks has now become 5 years."

Recently, Kabul-Luftbrücke has mainly focused on providing legal advice and support to Afghans. With success: They have won more than 200 lawsuits, and as a result, 1,018 people have been able to travel to Germany since September 1, 2025.

"About 75% of the people who are now still waiting are women and children. That means for all these women and children, who are not attending school, who can no longer build an independent life or pursue a career, the way to a secure future has been blocked," Beyer said.

She advocates for people who have already passed all security checks to quickly receive a visa. "There are also people who already had a visa in their passport and those whose visa had already been issued, but at the last minute they could not take the flight because it was canceled."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Donald Trump's Latin America allies open arms to Israel
World.content:
While the ongoing military actions in Gaza and settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank have largely isolated Israel globally, Latin America's authoritarian right sees an opening for a strategic alliance.

In 2009, Venezuela's Socialist president, Hugo Chavez, expelled the ambassador of Israel to protest the country's three-week military offensive in the Gaza Strip, which killed more than 1,400 people, including an estimated 1,100 civilians, severing diplomatic relations between the countries. Seventeen years later, Venezuela and Israel have agreed to establish a mechanism for the resumption of consular services. It's a limited step, but one that until recently would have been unthinkable.

In Colombia, the nationalist government of new President Abelardo de la Espriella reversed the decision by his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, to sever diplomatic relations with Israel in protest of the country's most recent war in Gaza, which killed more than 70,000 people, nearly one-third of them children. De la Espriella has even announced that Colombia will relocate its embassy to Jerusalem, and this week declared that Colombia would join the United States as the only two countries that recognize "Israeli sovereignty" over the Golan Heights, which is Syrian territory under international law, but has been occupied by Israel since 1967. The vast majority of the international community, including Germany and the UN, does not recognize the annexation of the Golan Heights by Israel.

"There is a trend toward rapprochement with Israel as a response to the surge of the radical right in the region," said Isaac Caro, a professor at Alberto Hurtado University in Chile. Caro said authoritarians in Latin America were linking relations with Israel to "an active alignment with US foreign policy." He said reinforcing ties with Israel had become a characteristic of Latin America's radical right in the region as part of the renewed discourse of region's place in Judeo-Christian Western civilization.

In Argentina, for example, ultraconservative President Javier Milei has made close relations with Israel a defining feature of both his foreign policy and his own political identity.

Daniel Wajner, associate professor of international relations at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said there had been a "surge" in diplomacy between Israel and Latin American governments. Wajner said Jair Bolsonaro, the neoliberal former president of Brazil, and El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the self-described "world's coolest dictator," were early adopters of warmer ties with Israel. They were followed by Milei and others.

Wajner said Latin America's authoritarians were actively "embracing" the national-conservative government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. He also said there were ideological, religious and strategic factors in governments' tightening of bonds with the country, such as the desire to signal a like-minded international orientation with the United States.

Gilberto Aranda, a political analyst from the University of Chile, said there had been a trend in Latin America of authoritarians' aligning with the United States under Donald Trump — and therefore also engaging in rapprochement with Israel.

Israel has sent more troops to the West Bank as settler attacks continue Image: Mussa Qawasma/REUTERS

Colombia's 'fundamental shift'

In 2024, under Petro, Colombia broke off relations because of the war in Gaza. In the week since de la Espriella assumed office on August 7, Caro said, there has been a "fundamental shift" in Colombia's foreign policy.

In Venezuela, the stated policies of the current government, which took power after US forces abducted the sitting president in early January, remain rooted in the socialist populism of Chavismo. However, the resumption of consular services has proved a symbolic diplomatic success for Israel.

Bolivia's Socialist government severed relations with Israel after the bombardment of a camp for displaced people in Gaze in 2023. When the conservative Rodrigo Paz assumed office 2025, he quickly restored them.

In Chile, the democratic socialist former president, Gabriel Boric, was highly critical of Netanyahu and his government. His successor, the national conservative, Jose Antonio Kast, is seeking, among other things, to revive Chile's defense cooperation with Israel.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brazil and Mexico

In Brazil, the social democratic government of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has taken a highly critical stance toward Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.

"The country with the most influence in the region, which maintains a critical stance toward Israel, is clearly Brazil," Aranda said. Brazil's demographic, economic and political clout are a major counterweight to the shift by other Latin American governments toward warmer relations with Israel.

Then there is Mexico, the other giant of Latin America. Whereas Lula, in Brazil, is particularly critical, Mexico, under President Claudia Sheinbaum, is trying to preserve greater neutrality as well as a diplomatic balance. Sheinbaum criticizes Israel's actions in Gaza, but she still maintains diplomatic relations. This shows that criticism of the Netanyahu government does not inevitably signify the breakdown of relations with the state of Israel.

Still, given the recent mass killings in Gaza, the shift in Israel relations with some governments in Latin America is significant. Israel is not just interested in winning over friendly governments. These bilateral relationships date back to the foundation of the state in 1948, and cover migration, trade, and security. The support of Latin America in multilateral organizations such as the United Nations has always been key in countering Israel's international isolation.

Wajner said Latin American governments' current warming of ties with Israel offered both sides "legitimacy, cooperation and influence." Israel needs international partners, and Latin American goverments also offer opportunities for economic, technological and military cooperation. For its part, Latin America can turn to Israel as a strong partner in areas such as cyber security, artificial intelligence, and defense.

Though Israel has managed to forge new bonds in Latin America for now, long-term relations will continue to depend on who is in power, where and when.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: India: Modi promises free exam coaching, AI training for youth after protests
World.content:
Speaking on India's Independence Day, PM Modi announced free online coaching for competitive exams and AI training for 10 million youths, weeks after protests over alleged exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on India's Independence Day announced training in artificial intelligence (AI) skills as well as free online coaching for young people for competitive exams just weeks after youth-led protests over exam paper leaks and recruitment irregularities.

Speaking at the Red Fort in New Delhi on Saturday, Modi said the coaching initiative would help ease the financial burden on poor and middle-class families.

"The competition surrounding coaching classes has become a huge burden for middle-class families," Modi said, adding that students could stay with their families while preparing for exams.

Modi's promise comes as last month the country was rocked by protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over alleged irregularities in competitive exams.

The protests ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan highlighting widespread concerns over access to education and jobs.

10 million youths to train in AI skills

The Indian prime minister also said 10 million young people would receive training in AI skills over the next year, in a move to appease the nation's youth that forced the Modi government to face its biggest challenge since coming to power in 2014.

Modi also said India will have eight more semiconductor chip plants in the coming years and five nuclear reactors which will generate 100 gigawatts of power by 2047.

In a speech lasting more than an hour, Modi outlined a seven-point growth and reform framework aimed at making India a developed country within 20 years. The plan focuses on manufacturing, agriculture, technology, defense and sectors including tourism and handicrafts.

Modi warns against 'intellectual Naxals'

At the same time, Modi also took aim at the latest enemy of the state — the "intellectual Naxals."

This was a reference to India's Naxal movement, which waged a guerrilla-style insurgency against the government, particularly in central and eastern India, leaving thousands dead and injured over nearly 60 years.

Modi said his government had defeated the armed movement but warned that the fight against the "Naxal mentality" remained, as its adherents looked for "opportunities to create violence and unrest."

Modi said these "intellectual Naxals" had to be identified and isolated to connect young people with the mainstream. Modi did not specify who these "intellectual Naxals" were in his speech.

In the past, Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has labelled rights activists, academics and intellectuals, journalists, political opponents, government critics and others with left-wing views as "urban Naxals."

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Germany news: Russia lists research body as 'undesirable'
World.content:
08/15/2026 August 15, 2026 Heightened security planned at Berlin techno parade

The Techno Parade, some of whose participants are seen here in 2023, is a major spectacle Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

The techno parade Rave the Planet is expected to draw tens of thousands of people in Berlin in Saturday, with police stepping up security at the event after last month's Islamist attack on fringes of the Pride march in the capital.

Participants in the parade will also have to contend with high temperatures of up to 37 C (98.6 F).

Police say they will deploy at least one water cannon to spray a cooling water mist and free drinking water is to be made available along the route of the parade, organizers have said.

The parade is to start in the early afternoon and run until late in the evening.

It is planned to run along the main boulevard through the Tiergarten park, between the Brandenburg Gate and the Victory Column, close to the site of the July 25 attack, in which an Islamist assailant killed a woman and injured at least 31 people, some seriously.

A police spokeswoman said some 1,500 officers would be deployed at the event, with Berlin police supported by colleagues from the states of Brandenburg and Saxony-Anhalt.

The techno parade was first held in Berlin in 2022 to celebrate electronic music culture and has taken place every year since then.

Organizers have registered 300,000 participants, though police have put the number closer to 100,000 at previous parades.

World.title: US: FDA recalls 19 million eggs over Salmonella risk
World.content:
The US has issued a serious health warning over the recalled eggs, saying exposure to the potentially contaminated products could cause severe illness or death.

Around 19 million eggs have been recalled in the United States over possible Salmonella contamination, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has said.

Midwest Poultry Services (MPS) voluntarily recalled 1,589,577 dozen eggs on July 22 after detecting potential Salmonella Enteritidis contamination at two Texas farms, the FDA said.

MPS Egg Farms said on its website that it had proactively recalled the eggs as a precautionary measure and initiated testing protocols to identify potential sources of Salmonella.

On Wednesday, the FDA said it was a Class 1 recall, indicating a reasonable probability of serious illness or death.

What did the FDA say about the egg recall?

The eggs were produced between June 6 and July 3 and distributed in the states of Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico and Mississippi.

These included both white shell eggs and brown cage-free shell eggs.

They were sold under several brand names, with sell-by or best-by dates from July 20 to August 17.

According to the FDA advisory :

Consumers should throw away the recalled eggs or return them for a refund

Restaurants and retailers should not serve or sell the eggs

Consumers, restaurants, and retailers who purchased or received recalled eggs should carefully clean and sanitize any surfaces or containers that the recalled eggs touched.

World.title: Indonesia: Strong earthquake hits off coast of Flores island
World.content:
At least 20 people have died and several buildings were damaged after the powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake, which was followed by dozens of aftershocks. A tsunami warning has been lifted.

A powerful earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 20 people and toppling buildings, authorities said.

At least two people were known to be trapped alive under rubble, rescue official Fathur Rahman told AFP news agency.

The epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), the US Geological Survey (USGS) said.

Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the country before the warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

Where did the earthquake strike?

Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded the first quake at 4:58 am (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 ⁠miles), followed by dozens of aftershocks.



People rushed out onto the street as the quake struck Image: Arnold Welianto/AFP

Video shared on social media from Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, showed part of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street.

"Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the Pelni port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, told AP.

Residents evacuated, tsunami warning lifted

The initial jolt was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same area, including one of magnitude 6.1.

Tourists evacuate after their hotel was severely damaged Image: REUTERS

BMKG issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.

The tsunami warning was later lifted.

Rescue workers searching for survivors in the rubble of a destroyed building Image: BASARNAS/AP Photo/picture alliance

"We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," Wijayanto, earthquake and tsunami director at BMKG, said.

Before the tsunami warning was lifted, residents of Maumere on Flores Island were told to move to higher ground, according to AFP.

State television also showed hundreds of people evacuating in nearby Nagekeo regency.

Local TV footage showed a hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province moving patients outside.

Patients and medical staff evacuated from a health center Image: Arnold Welianto/AFP

Authorities assessing damage, casualties

The quake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, causing power outages in cities and villages, severely hindering rescue operations.

"We are continuing to collect reports of damages and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko said.

Local television reports showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution.

"Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of Ritapiret Seminary on Flores said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake."

There were also damages reported in some part of southern Sulawesi island.

Indonesia's history of earthquakes

Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan.

Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region:

1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people

A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people 2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean

A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean 2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa

A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa 2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Donald Trump to declare Hormuz US territory 'soon'
World.content:
Donald Trump said the strait would become part of the US after Iran is defeated. He also told Americans to accept higher gas prices, which have soared since Iran closed Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.

President Donald Trump said Friday that he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.

"After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump said at a rally at a police academy in Garden City, New York state. "It's true," he added.

It was not clear whether his remarks were serious or whether they signal a new policy shift for Washington in its war against Tehran, which is more than five months old.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed Trump's remarks, saying the country would "not be intimidated" and that the strategic waterway would remain under its control and authority.

What is the situation in the Strait of Hormuz?

The US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28. At the time, senior White House officials, including Trump, said the aim was to end Iran's nuclear program and spark a popular uprising to force regime change in the Islamic Republic, among other goals.

Iran's response has been to target US allies across the Middle East with drone and missile strikes, as well as to impose a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments passed before the war.

The US responded to Iran's closure of the strait with its own naval blockade of Iranian ships and ports. The two countries have been locked in a stalemate over the vital waterway for months, causing energy prices to soar.

Rising oil and gas costs and the economic fallout from the war are likely to be leading issues in the midterm elections in November.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What else did Trump say during the rally in Garden City?

During the rally, the US president also urged Americans to accept that they would have to "pay a tiny little bit more" for their gasoline as a worthy price for preventing "a very evil country" from getting a nuclear weapon.

"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a ​great job," Trump told the crowd, adding that "no ships get through (the US blockade of Hormuz) unless we want them to."

On Friday, Trump also dismissed concerns over the living conditions aboard a US aircraft carrier that was deployed to the Middle East amid the war with Iran.

Relatives of service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln told US military media outlets that personnel are struggling with difficult living conditions and deteriorating mental health. There have also been reports of suicide attempts.

Trump denied that the deployment of the aircraft carrier , which has been at sea for nine months, had lasted too long, instead insisting that the aircraft carrier's deployment was "not nearly enough."

He also confirmed that the ship would be replaced by another "very similar" vessel.

World.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to let White House ballroom construction continue
World.content:
Justice Department lawyers echoed the US president's claim that the $400 million White House ballroom ​project is a security necessity.

The Trump administration on Friday asked the US Supreme Court to allow construction to continue on the president's $400 million White House ballroom.

It comes a week after an appeals court ruled Donald Trump's ballroom project, planned for the site of the White House's East Wing after it was demolished, lacked congressional approval and ordered above-ground construction to stop.

"This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security," Trump's Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court.

Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.

Trump assassination attempts and flight from Turkey mentioned

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the case after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom.

In a 2-1 ruling on August 7, the DC Circuit upheld a lower-court judge's order directing the administration to halt above-ground construction.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the appeals court panel wrote.

To justify the need for a secure ballroom, Justice Department lawyers pointed to the July 8 missile threat against Air Force One when Trump was flown out of Turkey aboard a secret flight and other recent assassination attempts.

The filing also claims the project is on time and under budget, funded by about $400 million in private donations. Democrats, however, say Trump's tax law is helping pay for the ballroom, while lawmakers in Congress have not approved a request by the administration for additional funding.

The ballroom is part of a broader set of projects planned by Trump for Washington D.C., including upgrades to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool as well as the construction of a large arch Image: Nathan Howard/REUTERS

Responding to the petition, the trust accused the White House of trying to "outrun the courts" by accelerating construction. It cited plans to install 1 million pounds (453,592.37 kilograms) of rebarand pour 3,000 cubic yards (81,000 cubic feet, 2,293.66 cubic meters) of concrete over the next week.

"The Administration's transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here," the plaintiffs said.

The National Trust has urged the Supreme Court to reject the administration's appeal.
