World.title: An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.content:
“My contact lenses are comfortable even after wearing them all day. Do you want to try them?”

So says a young woman in glasses with transparent lenses, in response to a friend who says her contacts are painful. She then takes a contact box out of a black handbag, offers it, and says, “You can blink without worry.”

The endorsement seems genuine enough — except neither woman is real.

This , featuring the popular AI actress Fang Taozi endorsing colored contacts, has recently sparked controversy in China over whether an AI character can vouch for a product’s quality.

Released in late July on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by domestic contact lens brand Nutnutlook, the ad was taken down without comment last week.

In response, Chinese netizens criticized the  for using an AI avatar instead of a human actress. “What makes me uncomfortable is that someone without eyes now has the right to speak about eyes,” one user commented.

“AI doesn’t even know what it feels like to actually wear the product,” another wrote.

Neither the company behind the AI actress, Guangzhou-based World Media Film and TV Culture, nor the contacts brand has responded to the controversy.

The fictional 20-year-old Fang Taozi was unveiled in the AI short drama “The Laid-off Girl” in June this year. The series, which tells the story of a small-town girl moving to a fictional city to pursue a modeling career, has been viewed more than 320 million times on Douyin.

In the months following the series’ release, directed by popular content creator Fei Feifei, Fang’s personal Douyin account — created by companies to boost AI actors’popularity — gained more than 470,000 followers. Her account posts content ranging from so-called “behind-the-scenes” footage during the show’s production to snippets of her supposed daily life, such as making breakfast.

Fang has been lauded by fans for having, unlike many AI characters, moles and blemishes, giving her an imperfect and realistic appearance. In “The Laid-off Girl,” she struggles with relatable Chinese workplace challenges, such as pressure to attend business dinners and getting bullied by her colleagues.

Domestic media reported that on Juliang Xingtu, Douyin’s influencer marketing platform, Fang Taozi’s advertising rates are 168,000 yuan ($24,900) per video for clips under 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan for videos between 21 and 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan for videos over 60 seconds — significantly higher than ad rates charged by most human influencers.

Ma Lihong, a senior partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, told domestic media that, despite AI avatars not being considered people under Chinese law and therefore not legally considered  endorsers, the video could still constitute false advertising.

Ma added that advertisers are responsible for the truthfulness of their content and that by making a first-person claim about experiencing a product, the AI character could be seen as fabricating user experience. As such, the brand and the ’s producer could potentially be in violation of the law.

Compounding the severity of the issue, colored contact lenses are classified as Class III medical devices under China’s regulatory system, reserved for items that pose the highest risk to consumers. Actors are prohibited from recommending such products in s, a rule aimed at preventing brands from misleading consumers.

This is not the first time Chinese brands have experimented with AI-generated figures in advertising. Major bottled water company Nongfu Spring made headlines last year for using AI-generated images in promotional posters, while companies ranging from yogurt brands to office chair suppliers have collaborated with various AI-generated actors to endorse products and use slogans. Tutorials on using AI-generated videos for livestream commerce have also become common.

Entertainment law expert Qiu Zhimiao said AI-powered endorsements will become increasingly common, and regulating them is a new frontier. As s endorsed by virtual influencers exist in a legal gray area, he said, there is a need for clearer regulations.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of the AI actress Fang Taozi in the  promoting colored contact lenses. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.title: 1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.content:
On a rain-washed weekend morning, mist clings to the peaks surrounding Ze’e Village in the southwestern Sichuan province. Over the sound of a rushing mountain stream, 24-year-old Jifu Lama leads a procession of children in matching kits. They navigate through rice paddies, along irrigation canals and over earthen mounds until they reach their destination: a soccer pitch carved out of a former cornfield.

Perched halfway up a mountain at an altitude of 1,300 meters, Lama’s pitch looks like a vibrant green terraced field folded into the sweeping landscape of Sichuan’s Daliangshan region. Standing in the center circle, the young coach directs his players — mostly children aged 6 to 13 from six neighboring Yi ethnic villages — to lace up their boots, arrange the cones and begin their warm-ups.

Ze’e Village is remote, accessible only by winding mountain roads, but the children’s imaginations stretch far beyond the peaks. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, the young athletes devoured match highlights on smartphones. Winning and losing are secondary to the star players: the children argue passionately over the goals scored by superstars like Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi and Harry Kane.

Seven-year-old Aluo, a first-grader with lightning-fast footwork, idolizes France’s Mbappé. His cousin, Yang Xiaojun, a skinny third-grader, became a die-hard Gareth Bale fan after watching a clip of the Welshman’s legendary bicycle kick.

When they score on this mountain pitch, the kids leap into the air, spinning to land in Cristiano Ronaldo’s iconic, arms-down “Siu” celebration.

For these children, soccer is bright spot in childhood marked by economic hardship. Local data shows rural per capita income in Daliangshan is around just 12,700 yuan ($1,770) a year. To make a living, parents migrate to factories in the southern Guangdong province, Wuhan in the central Hubei province, and the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, returning only once a year for the traditional Yi New Year.

Raised by aging grandparents in households with multiple siblings, these “left-behind” children have few outlets for their energy. A piece of candy or a lucky draw at the school gate used to be the highlight of their week. Now, soccer offers them friendship, structure and a window to the outside world.

To keep them invested, Lama implemented a reward system. Players earn four points for every practice they attend, which they can exchange for free gear. That is how Hu Feifei, one of the girls who recently joined the squad, earned her jersey, socks and boots.

Hu remembers when the pitch was nothing but sand dumped over uneven soil. When it rained, they played in puddles and went home with scraped knees, but they were happy. Today, thanks to a corporate sponsor moved by the team’s story, they play on an artificial turf pitch that Lama proudly claims is “better than the ones in the county town.”

The sponsor discovered them because of Lama, who is no stranger to the spotlight. But his viral fame is a chapter of his life tinged with both pride and heartbreak.

Lama’s obsession began in middle school when a friend gifted him a Neymar Barcelona jersey. The self-described rebellious teen found his anchor in soccer. To play, he transferred to a vocational school with a pitch.

To master the game, he did the unthinkable and dropped out, hiked to an altitude of 2,000 meters, and built a wooden hut on a flat peak. There, with no electricity and relying on a wood fire to cook, he trained alone for days at a time. His goal was to become a professional soccer player within five years.

He documented his solitary, high-altitude drills on short-video platforms. The stark contrast between the primitive, breathtaking environment and the boy’s fluid footwork captivated the internet. He amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, drawing the attention of FIFA on the eve of the 2022 Qatar World Cup. At his peak, he was earning up to 6,000 yuan a month from his videos.

But soon this felt wrong, money was not why he played soccer. “It felt like I was using soccer to make a profit,” Lama says. “It betrayed my original love for the game.”

However, his online presence earned him a spot in professional tryouts. It was here that Lama’s dream collided with reality. “My technique was too poor, I couldn’t understand the tactics, and my receiving and passing were all wrong,” he said.

In May 2023, he finally earned a spot with Jingchuan Wenhui, a fourth-tier club in the Chinese Champions League. Stepping onto the pitch, the cheers of the fans made the experience feel unreal.

It lasted exactly 45 minutes. Half a match that Lama doesn’t dare to rewatch. “My muscles were constantly tense, and I felt I performed too poorly,” he said.

The experience made clarified the insurmountable chasm between himself and real professional players, he said he could “never keep up with the rhythm and physical confrontation.”

The failure was a brutal watershed moment. But instead of continuing to chase trials across the country, Lama packed his bags and looked back to the dirt fields of Ze’e Village.

Today, he serves as an unpaid, unofficial soccer coach for two local primary schools. He runs training sessions five days a week and spends his weekends driving his minivan across the mountains to ferry kids to and from practice.

The transition from viral star to grassroots coach hasn’t been easy. The internet money has dried up, and his public welfare coaching model is financially unsustainable. He is considering charging a modest annual fee of 1,200 yuan for new recruits this fall, but he agonizes over whether the cost will price out the very kids who need the game most. He regularly visits skeptical parents, trying to convince them that soccer isn’t a distraction, but a vital tool for development.

“I want these children to start changing from this generation,” Lama said. “I want them to learn manners and be driven.”

In a region where educational resources are sparse and academic struggles are common, Lama sees soccer as a safety net. His vision is already bearing fruit: four of his sixth-graders recently passed a specialized sports exam, securing them spots in a superior middle school in the county town.

Eventually, Lama plans to build a fully registered professional club. He has already chosen the name: Leke, the Yi word for plowshare.

It is a fitting moniker for a young man breaking tough ground. “I don’t even have a first team yet,” Lama said, looking out over the mist-covered pitch. “I’ve only just lifted my foot to take the first step, and it hasn’t even landed yet.”

This piece was originally published by Caixin Global. It is republished here with permission.

Reporter: Zheng Haipeng.

(Header image: Players from Jijia Primary School pose for a group photo, imitating the signature moves of their favorite soccer stars, Ze’e Village, Sichuan province, June 2026. Zheng Haipeng/Caixin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: New challenge: Why BT Toews wants to coach Gilas Women
World.content:
After decades in Japan where he helped shape its thriving women’s basketball scene, Burke "BT" Toews hopes to do the same in the Philippines, convinced that Gilas Women have what it takes to reach new heights

The quest for a new challenge has led Burke “BT” Toews to coach Gilas Women.

After decades in Japan where he helped shape its thriving women’s basketball scene, the 60-year-old mentor hopes to do the same in the Philippines, convinced that Gilas Women have what it takes to reach new heights.

Toews takes over the coaching reins from Patrick Aquino, whose decade-plus tenure with Gilas Women saw the team achieve several milestones and multiple firsts.

Under Aquino, Gilas Women ruled three of the last four Southeast Asian Games, earned promotion to the Division A of the FIBA Women’s Asia Cup, and beat a non-Asian team for the first time when they stunned Colombia in the FIBA Women’s World Cup Qualifying Tournament in March.

While those accomplishments reflect a steady growth, Toews believes there is still another level for Gilas Women to unlock.

“I’m very familiar with all the teams in Asia, whether they’re national team or pro team. And of all the teams that I thought about — and I’ve had some other offers in Asia to coach national teams — I thought that the Philippines, the women’s, were a team that had a really high ceiling,” said Toews.

“Not just because of what happened in the last few years with coach Pat and the success they had. But if things could be changed not just on the court but off the court, I thought that the Philippines could really get to the top tier and be a perennial contender.”

Change of scenery

Originally from Canada, Toews moved to the Land of the Rising Sun, where he carved out a prolific career as head coach of the Fujitsu Red Wave in the Women’s Japan Basketball League.

Across his two stints with the Red Wave spanning nearly a decade — first from 2014 to 2016 and again from 2018 to 2025 — Toews steered Fujitsu to five finals appearances and two championships.

Following three unsuccessful bids for the elusive crowns, the Red Wave finally broke through in 2023–24 and successfully defended their title in 2024–25, with Toews earning Coach of the Year honors in both seasons.

But even with his success in Japan, Toews left Fujitsu in 2025 in pursuit of new horizons elsewhere.

“It seemed like kind of a strange time to step down as a coach at the peak of my Spider-Man powers, so to speak. I really felt strongly at this stage of my career, I still had some personal goals that were more than just championships,” said Toews.

Toews made Japan his home.

He married Eiko, a Japanese national, and their two sons, Kai and Luka, have followed in his basketball footsteps, representing Japan on the international stage.

A change of scenery, however, felt necessary.

“I accomplished two things right there: I got the job of the Philippines, and second of all, I’m able to coach in English. The third thing was I wanted to live outside of Japan because I’ve been there for 30-some years. I think it’s 35, actually. Both my wife and I wanted to experience a different country in Asia, so that brings me here,” he said.

Built over time

When it comes to women’s basketball in Asia, Japan is a prime example of sustained development.

Ranked outside the world top 15 in 2015, Akatsuki Japan made consistent improvements that culminated in a historic silver medal in the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

It marked the first time an Asian team won an Olympic medal in women’s basketball since China bagged silver as well in the 1992 Barcelona Games.

Japan also reached the finals in each of the last seven Women’s Asia Cup editions, capturing five consecutive championships from 2013 to 2021 before settling for runner-up finishes in 2023 (lost to China) and 2025 (lost to Australia).

The philosophies that have made Japan a force to be reckoned with are among the lessons Toews hopes the Filipinas can learn from.

“I scouted the Philippines for a long time, even before I got this job, even more so after. My impressions and my take is accurate, I believe. It shouldn’t be news to anybody. I think that the players’ individual offensive skills are very good, in some ways better than Japanese players’ individual skill,” said Toews.

“But the Japanese, to make a direct comparison, play with the team, in every sense. They sprint together, they play defense together, they’re all in charge of stopping the ball, they’re all on a string. Offensively, the ball moves quickly, people are cutting and flying all over the place. It’s dizzying.”

Although Toews brings with him the practices and principles that have contributed to the rise of Japanese women’s basketball, having coached national team players such as Rui Machida, Yuki Miyazawa, and Monica Okoye at Fujitsu, he wants Gilas Women to forge an identity of their own.

“I don’t want to say that we can just bring what Japan does to the Philippine national team, to Gilas. Not only should you not copy someone completely because you lose the essence of the players that you’re coaching and what they do well, but at the same time, I feel like there’s a lot of areas that we can tune up and we will imitate,” he said.

And success takes time, as Toews learned during his second stint with Fujitsu.

The Red Wave finished seventh in 2018-19, placed third in the next two seasons, fell short of the crown in 2021-22, and slipped to sixth in 2022-23 before going on to win back-to-back championships.

“It doesn’t happen overnight,” he said.

Long road ahead

Toews gets to see how far Gilas Women have come since he took over the helm in June as the Philippines takes part in the FIBA Women’s Olympic Pre-Qualifying Tournament in Mexico scheduled from August 17 to 23.

Currently ranked 30th in the world, the Filipinas will take on No. 7 Canada, No. 22 Senegal, and No. 31 Mexico in the group stage, needing a top-two finish to advance to the knockout rounds.

After that, Toews and Gilas Women travel to Japan for the Asian Games in September as they shoot for a first-ever medal.

The road leads to the next Asia Cup, which the Philippines will host in 2027 in Cebu City.

“We have high goals and we want to win every game we play. We’ll take it one game at a time. I won’t make predictions but my standards are high. The players know that. They hear me in practice when I talk about what I accept, what I don’t accept. But they’re human and it’s going to take time. But we want to win while we’re learning,” Toews said.

“The long range plan is to be the best team we can be in the Asia Cup in Cebu.” – Rappler.com

World.title: A lot of casual friends, or only a few you’re really close with? New research questions that trade‑off
World.content:
'Our interpretation is that everyone wants emotional closeness, but that people pay more attention to that desire when they’re feeling less satisfied with their friendships,' a researcher says

Is there a natural trade-off between quantity and quality when it comes to the friends in your circle?

Between family, work, chores and other responsibilities, people often feel left with very little time to connect with friends — let alone to make new ones. With time as a limited resource, people often think they must choose between having a few emotionally close friendships or a lot of friends they’re less invested in.

But our new research published in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior suggests people don’t actually pick between having many friends and being emotionally close with them.

What people say they prioritize

Across five studies with over 5,000 international participants, we asked people about their friendship-making preferences. We were interested in how someone’s preferences matched how many friends they had, if they want to make new friends, and their personality in general.

For example, people who had stronger preferences for wide networks of friends also reported that they were more extroverted, had more friends, and had more people who would help them if they needed it.

On the other hand, those with stronger preferences for emotional intimacy with their friends reported having fewer friends willing to help them, more concern about exclusion and loneliness, and less satisfaction with their friends. They were also more willing to share personal and contact information with potential friends, suggesting they were motivated to make new friends.

But one of the most interesting things we saw was that people didn’t seem to make a simple quantity-versus-quality choice. Instead, participants generally wanted both wide friendship networks and emotional intimacy with their friends. Rather than one or the other, what we found is that our participants held both preferences simultaneously.

Interested in both

This finding suggests that people may not pick between the quantity and quality of their friendships, as previously thought, but rather pursue strategies that allow them to have many friends as well as be emotionally close with them. People weren’t telling us they wanted a wide but shallow pool of friends.

We’re left wondering how these preferences influence someone’s approach toward friendships. Our research suggested that a desire for intimacy with friends wasn’t specific to wanting only close relationships with a few friends. It was associated, however, with more concern about loneliness.

Our interpretation is that everyone wants emotional closeness, but that people pay more attention to that desire when they’re feeling less satisfied with their friendships. People who feel OK friendwise don’t need to express this desire. They can instead focus on their existing wider network of friends.

This preference for closeness, therefore, might function to warn you when you aren’t getting what you need from your friendships and motivate you to seek out new opportunities. If this is the case, then it could be like a gentle alarm that you’re close to experiencing loneliness and would benefit from more social interactions.

What still isn’t known

Friendships are integral to human health and well-being, yet researchers know very little about how people make friends. Many open questions remain.

We didn’t look at people’s behavior, so we can’t compare the overall levels of emotional intimacy people who had a lot of friends actually experienced as compared to those with just a few.

Other research shows that men and women approach friendships differently and prioritize different things when making same-sex friends. However, we found no sex differences in our study. Maybe while men’s and women’s friendships may differ in specifics, the benefits people gain from these relationships are things that are universally valued and prioritized.

On a grander scale, preferences for intimacy with many friends could also indicate the extent of loneliness felt by individuals within different social groups, such as first-year college students, med students and working professionals. We imagine public health workers could use this metric to suggest appropriate interventions to help reduce loneliness.

Finally, we saw that extroversion was the only personality trait associated with these preferences. While it seems obvious that personality influences whether you become friends with someone, there is almost no empirical research on the topic.

If extroversion is the force that drives the number of friends you have and how close you are to them, what do other aspects of personality influence in friendships? Could conscientiousness be related to satisfaction with your friendships? Openness to the variety of interests your friends have? Agreeableness to conflict resolution, and neuroticism to avoidance?

There are many unanswered questions in friendship research, but friendship-making orientation provides a useful step toward answering them. – Rappler.com

This article originally appeared on The Conversation.

Jessica D. Ayers, Assistant Professor of Psychological Science, Boise State University

Diego Guevara Beltran, Assistant Professor of Social Psychology, University of Arizona

World.title: Meet Vahn Pascual, the debuting director behind Cinemalaya hit ‘Status: Rejected’
World.content:
Even as this year’s youngest Cinemalaya main competition director, Vahn Pascual proves with ‘Status: Rejected’ that a modestly scaled debut can be boldly cinematic

Vahn Leinard Pascual’s interest in moving images only began upon the demise of his grandfather Leonardo “Ding” Pascual, a once active filmmaker in the late 1970s through the 1990s known for hyper-masculine action movies, including Final Showdown (1979), The Five Style Fist (1978), and Brusko (1981), which were all the rage then.

“Nanghihinayang ako kasi hindi ako nakapag-usap sa kanya tungkol sa paggawa ng pelikula (I regret that I wasn’t able to have any conversations with him about filmmaking),” Pascual said in a Zoom interview.

Now at 26, Pascual is the youngest main competition director in this year’s Cinemalaya Philippine Independent Film Festival, making his feature debut Status: Rejected fresh off college.

And yet, the Ani ng Dangal awardee wasn’t exactly a complete newbie to moviemaking and was even once tagged as among the “eight emerging Filipino directors to watch out for.”

Pascual’s earliest exposure to cinema was through bootleg DVDs of mostly commercial comedies, such as those from Wenn V. Deramas and the Enteng Kabisote film franchise. He would write and direct his first film for a campus festival in his high school years, until he entered film school at De La Salle – College of Saint Benilde, under which he’d direct nearly 20 shorts prior to his Cinemalaya debut.

“Most Benilde people would focus on the technicalities of moviemaking because of the equipment and budgets that they have, but I really insist on the importance of making stories with heart, and at the same time, grounded on lived realities,” Pascual told Rappler, recalling how he began making movies armed only with a mobile phone.

VETERAN. Ruby Ruiz leads Vahn Pascual’s Cinemalaya feature debut ‘Status: Rejected.’

Among his directing credits include Blue Is Not My Favorite Color (2020), Sina Alexa, Xander at ang Universe (2020), and Ang mga Sisiw sa Kagubatan (2022), all premiering to various acclaim in the Philippines and abroad. His 2021 black-and-white silent short Alingasngas ng mga Kuliglig, in particular, entered the library of The Criterion Channel in May 2024 as part of the film program “When the Apocalypse is Over: New Independent Cinema” curated by Filipino-American critic Aaron Hunt.

Much of Pascual’s work, produced largely during the COVID-19 pandemic amid bouts of depression, invokes the personal and the vicissitudes of growing up a queer boy. In fact, his first two submissions to Cinemalaya are queer-themed concepts, which riff on his thesis film My Dearest Darling, and the work-in-progress Don’t Mess With My Hormones. But what resonated with the selection committee was his concept for Status: Rejected, initially titled Friend Request Sent.

Loosely described by the director as a “love scam movie,” Status: Rejected follows Biring (played with lacerating clarity and dignified quietude by Ruby Ruiz), a widow in her late 60s who is left existentially adrift by her distant daughter Anna (Alessandra de Rossi), whose own child Sophia (Yani Villarosa) inherits the swelling generational trauma. Soon enough, Biring resorts to the illusory promise of digital ephemera, finding some sense of belongingness in a faceless American serviceman she can only embrace by proxy.

Drawing inspiration from the women in his life, especially his grandmother, Pascual builds his commentary to a hopeful endnote in which Biring reconciles the ideals the American empire fleetingly, deceptively offers with the realities of the world around her.

IN ACTION. Ruby Ruiz behind the scenes of the film.

It was in the Cinemalaya lab when the director realized he had to work within the operations of family drama and romance for the vision he had in mind, at which point Jaymar Santos Castro and Ivan Villacorta Gentolizo — who likewise penned another Cinemalaya entry, Jenn Romano’s Padamlágan (2025) — joined the crew as co-writers.

Then, Pascual was dreading the idea that the concept would not work as a full-fledged feature. “Because I was so exposed to short films, people might think, ‘If it works as a short film, then why not make it a short film?’” he explained. But with experienced writers and veterans in the workshop working alongside him, Pascual grew less and less anxious, confident that the material would eventually snap into focus.

While shopping the material around, he likewise lamented the limitation of having to cast bankable and therefore mainstream actors for production houses to be on board with the project, given that it’s from an independent artist. In fact, Pascual’s team initially considered Vilma Santos and Chanda Romero in the lead role.

“It’s disheartening, actually,” Pascual admitted. “I and my producer Fea Fortuna struggled with impostor syndrome from time to time.”

Luckily, the rejections led to some newfound allies in the industry, such as producer Micah Tadena and production outlets Clever Minds Inc. and Black Cap Pictures. Upon their attachment to the project came the casting of Ruby Ruiz, who had starred in Iska, a 2019 Cinemalaya entry directed by Theodore Boborol, Pascual’s mentor.

Also among those allies was cinematographer and Leonor Will Never Die director Martika Ramirez Escobar, whom Pascual already worked with in Gab Rosique’s QCinema 2025 entry Yelo. “I’m really a fan of her work because Pusong Bato was the first short film I saw when I was still starting out as a filmmaker,” said Pascual. “That’s when I realized that that kind of storytelling was possible.”

On set, Pascual described his process with the seasoned cinematographer as “very collaborative.” “She would always ask about my intentions in terms of the framing and story,” he added.

Indeed, Escobar’s signature lensing lifts the film to a greater aesthetic delight, generating stunning vistas occasionally punctuated with experimental flourishes, which are already part of Pascual’s own lexicon.

Pascual never thought of his feature debut not being a queer film, but just by virtue of the movie being so personal to him and the women around him allowed for a kind of shared understanding about minoritized struggles to come through.

Such sensibility proves crucial to the many different ways in which he facilitates the tensions among the female protagonists, deeply locating us in their chaotic, at-times needy and embarrassing, yet profound interior lives.

And while Status: Rejected is a modestly scaled debut, it somehow never feels contained or limited as far as filmic daring is concerned. If anything, it is proof that putting faith in new voices remains, more often than not, a worthy venture.

With so much promise still ahead of him, we certainly won’t be done with Vahn Leinard Pascual anytime soon. – Rappler.com

Note: Some quotes in Filipino have been translated into English for brevity.

World.title: P241-billion budget proposed for DSWD in 2027 is below 2026 level
World.content:
AID. Tricycle drivers queue to receive cash assistance distributed by the Department of Social Welfare and Development at the Cuneta Astrodome in Pasay City on March 17, 2026.

Will lawmakers again push for a higher amount for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program?

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), along with its attached agencies, is seeking a budget of P241.6 billion for 2027, the National Expenditure Program (NEP) showed.

It is among the top agencies with the biggest proposed allocations for next year, ranking eighth. But the 2027 figure is 8.6% lower than the P264.45 billion approved under the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA) or national budget.

One of the programs which would have a funding cut is the Protective Program for Individuals and Families in Especially Difficult Circumstances, where the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) is lodged.

It would only get P33.29 billion under next year’s spending plan to assist around 4.6 million beneficiaries. The amount was nearly halved from the P63.9 billion under the 2026 GAA.

Initially, only P27.04 billion was proposed for AICS under the 2026 NEP. But the House of Representatives was persistent up to the bicameral conference committee level that the funding should be much higher.

Civil society groups have tagged the controversial AICS program as “soft pork.”

Congress introduced a provision in the 2026 national budget barring politicians from taking part in any cash aid distribution, including for AICS. Such a provision is also present in the 2027 NEP.

However, even the administration’s pet bill seeking to institutionalize the AICS program was stuck at the bicam level amid differences in the Senate and House versions, including the “anti-epal” clause.

Comparing the 2027 NEP against the 2026 GAA, decreases in funding allocations are also seen in other DSWD programs:

Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program – P99.08 billion (from P113 billion)

Social Pension for Indigent Senior Citizens – P51.64 billion (from P51.86 billion)

Supplementary Feeding Program – P6.36 billion (from P9.56 billion)

Sustainable Livelihood Program – P5.12 billion (from P5.31 billion)

Disaster Response and Management Program – P3.32 billion (from P5.27 billion)

Next year, the DSWD could receive P1.89 billion for the Walang Gutom Program, where the agency provides a monthly food credit of P3,000 to household beneficiaries. So far, the program has reached a total of 600,000 families, and the government aims to boost this figure to 750,000 by 2028.

Another P900 million is earmarked for the Tara, Basa! Tutoring Program, which helps struggling readers in public elementary schools.

Meanwhile, the National Commission of Senior Citizens is asking for P3.83 billion for 2027, which is around 6% higher than the P3.6 billion provided under the 2026 national budget. The commission became an attached agency of the DSWD in 2025.

Under the 2027 NEP, P2.456 trillion is allocated for social services to strengthen the sectors of education, culture, and manpower development; social security, welfare, and employment; and health.

2027 is the last full year of the Marcos administration before the May 2028 presidential election.

Will lawmakers fight tooth and nail for a higher DSWD budget, especially for the AICS program? The House appropriations committee is conducting its budget hearing for the agency on September 8. – Rappler.com

World.title: The renovation is done. Now Ayala is changing the shops inside its malls.
World.content:
As malls complete their glow-up, Ayala Land hopes it can ‘bring in the concepts to kind of match the new physical experience’

MANILA, Philippines – The construction dust may finally be settling at some of Ayala Land’s biggest malls, but the makeover isn’t quite over.

After spending the past two years renovating flagship properties such as Glorietta, Greenbelt, TriNoma, and Ayala Center Cebu, the scaffolding and temporary walls are finally coming down. Ayala Land is now moving into what it calls the “merchant replacement phase,” which involves changing the mix of shops, restaurants, and other concepts that customers will find inside.

“The physical works have been completed. So now it’s about ensuring that we can bring in the concepts to kind of match the new physical experience,” said Mariana Beatriz Zobel de Ayala, Ayala Land senior vice president and head of its leasing and hospitality group, during the company’s H1 2026 briefing on Monday, August 10.

Glorietta has mostly finished its glow-up. The mall, last majorly renovated in 2012, has a new look to its cinemas and refreshed decors throughout. The biggest change is a new pedestrian park connecting the outside part of Glorietta 3, replacing what used to be the car mall entrance. Portions, such as the food court, remain under renovation.

NEW PARK. After a year, Glorietta has completed the renovation of its new park. Photos by Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler.

Zobel de Ayala had also previously said that after the renovations, the refreshed Glorietta and Greenbelt malls should have a more “intuitive wayfind and circulation.” If you’ve ever gotten lost in Glorietta’s maze-like interior, this should come as welcome news.

Where stores and concepts have already been replaced or refreshed, rental rates have risen by an average of 25%. (FIRST LOOK: How Glorietta, Greenbelt, TriNoma, Ayala Center Cebu will be redesigned)

Ayala Center Cebu, the most advanced of the four mall reinventions, is already seeing around 10% year-on-year rental-rate growth. Ayala Land president and CEO Anna Ma. Margarita Dy said the full benefits of the overhaul could still take another two to three years to materialize.

New look, new shops

For shoppers, some of that next phase is already becoming visible.

At Greenbelt, Ayala recently soft-opened about 3,000 square meters of Greenbelt 2. The former Greenbelt townhomes, meanwhile, are being repurposed into T:28, which management described as a nightlife concept. TriNoma is also getting additional retail space.

Then there is, of course, still Greenbelt 1. The decades-old mall was designed by National Artist for Architecture Leandro Locsin and first opened in 1982. It has since been demolished, but Ayala is expected to unveil its new look in 2028.

In its other spaces, Ayala is also bringing in brands both new and old to many Filipino shoppers as its retail footprint expands. Management highlighted Makro, the Thai wholesale-retail chain, at Ayala Malls Arca South; premium grocery chain Spinneys at Parklinks and San Antonio Plaza Arcade; and IKEA as an anchor at Gatewalk in Cebu.

Ayala Malls Arca South formally opened in 2026 as a mixed-format retail development, while the company is preparing another major mall opening in Nuvali in November. Gatewalk is targeted to open in December.

Ayala’s numbers suggest that customers are responding. Same-mall sales grew 7% in the first half of 2026, while foot traffic rose 5%. Traffic at premium malls increased 8%, compared with 3% at its core malls.

Betting more on malls

The reinvention is becoming more important to Ayala Land at a time when its residential development business is facing a tougher market.

Shopping center revenues reached P12 billion in the first half, up 4% year-on-year. Strip out Alabang Town Center (ATC), which Ayala no longer owns, and mall revenues grew by about 9%. (READ: Refreshed Alabang Town Center? What shoppers can expect now that Rockwell has near-full control.)

Ayala Land sold its stake in Alabang Commercial Center Corporation, the company behind Alabang Town Center, to the Madrigal family for P13.5 billion in December 2025. ATC has since been acquired by the Lopez’s Rockwell Land. Ayala described the transaction as a way to unlock capital for new commercial developments.

The sale is part of a broader shift toward putting capital where Ayala sees more room to grow. In the first half, spending on malls surged 62% to P9.2 billion, even as residential capital expenditures fell 24%. – Rappler.com

A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

MANILA, Philippines — Bad weather conditions due to southwest monsoon or habagat prevailed over the week affecting Luzon and Western Visayas. On August 9, five young students died after a landslide struck Barangay Guisad Surong in Baguio City. 13 people were buried by thick mud and debris while three houses were hit by the landslide, affecting five families.

Nonstop rain disrupted the schooling of around 6.7 million students on August 10, following the suspension of face-to-face classes. The heavy downpour also forced the Senate to postpone the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte and the chamber’s regular session.

On August 11, a massive accumulation of floodwater and garbage at the Baclaran-Redemptorist Water Channel happened after its trash trap broke off, allowing waste to enter the waterway. Over 700 metric tons of waste and debris, equivalent to around 203 truckloads of garbage were collected after clearing operations.

Meanwhile, state auditor Xylene Mae del Campo testified before the impeachment court on August 11, saying that the Office of the Vice President spent confidential funds on Christmas parties, tree-planting, and gift-giving activity.

On August 12, counsels for the opposing parties — private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan and defense lawyer Kristine Ferrer — butted heads numerous times. Disputes arose over the use of documents for cross-examination, leading to objections and accusations of misleading questions, prompting interventions from the presiding officer Chiz Escudero.
